\mu_{A,-}:\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{C},\;\;\mu_{-,A^{\prime}}:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}

are both exact morphisms. Let
\mathcal{A}\boxtimes\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be the
\tau_{\leq 0}
-truncation of the extension closure of
the quasi-essential image of the morphism in
\mathrm{Hqe}

F:\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})\otimes\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})\rightarrow\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})\otimes\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime}))

Proposition 2.17

(Proposition
6.51
)
.

The natural morphism
\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}\boxtimes\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is the universal biexact morphism in
\mathrm{Hqe}
from
\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
to an exact dg category.

Let
\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
be connective exact dg categories.
Let
\mathrm{rep}_{dg}^{ex}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
be the full dg subcategory
\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
consisting of exact morphisms.
It is shown in Lemma
6.50
that
\mathrm{rep}_{dg}^{ex}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
is stable under extensions in
\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})
and thus inherits a canonical exact dg structure.

Corollary 2.18

(Corollary
6.52
)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
be small connective exact dg categories. Let
\mathcal{C}
be a small exact dg category.
Then we have the following natural bijection

\mathrm{Hqe}_{ex}(\mathcal{A}\boxtimes\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hqe}_{ex}(\mathcal{A},\mathrm{rep}_{dg}^{ex}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})).

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
be a small extriangulated category.
The
defect
of an
\mathfrak{s}
-conflation

A\xrightarrow{x}B\xrightarrow{y}C

is defined to be the cokernel of the morphism of right
\mathcal{C}
-modules
\mathcal{C}(?,B)\xrightarrow{(?,y)}\mathcal{C}(?,C)
.
The full subcategory of the module category
\mathrm{Mod}\,\mathcal{C}
whose objects are the defects is denoted by

\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{E}
. It was introduced in this generality by Ogawa in
[
117
]

and further studied by Enomoto
[
33
]
, who showed that
\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{E}
is
a Serre subcategory of the abelian category of coherent
\mathcal{C}
-modules and that the map
taking a closed subbifunctor of
\mathbb{E}
to its category of defects is a poset
isomorphism onto the poset of Serre subcategories of
\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{E}
.
If
\mathcal{A}
is a connective exact dg category, then
\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006ptH^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is equivalent
to the heart of a
t
-structure on the category
\mathcal{N}
of ‘acyclic complexes’, cf.
the remark after Theorem
2.13
.

Theorem 2.19

(Theorem
6.61
)
.

Let
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
be an exact dg category and
(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
the associated algebraic extriangulated category.
The following posets (where the order relations are given by inclusion) are canonically isomorphic:

(1)

The poset of exact substructures of
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
.

(2)

The poset of closed subbifunctors of
\mathbb{E}
.

(3)

The poset of Serre subcategories of
\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{E}
.

Here, the isomorphism between the posets in (2) and (3) follows from Enomoto’s theorem
[
33
]
.

In
[
125
]
, Rump proved that every additive category has the greatest exact structure, which generalized the results in
[
129
,
25
]
.
The following theorem generalizes Rump’s result to additive dg categories.

Theorem 2.20

(Theorem
7.10
)
.

Each additive dg category
\mathcal{A}
admits a greatest (i.e. unique maximal) exact dg structure.

It is not clear how to formulate, let alone prove, an analogous statement for extriangulated
structures.

3.
Homotopy diagrams

3.1.
Notations and terminology

In this subsection, we collect basic notations and terminology needed in this paper. The standard references for dg categories are
[
79
,
85
,
28
,
135
,
15
]
.

Throughout we fix a commutative ring
k
.
We write
\otimes
for the tensor product over
k
.
We denote by
\mathcal{C}_{dg}(k)
the dg category of complexes of
k
-modules and by
\mathcal{C}(k)
the category of complexes of
k
-modules.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a dg
k
-category.
For two objects
A_{1}
and
A_{2}
, the Hom complex is denoted by
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A_{1},A_{2})
or

\mathcal{A}(A_{1},A_{2})
. An element
f
of
\mathcal{A}(A_{1},A_{2})^{p}
will be called a
homogeneous
morphism of degree
p
with the notation
|f|=p
.
A homogeneous morphism
f:A_{1}\rightarrow A_{2}
is
closed
if we have
d(f)=0
.

Let
M
be complex of
k
-modules. We put

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}M=(\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M^{-2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M^{-1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z^{0}M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots).}

For a dg category
\mathcal{A}
, denote by
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}
the dg category with the same objects as
\mathcal{A}

and whose morphism complexes are given by

(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})(A_{1},A_{2})=\tau_{\leq 0}(\mathcal{A}(A_{1},A_{2})).

The composition is naturally induced by that of
\mathcal{A}
.

A dg category
\mathcal{A}
is
connective
if for each pair of objects
A_{1},A_{2}\in\mathcal{A}
, the
complex
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A_{1},A_{2})
has cohomology concentrated in non-positive degrees.
It is called
strictly connective
if the components of the complex
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A_{1},A_{2})
vanish
in all positive degrees.

We denote by
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
the category with the same objects as
\mathcal{A}
and whose morphism
spaces are defined by

(Z^{0}\mathcal{A})(A_{1},A_{2})=Z^{0}(\mathcal{A}(A_{1},A_{2})),

where
Z^{0}
is the kernel of
d:\mathcal{A}(A_{1},A_{2})^{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}(A_{1},A_{2})^{1}
.
Similarly, we denote by
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
the category with the same objects as
\mathcal{A}
and whose
morphism spaces are given by

(H^{0}\mathcal{A})(A_{1},A_{2})=H^{0}(\mathcal{A}(A_{1},A_{2})),

where
H^{0}
denotes the zeroth cohomology of the complex.

The
oppositie dg category

\mathcal{A}^{op}
has the same objects as
\mathcal{A}
and its morphism spaces are defined by

\mathcal{A}^{op}(X,Y)=\mathcal{A}(Y,X);

the composition of
f\in\mathcal{A}^{op}(Y,X)^{op}
with
g\in\mathcal{A}^{op}(Z,Y)^{q}
is given by
(-1)^{pq}gf
.
By a dg
\mathcal{A}
-module
M
, we mean a right dg
\mathcal{A}
-module, i.e. a dg functor
\mathcal{A}^{op}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{dg}(k)
.
We denote by
\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
the dg category of right dg
\mathcal{A}
-modules and by
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
the category of dg

\mathcal{A}
-modules. Note that
Z^{0}(\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))=\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
.
The category up to homotopy of dg
\mathcal{A}
-modules is

\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{A})=H^{0}(\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})).

An object
A
in
\mathcal{A}
is
contractible
if it is a zero object in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
, or equivalently if we have
\mathrm{id}_{M}=d(h)
for some morphism
h:M\rightarrow M
of degree
-1
.
A dg category
\mathcal{A}
has
contractible pre-envelopes
provided for each object
A
in
\mathcal{A}
, there exists a closed morphism
f:A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
of degree
0
such that
A^{\prime}
is contractible and for each morphism
h:A\rightarrow B
in
\mathcal{A}
, there exists some
h^{\prime}:A^{\prime}\rightarrow B
satisfying
h^{\prime}\circ f=h
(hence
d(h^{\prime})\circ f=d(h)
).
Dually one has the notion of a dg category having
contractible pre-covers
.
A dg
\mathcal{A}
-module is
contractible
if it is contractible in the dg category
\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.

For each object
A\in\mathcal{A}
, we have the right dg module
represented by

A

A^{\wedge}=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(-,A).

A dg
\mathcal{A}
-module
M
is
representable
if it is isomorphic to
A^{\wedge}
for some

A\in\mathcal{A}
and
quasi-representable
if it is quasi-isomorphic to
A^{\wedge}
for some
A\in\mathcal{A}
.

For a dg
\mathcal{A}
-module
M
, put
IM=\mathrm{Cone}(\mathrm{id}_{M})
and
PM=\mathrm{Cone}(\mathrm{id}_{\Sigma^{-1}M})
.
Explicitly, we have
IM=\Sigma M\oplus M
and
PM=M\oplus\Sigma^{-1}M
as graded
\mathcal{A}
-modules.
We have the natural inclusion
i=[0,1]^{\intercal}:M\rightarrow IM
and projection
p=[1,0]:PM\rightarrow M
.

A dg functor
F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
is a
quasi-equivalence
if

a)

it is
quasi-fully faithful
, i.e. for all objects
A,A^{\prime}\in A
, the morphism

F_{A,A^{\prime}}:\mathcal{A}(A,A^{\prime})\rightarrow\mathcal{B}(FA,FA^{\prime}).

is a quasi-isomorphism and

b)

the induced functor
H^{0}(F):H^{0}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow H^{0}(\mathcal{B})
is an equivalence of categories.

The
Yoneda dg functor

\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}),\;\;A\mapsto A^{\wedge}

is fully faithful.
Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be the full dg subcategory of
\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
consisting of objects
A^{\wedge}
,
\mathrm{Cone}(\mathrm{id}_{A^{\wedge}})
and
\mathrm{Cone}(-\mathrm{id}_{\Sigma^{-1}A^{\wedge}})
for each
A\in\mathcal{A}
.
The dg category
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
has contractible pre-covers and contractible pre-envelopes and the inclusion
\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a quasi-equivalence.
Thus, up to quasi-equivalence, we may assume
\mathcal{A}
has contractible pre-covers and contractible pre-envelopes.

The category
\mathrm{dgcat}
of small dg categories admits the Dwyer-Kan model structure (cf.
[
130
]
),
whose weak equivalences are the quasi-equivalences. Its homotopy category is denoted by
\mathrm{Hqe}
.
There exists a cofibrant replacement functor
Q
on
\mathrm{dgcat}
such that for any
\mathcal{A}\in\mathrm{dgcat}
, the natural dg functor
Q(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
is the identity on the set of objects.
In particular, the Hom-complexes of
Q(\mathcal{A})
are cofibrant over
k
.
The
tensor product

\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}
of two dg categories
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
has the class of objects
\mathrm{obj}(\mathcal{A})\times\mathrm{obj}(\mathcal{B})
and the morphism spaces

(\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B})((A,B),(A^{\prime},B^{\prime}))=\mathcal{A}(A,A^{\prime})\otimes\mathcal{B}(B,B^{\prime})

with the natural compositions and units.
This defines a symmetric monoidal structure
-\otimes-
on
\mathrm{dgcat}
which is closed.
For
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\in\mathrm{dgcat}
, put
\mathcal{A}\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{A}\otimes Q(\mathcal{B})
.
This extends to a bifunctor
-\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}-:\mathrm{dgcat}\times\mathrm{dgcat}\rightarrow\mathrm{dgcat}
and then passes through the homotopy categories

-\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}-:\mathrm{Hqe}\times\mathrm{Hqe}\rightarrow\mathrm{Hqe}.

Let
\mathrm{Cat}
be the category of small categories.
Let
[\mathrm{Cat}]
be the category with objects small categories and with morphisms isomorphism classes of functors.
In particular the isomorphism class of an equivalence of categories is an isomorphism in
[\mathrm{Cat}]
.
So the functor
H^{0}:\mathrm{dgcat}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}
induces a functor

H^{0}:\mathrm{Hqe}\rightarrow[\mathrm{Cat}].

For a category
\mathcal{C}
, we denote by
\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{C})
its isomorphism classes of objects.

For a dg category
\mathcal{A}
, we denote by
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
its
derived category
, a triangulated category.
By definition
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
is the localization of
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
at the class of
quasi-isomorphisms
, i.e. morphisms of dg
\mathcal{A}
-modules which induce quasi-isomorphisms of complexes when evaluated at any object in
\mathcal{A}
.
Let
\pi:\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
be the quotient functor.
For a morphism
j:M\rightarrow N
in
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
, we denote by
\overline{\jmath}=\pi(j):M\rightarrow N
the corresponding morphism in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
.
A dg functor
F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
induces a triangle functor
F_{*}:\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{B})
which is an equivalence of triangulated categories if
F
is a quasi-equivalence.
The
dg derived category

\mathcal{D}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
of
\mathcal{A}
is defined to be the full dg subcategory of
\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
consisting of cofibrant dg
\mathcal{A}
-modules in the
projective model structure
of
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
(cf.
[
85
, Theorem 3.2]
).
The canonical functor
H^{0}(\mathcal{D}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
is an equivalence of triangulated categories.

For dg categories
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
, we define
\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
to be the full subcategory of
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}\mathcal{B}^{op})
whose objects are the dg bimodules
X
such that
X(-,B)
is quasi-representable for each object
B
of
\mathcal{B}
.
We define the canonical dg enhancement
\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
to be the full dg subcategory of
\mathcal{D}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}\mathcal{B}^{op})
whose objects are those of
\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
.

A dg category
\mathcal{A}
is
pretriangulated
if the canonical inclusion
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
is a triangulated subcategory.
Note that
\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
is pretriangulated if
\mathcal{A}
is pretriangulated.
For a dg category
\mathcal{A}
, its
pretriangulated hull

\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
(
[
15
,
28
,
16
]
) is defined as follows.
The objects of
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
are “one-sided twisted complexes”, i.e. formal expressions
(\oplus_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}[r_{i}],q)
, where
A_{i}\in\mathcal{A}
,
r_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}
,
n\geq 0
,
q=(q_{ij})
,
q_{ij}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}^{r_{i}-r_{j}+1}(A_{j},A_{i})
,
q_{ij}=0
for
i\geq j
and
dq+q^{2}=0
.
Here we adopt the convention
(dq)_{ij}=(-1)^{r_{i}}d_{\mathcal{A}}(q_{ij})
and
(q^{2})_{ij}=\sum_{k}q_{ik}\circ q_{kj}
.
If
A
and
A^{\prime}
are two objects in
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
with
A=(\oplus_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}[r_{i}],q)
and
A^{\prime}=(\oplus_{i^{\prime}=1}^{n^{\prime}}A_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime}[r_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime}],q^{\prime})
, the complex
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})}(A,A^{\prime})
has as the degree
m
component the space of matrices
f=(f_{ij})
,
f_{ij}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}^{m+r_{i}^{\prime}-r_{j}}(A_{j},A_{i}^{\prime})
.
The differential
d
carries a morphism
f=(f_{ij})
of degree
m
to
df=((df)_{ij})
where

(df)_{ij}=(-1)^{r_{i}^{\prime}}d_{\mathcal{A}}(f_{ij})+\sum_{k}q^{\prime}_{ik}\circ f_{kj}-(-1)^{m}\sum_{k}f_{ik}\circ q_{kj}.

The composition map

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})}(A^{\prime},A^{\prime\prime})\otimes\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})}(A,A^{\prime})\rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})}(A,A^{\prime\prime})

is the matrix multiplication:
f^{\prime}\otimes f\mapsto f^{\prime\prime}
where
f^{\prime\prime}_{ij}=\sum_{k}f^{\prime}_{ik}\circ f_{kj}
.
We denote the triangulated category
H^{0}(\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A}))
by
\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{A})
.
The Yoneda dg functor
\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
extends to a fully faithful dg functor
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.
It induces a fully faithful triangle functor
\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
whose essential image is the triangulated subcategory of
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
generated by the representable dg modules.

A
quiver
(or
directed graph
)
Q
is a quadruple
(Q_{0},Q_{1},s,t)
where
Q_{0}
is a set whose elements are called
objects
or
vertices
of
Q
,
Q_{1}
is a set of
arrows

f
(or
edges
), and
s,t
are maps
Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0}
where
s(f)
is the
source
of the arrow
f
and
t(f)
is the
target
of
f
.
A morphism between quivers is defined in the obvious way.
We denote the category of quivers by
\mathrm{Quiv}
.

Each small category
\mathcal{C}
has an
underlying quiver

F(\mathcal{C})
and this extends to the forgetful functor
F:\mathrm{Cat}\rightarrow\mathrm{Quiv}
.
This functor admits a left adjoint
P:\mathrm{Quiv}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}
which associates to a quiver
Q
the
path category

P(Q)
of
Q
.
The path category
P(Q)
has the same objects as
Q
and its morphisms
x_{1}\rightarrow x_{n}
are finite paths

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n-1}}

consisting of
n\geq 1
objects
x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}
of
Q
which are connected by arrows
f_{i}:x_{i}\rightarrow x_{i+1}
of
Q
.
The composite of two paths is defined by concatenation:
\mathrm{concat}(f,g)=g\circ f
.

Let
Q
be a quiver and
R
a function which assigns to each pair of objects
x,y
of
Q
a binary relation
R_{x,y}
on the set of finite paths from
x
to
y
.
Then the path category of the quiver
Q
with relations
R
is defined to be the quotient category
P(Q)/\overline{R}
, where
\overline{R}
is the smallest family of equivalence relations
\overline{R}_{x,y}
,
x,y\in Q_{0}
, containing
R
and stable under pre- and postcomposition with morphisms.
Often we only write down nontrivial relations in
R
.

For a small category
\mathcal{I}
, we have the
k
-category
k\mathcal{I}
whose set of objects is the same as that of
\mathcal{I}
and for each pair of objects
x,y
in
\mathcal{C}
, the space
k\mathcal{I}(i,j)
is the free
k
-module generated by the set
\mathcal{I}(i,j)
.
In particular, if we view
k\mathcal{I}
as a dg category concentrated in degree 0, then it is
k
-cofibrant
, i.e. the Hom complexes are
k
-cofibrant.
Let
\mathcal{B}
be a
k
-cofibrant dg category.
We have a quasi-equivalence
\mathcal{A}\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}\mathcal{B}\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}
.
A dg functor
F:\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
gives rise to a
\mathcal{B}
-
\mathcal{A}
-bimodule
{}_{F}\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{A}}
defined by

(A,B)\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A,FB).

The assignment
F\mapsto{{}_{F}\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{A}}}
passes to the following map

\mathrm{Hqe}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{Iso}(\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}))

which is a bijection, cf.
[
134
]
.
It is shown in loc. cit that
\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
is the internal Hom of the monoidal category
(\mathrm{Hqe},-\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}-)
, i.e. for small dg categories
\mathcal{A}
,
\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
, we have

\mathrm{Hqe}(\mathcal{A}\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hqe}(\mathcal{A},\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})).

3.2.
Preliminaries

Throughout we fix a dg
k
-category
\mathcal{A}
.
Consider the derived category
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
of the dg category
\mathcal{A}
.
Our first aim is to formulate proper definitions of homotopy (co)cartesian squares in the dg category
\mathcal{A}
(not
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
).

Notation 3.3
.

For a small category
\mathcal{I}
, put

\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{I})=\mathcal{D}(k(\mathcal{I}^{op})\otimes\mathcal{A}),\;\;\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{I})=\mathcal{C}(k(\mathcal{I}^{op})\otimes\mathcal{A}),\;\;\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{I})=\mathrm{rep}(k(\mathcal{I}),\mathcal{A})

and

\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{I})=\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(k(\mathcal{I}),\mathcal{A}).

We are mainly concerned with the case when
\mathcal{I}
is the category with one object and one morphism or one of the following categories:

The
square
category

We identify objects
X\in\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sq})
with commutative squares

(3.3.1)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{00}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{01}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{10}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{11}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}

in
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
.

In general we identify an object
X\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{I})
with an
\mathcal{I}
-shaped diagram
X
in
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
, i.e. a functor

X:\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}),\;\;i\mapsto X_{i}.

Let
Q:\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
be the canonical quotient functor.
The map sending
X
to
Q\circ X
defines the canonical
diagram functor

\mathrm{Dia}:\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{I})\rightarrow\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}))
which is
conservative
, i.e. detects isomorphisms. Note that it is not full in general.

We have the following diagram with the obvious functors
i:\mathrm{Cosp}\rightarrow\mathrm{Sq}
and
s:\mathrm{Mor}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cosp}
.

It fits into a short exact sequence in
\mathcal{C}(k\mathrm{Cosp}^{op})

0\rightarrow 11^{\wedge}\rightarrow 01^{\wedge}\oplus 10^{\wedge}\rightarrow M(-,00)\rightarrow 0.

So it is quasi-isomorphic to the cokernel
N
of the graded-injective map

11^{\wedge}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cone}(\mathrm{id}_{11^{\wedge}})\oplus 10^{\wedge}\oplus 01^{\wedge}.

Let
M^{\prime}
be the dg
k\mathrm{Cosp}^{op}\otimes k(\mathrm{Sq})
-module given by the following diagram in
\mathcal{C}(k\mathrm{Cosp}^{op})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 10^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 01^{\wedge}\oplus\mathrm{Cone}(\mathrm{id}_{11^{\wedge}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 11^{\wedge}\mathrlap{\;.}}

Then we get the desired quasi-isomorphism
M^{\prime}\rightarrow M
.
So the functor
R
takes
S
to
\mathrm{Hom}_{k\mathrm{Cosp}^{op}}(M^{\prime},S)
which is given by the following diagram in
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C\oplus\mathrm{Cone}(-\mathrm{id}_{\Sigma^{-1}D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(k\ p)}

such that
p:\mathrm{Cone}(-\mathrm{id}_{\Sigma^{-1}D})\rightarrow D
is the canonical projection map and that the diagram fits into the following graded split short exact sequence in
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})

0\rightarrow K\rightarrow\mathrm{Cone}(-\mathrm{id}_{\Sigma^{-1}D})\oplus B\oplus C\xrightarrow{[p\;\;j\;\;k]}D\rightarrow 0.

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L^{\prime}}

Since the cofibrant objects are direct summands, as graded modules, of sums of modules which are shifts of representable modules, we have that cofibrant objects in
\mathcal{C}(\mathrm{Sq})
are of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{00}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{01}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{10}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{11}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}

where
f,g,j,k
are graded-split injections and all
X_{i}
are cofibrant dg
\mathcal{A}
-modules.

Lemma 3.4

(
[
86
,
11
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a dg category.
There is a canonical t-structure

(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\leq 0},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\geq 0})

on
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
such that
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\geq 0}
is formed by those dg modules whose cohomology is concentrated in non-negative degrees.

Note that we have
A^{\wedge}\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\leq 0}
for each
A\in\mathcal{A}
.

Let
\mathcal{B}
be a connective dg
k
-category.
Put
\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}^{op})
.
Let
(\mathcal{T}^{\leq 0},\mathcal{T}^{\geq 0})
be the canonical t-structure on
\mathcal{T}
.

Let
X
be a dg
\mathcal{B}-\mathcal{A}
-bimodule. It is clear that
X\in\mathcal{T}^{\geq 0}
if and only if
X(-,B)\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\geq 0}
for each
B\in\mathcal{B}
.

Lemma 3.5
.

We have
X\in\mathcal{T}^{\leq 0}
if
X(-,B)\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\leq 0}
for each
B\in\mathcal{B}
.

Proof.

Suppose
X(-,B)\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\leq 0}
for each
B\in\mathcal{B}
. Let
Y\in\mathcal{T}^{\geq 1}
.

Then we have
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})}(X(-,B),Y(-,B^{\prime}))=0
for
B,B^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}
.

So we have
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y)=0
and we have

\displaystyle\mathrm{RHom}_{\mathcal{B}^{op}\otimes\mathcal{A}}(X,Y)=

\displaystyle\mathrm{RHom}_{\mathcal{B}^{op}\otimes\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{B},\mathrm{RHom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathrm{RHom}_{\mathcal{B}^{op}\otimes\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{B},\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}_{\mathcal{A}}(X,Y))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Hence
X\in\mathcal{T}^{\leq 0}
.
∎

In particular, for a small category
\mathcal{I}
, the category
\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{I})
is a full subcategory of
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{I})^{\leq 0}
.

Definition 3.6

(
[
17
,
118
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{T}
be a triangulated category.
A co-t-structure on
\mathcal{T}
is a pair of full additive subcategories
(\mathcal{T}^{w\leq 0},\mathcal{T}^{w\geq 0})
such that the following properties hold:

(i)

\mathcal{T}^{w\leq 0}
and
\mathcal{T}^{w\geq 0}
are stable under forming direct summands;

(ii)

\Sigma^{-1}\mathcal{T}^{w\geq 0}\subset\mathcal{T}^{w\geq 0}
;
\Sigma\mathcal{T}^{w\leq 0}\subset\mathcal{T}^{w\leq 0}
;

(iii)

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{T}}(\Sigma^{-1}\mathcal{T}^{w\geq 0},\mathcal{T}^{w\leq 0})=0
;

(iv)

For any object
X
of
\mathcal{T}
there exists a triangle

(2.1)

\displaystyle\Sigma^{-1}B\rightarrow X\rightarrow A\rightarrow B

such that
A\in\mathcal{T}^{w\leq 0}
and
B\in\mathcal{T}^{w\geq 0}
.

The triangle (
2.1
) is called a weight decomposition of
X
.

Let
(\mathcal{T}^{w\leq 0},\mathcal{T}^{w\geq 0})
be a co-t-structure on a triangulated category
\mathcal{T}
.

Definition 3.7

(
[
17
,
118
]
)
.

—

The full subcategory
\mathcal{H}{\coloneqq}\mathcal{T}^{w\leq 0}\cap\mathcal{T}^{w\geq 0}
is called the coheart of the co-t-structure.

—

\mathcal{T}^{w\geq l}{\coloneqq}\Sigma^{-l}\mathcal{T}^{w\geq 0}
and
\mathcal{T}^{w\leq l}{\coloneqq}\Sigma^{-l}\mathcal{T}^{w\leq 0}
.

—

For any
i,j\in\mathbb{Z}
,
i\leq j
, we define
\mathcal{T}^{[i,j]}{\coloneqq}\mathcal{T}^{w\leq j}\bigcap\mathcal{T}^{w\geq i}
.

—

The co-t-structure
(\mathcal{T}^{w\leq 0},\mathcal{T}^{w\geq 0})
is called bounded if

\mathcal{T}=\bigcup_{l\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{T}^{w\leq l}=\bigcup_{l\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{T}^{w\geq l}.

Example 3.8

(
[
17
,
118
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{B}
be an additive category.
We denote by
\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{B})^{\leq 0}
(resp.
\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{B})^{\geq 0}
) the full subcategory consisting of complexes that are homotopy equivalent to complexes concentrated in degrees
\leq 0
(resp.
\geq 0
).
The pair of subcategories
(\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{B})^{\leq 0},\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{B})^{\geq 0})
is a co-t-structure on
\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{B})
.
Its coheart is the Karoubi-closure of
\mathcal{B}
in
\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{B})
, i.e. the full subcategory consisting of the objects
X\in\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{B})
which are retracts of objects in
\mathcal{B}
.
For example, suppose
p:Y^{0}\rightarrow Y^{1}
is an epimorphism in
\mathcal{B}
with a left inverse
s:Y^{1}\rightarrow Y^{0}
.
Then the complex

\cdots\rightarrow 0\rightarrow 0\rightarrow Y^{0}\xrightarrow{p}Y^{1}\rightarrow 0\rightarrow\cdots

where
Y^{0}
is in degree 0, is a retract of the stalk complex
Y^{0}
and hence belongs to the coheart.
Each such complex belongs to
\mathcal{B}
if and only if
\mathcal{B}
is weakly idempotent complete.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a dg
k
-category.
Recall that we denote by
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
its pretriangulated hull and by
\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{A})
the triangulated category
H^{0}(\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A}))
and that the Yoneda embedding induces a fully faithful triangle functor
\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
.

Proposition 3.9
.

(
[
17
, Proposition 6.2.1]
)

Suppose
\mathcal{A}
is a strictly connective dg category.
Put
\mathcal{T}=\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{A})
.
Let
\mathcal{T}^{\leq 0}
(resp.
\mathcal{T}^{\geq 0}
) be the full subcategory of
\mathcal{T}
which consists of objects isomorphic to those of the form
A=(\oplus_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}[r_{i}],q)
for
n\geq 0
and
r_{i}\geq 0
(resp.
r_{i}\leq 0
) for each
i
.
Then
(\mathcal{T}^{\leq 0},\mathcal{T}^{\geq 0})
is a co-t-structure on
\mathcal{T}
, the canonical co-t-structure.

3.10.
Homotopy cartesian squares for triangulated categories

Let
\mathcal{T}
be a triangulated category. Consider a commutative square in
\mathcal{T}

(3.10.1)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z^{\prime}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}

It is
homotopy cartesian
(
[
113
, Definition 1.4.1]
) if there is a (distinguished) triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}\oplus Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(g,-f)^{\intercal}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f^{\prime}\ g^{\prime})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\partial}

for some
\partial:Z^{\prime}\rightarrow\Sigma Y
.
For a general commutative square as above, let
u=(g,-f)^{\intercal}
.
We complete it to a triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}\oplus Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma Y.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}

Then we have a map
t:W\rightarrow Z^{\prime}
such that
(f^{\prime}\ \ g^{\prime})=t\circ v
.
However this map is not canonical and we do not know if this map is an isomorphism.
Therefore we cannot determine whether the commutative square is homotopy cartesian from this map.

It turns out that we have a satisfactory definition of homotopy cartesian squares provided
\mathcal{T}
is algebraic, i.e.
\mathcal{T}
is equivalent, as a triangulated category, to
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
for a pretriangulated dg category
\mathcal{A}
.
In this case, the adjunction
(L,R)
in the diagram
3.3.2
restricts to an adjuntion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{rep}(k(\mathrm{Sq}),\mathcal{A})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{rep}(k(\mathrm{Cosp}),\mathcal{A}).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}

Definition 3.11
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a pretriangulated dg category.
An object
X\in\mathrm{rep}(k(\mathrm{Sq}),\mathcal{A})
is homotopy cartesian if the adjunction morphism

The object
X
is homotopy cartesian if and only if the canonical morphism

X_{00}\xrightarrow{(f,g,0)^{\intercal}}\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}((-j,k))

is an isomorphism in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
(cf. the proof of Lemma
3.16
).
Note that this implies
\mathrm{Dia}(X)\in\mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Sq},H^{0}(\mathcal{A}))
is a homotopy cartesian square in
\mathcal{T}=H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.

Conversely, let
Y\in\mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Sq},H^{0}(\mathcal{A}))
be a square in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
. If it is a homotopy cartesian square, then it is isomorphic to
\mathrm{Dia}(X)
for some homotopy cartesian object
X\in\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A})
.
Indeed, by Lemma
3.12
below, the object
\mathrm{Res}(Y)\in\mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Cosp},H^{0}(\mathcal{A}))
is isomorphic to
\mathrm{Dia}(V)
for some
V\in\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Cosp},\mathcal{A})
.
Then the object
X\coloneqq R(V)\in\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A})
is homotopy cartesian and satisfies
\mathrm{Dia}(X)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}Y
.

Recall that for a small category
\mathcal{I}
, the canonical diagram functor

\mathrm{Dia}:\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{I})\rightarrow\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{D}({\mathcal{A}}))

sends an object
X:\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
to the corresponding diagram
\mathrm{Dia}(X)=\pi\circ X
where
\pi:\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
is the canonical quotient functor.

Recall that, for a category
\mathcal{C}
, we denote by
\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{C})
the class of isomorphism classes of objects in
\mathcal{C}
.
The following lemma is well-known.
Here we include a proof for the convenience of the reader.

Lemma 3.12
.

Let
\mathcal{I}
be the path category
P(Q)
of a quiver
Q
(without relations).
The functor
\mathrm{Dia}:\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{I})\rightarrow\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}))
is an epivalence, i.e. it is full and dense and detects isomorphisms.
In particular, it induces a bijection

\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{D}(I))\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Iso}(\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}))).

Proof.

The functor
\mathrm{Dia}
clearly detects isomorphisms.
Let us first show that it is dense.

Let
S:\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
be an object in
\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}))
.
For each object
i\in\mathcal{I}
, we take a cofibrant resolution
\theta_{i}:X_{i}\rightarrow S(i)
.
Then for each arrow
\alpha:i\rightarrow j
in
Q
, we have a morphism
X_{\alpha}:X_{i}\rightarrow X_{j}
in
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
such that
\theta_{j}\circ\pi(X_{\alpha})\circ\theta_{i}^{-1}=S(\alpha)
where
\pi:\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
is the quotient functor.
This extends to a functor
X:\mathcal{I}=kQ\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
such that
\mathrm{Dia}(X)=\pi\circ X\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}S
.
This shows that the functor
\mathrm{Dia}
is dense.

Let us now show that it is full.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an additive category with coproducts and
\mathcal{I}
a small category.
For each object
i\in\mathcal{I}
, the map sending a functor
F:\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
to
F(i)
determines the
evaluation functor at
i

i^{*}:\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C})\rightarrow\mathcal{C},\;\;F\mapsto F(i).

It admits a left adjoint

i_{!}:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C})

sending an object
X
to the functor
j\mapsto\coprod_{p:i\rightarrow j}X
, where
p
runs through morphisms from
i
to
j
in
\mathcal{I}
.

Suppose
\mathcal{I}
is the path category
P(Q)
of a quiver
Q
.
Then for each
F\in\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C})
, we have the following sequence

0\rightarrow\coprod_{\alpha:i\rightarrow j\text{ in $Q$}}j_{!}i^{*}F\rightarrow\coprod_{i\in Q}i_{!}i^{*}F\rightarrow F\rightarrow 0.

which splits when evaluated at each object
i\in\mathcal{I}
.

Now suppose
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
.
The above sequence is a short exact sequence in
\mathrm{Fun}(P(Q),\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}))\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}\otimes k(P(Q))^{op})
.
Thus it induces a triangle in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes k(P(Q))^{op})

(3.12.1)

\bigoplus_{\alpha:i\rightarrow j\text{ in $Q$}}j_{!}i^{*}F\rightarrow\bigoplus_{i\in Q}i_{!}i^{*}F\rightarrow F\rightarrow\Sigma\bigoplus_{\alpha:i\rightarrow\text{ in $Q$}}j_{!}i^{*}F.

Notice that the adjunction
(i_{!},i^{*})
is a Quillen adjunction with respect to the projective model structures on both categories.
Thus we have

\mathrm{RHom}(i_{!}X,F)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{RHom}(X,i^{*}F).

Let
G
be another object in
\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}))
.
If we apply
\mathrm{RHom}(-,G)
to the triangle
3.12.1
, we otain the following triangle in
\mathcal{D}(k)

\mathrm{RHom}(F,G)\rightarrow\prod_{i\in Q}\mathrm{RHom}(F(i),G(i))\xrightarrow{\varphi}\prod_{\alpha:i\rightarrow j\text{ in $Q$}}\mathrm{RHom}(F(i),G(j))\rightarrow\Sigma\mathrm{RHom}(F,G).

By direct inspection, we see that the kernel of
H^{0}(\varphi)
is the space of morphisms of diagrams from
\mathrm{Dia}(F)
to
\mathrm{Dia}(G)
.
Thus by applying
H^{0}
to the triangle we see that the map

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes k(P(Q))^{op})}(F,G)\rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Fun}(P(Q),\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}))}(\mathrm{Dia}(F),\mathrm{Dia}(G))

is a surjection.
∎

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a pretriangulated dg category.
In summary, we have the following diagram of functors

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{rep}(k(\mathrm{Sq}),\mathcal{A})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Sq},H^{0}(\mathcal{A}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{rep}(k(\mathrm{Cosp}),\mathcal{A})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Cosp},H^{0}(\mathcal{A}))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Dia}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Res}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Dia}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}

where

—

\mathrm{Res}\circ\mathrm{Dia}=\mathrm{Dia}\circ L
and
\mathrm{Res}\circ\mathrm{Dia}\circ R\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Dia}
;

—

by Lemma
3.12
, the bottom horizontal functor induces a bijection between the isomorphism classes of objects;

—

the functor
R
is fully faithful and by definition, an object
X
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A})
is homotopy cartesian if and only if it is in the essential image of
R
;

—

for each homotopy cartesian square
X
in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
, there exists a non-unique homotopy bicartesian object in
\mathcal{A}
whose image under
\mathrm{Dia}
is isomorphic to
X
;

—

the right vertical functor does not admit a right adjoint because maps in the triangulated category
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
do not have kernels in general.

3.13.
Homotopy pullbacks/pushouts

In this subsection, we extend the definitions of homotopy (co)cartesian squares to the general case when
\mathcal{A}
is not necessarily pretriangulated.

Definition 3.14
.

An object
X\in\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
is a
homotopy cartesian square
with respect to
\mathcal{A}
if the canonical map
X_{00}\rightarrow\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}((-j,k))
induces an isomorphism

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\wedge},X_{00})\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\wedge},\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}((-j,k)))

in
\mathcal{D}(k)
for each
A
in
\mathcal{A}
.

Remark 3.15
.

Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be a full dg subcategory of
\mathcal{A}
.
Let
F:\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A}^{\prime})\rightarrow\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A})
be the inclusion functor induced by the inclusion dg functor
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
.
Let
X
be an object in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
.
If
F(X)
is homotopy cartesian with respect to
\mathcal{A}
, then
X
is homotopy cartesian with respect to
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

In the rest of the chapter, we will only use this relative version of homotopy (co)cartesian squares.

For an object
X\in\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
, by Lemma
3.5
the unit morphism
X\rightarrow RLX
induces a canonical morphism
X\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}RLX
in
\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sq})
.

Lemma 3.16
.

Let
X
be an object in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
. If the canonical map
X\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}RLX
is an isomorphism, then
X
is homotopy cartesian. If
\mathcal{A}
is a connective dg category, then the converse also holds.

Proof.

Let
X
be the object

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}

in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
. Let
p:\mathrm{Cone}(-\mathrm{id}_{\Sigma^{-1}D})\rightarrow D
be the canonical projection.

Then the canonical map
X\rightarrow RLX
can be described by the following commutative diagram in
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\oplus C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cone}(-\mathrm{id}_{\Sigma^{-1}D})\oplus B\oplus C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}f\\
g\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}0\ 1\ 0\\
0\ 0\ 1\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}-j{,}k{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}p{,}-j{,}k{]}}

where the second row is a short exact sequence in
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})
.
By Lemma
3.5
, we have
(\tau_{\leq 0}RLX)_{00}\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\tau_{\leq 0}K
.

We have a canonical commutative diagram in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})

The map

induces a canonical map

in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
.
It is an isomorphism in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
if and only if the canonical map

is an isomorphism in
\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sq})
.

The object
X
is a homotopy cartesian square if and only if
u:A\rightarrow K
induces an isomorphism in
\mathcal{D}(k)

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\prime\wedge},A)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\prime\wedge},K)

for each

in
\mathcal{A}
.

Note that we have

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\prime\wedge},\tau_{\leq 0}K)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\prime\wedge},K).

So if the canonical map
A\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}K
is an isomorphism in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
, then
X
is homotopy cartesian.

When the dg category
\mathcal{A}
is connective, we have

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\prime\wedge},A)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\prime\wedge},A)

and

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\prime\wedge},\tau_{\leq 0}K)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\prime\wedge},\tau_{\leq 0}K).

So the converse also holds.

∎

The following lemma was obtained independently by Genovese, Lowen and Van den Bergh, c.f.
[
48
, Lemma 2.5.5]
.

Lemma 3.19
.

Let
\mathcal{B}
be a connective dg category. Then the natural functor

F:\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{B},\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})

is an equivalence of categories.
Let
H:\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}\mathcal{B}^{op})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}\mathcal{B}^{op})
be the restriction functor.
Then a quasi-inverse of
F
is given by
G=\tau_{\leq 0}\circ H
.
Moreover, for any
X,Y\in\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{B},\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})
, we have
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(X,Y)\xrightarrow{\sim}\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(FX,FY)
.

Proof.

Let
\mathrm{dgcat}_{\leq 0}
be the category of small strictly connective dg categories.
Then we have the following adjunction

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{dgcat}_{\leq 0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{dgcat}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}}

where the left adjoint
i:\mathrm{dgcat}_{\leq 0}\rightarrow\mathrm{dgcat}
is the inclusion functor and the right adjoint
\tau_{\leq 0}:\mathrm{dgcat}\rightarrow\mathrm{dgcat}_{\leq 0}
sends a small dg category
\mathcal{A}
to
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}
.

Let
\mathrm{Hqe}_{\leq 0}
be the localization of
\mathrm{dgcat}_{\leq 0}
at the class of quasi-equivalences of strictly connective dg categories.
The functors
i
and
\tau_{\leq 0}
clearly preserve quasi-equivalences.
Hence by the universal properties of localizations of categories, the above adjunction induces the following adjunction

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hqe}_{\leq 0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hqe}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}}

where
i
is fully faithful.

We claim that the canonical morphism in
\mathrm{Hqe}_{\leq 0}

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B},\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})

is an isomorphism.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an arbitrary small strictly connective dg category.
Recall that the tensor product of strictly connective dg categories remains strictly connective and
that each connective dg category admits a cofibrant replacement which is strictly connective.
Recall that
\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
is the internal Hom of the monoidal category
(\mathrm{Hqe},-\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}-)
.
Then we have

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Hqe}_{\leq 0}}(\mathcal{C},\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(i(\mathcal{B}),i(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})))

\displaystyle=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Hqe}}(i(\mathcal{C}),\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(i(\mathcal{B}),i(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})))

\displaystyle=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Hqe}}(i(\mathcal{C})\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}i(\mathcal{B}),i(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}))

\displaystyle=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Hqe}_{\leq 0}}(\mathcal{C}\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}\mathcal{B},\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Hqe}}(i(\mathcal{C})\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}i(\mathcal{B}),\mathcal{A})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Hqe}}(i(\mathcal{C}),\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(i(\mathcal{B}),\mathcal{A}))

\displaystyle=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Hqe}_{\leq 0}}(\mathcal{C},\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(i(\mathcal{B}),\mathcal{A})).

∎

The following lemma allows us to reduce, in many cases, to the connective case when considering homotopy (co)cartesian squares.

By applying
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})}(A^{\wedge},-)
to the above triangle for each
A\in\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}
, we get the associated long exact sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}(A^{\wedge},X_{00})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}(A^{\wedge},\Sigma^{-1}X_{11})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}(A^{\wedge},\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(\psi))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}(A^{\wedge},X_{10}\oplus X_{01})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dots}

We have
\mathrm{Hom}(A^{\wedge},\Sigma^{-n}X_{ij})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hom}(FA^{\wedge},\Sigma^{-n}FX_{ij})
for
n\geq 0
where
F:\mathcal{D}(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
is the induction functor.
By the Five-Lemma, it is then clear that an object
X
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})
is homotopy cartesian if and only if its image under
F
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A})
is homotopy cartesian.
∎

Definition 3.21
.

An object
S
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Cosp})
is said to admit a homotopy pullback if there is a homotopy cartesian square
X
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
with an isomorphism
\varphi:LX\rightarrow S
in
\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Cosp})
.
In this case, the pair
(X,\varphi)
is called a homotopy pullback of
S
.
We will also abuse the notation and say that
X
is a homotopy pullback of
S
.

Remark 3.22
.

The isomorphism
\varphi:LX\rightarrow S
in the definition of a homotopy pullback is in general not the identity.
For example, let
\mathcal{A}
be the dg category of two-term complexes of finitely generated projective modules over a finite dimensional algebra
A
.
The cospan

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cone}(\mathrm{id}_{A})}

where
A
denotes the corresponding stalk complex, does not admit a homotopy pullback
(X,\varphi)
with
\varphi
being the identity.
It admits a homotopy pullback with
X
given by

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

and
\varphi^{-1}
given by the obvious morphism

Proposition 3.23
.

The functor
L:\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sq})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Cosp})
restricted to
the full subcategory consisting of homotopy cartesian squares is fully faithful.
In particular, the homotopy pullback of an object
S
in
\mathrm{rep}(k\mathrm{Cosp},\mathcal{A})
,
if it exists, is unique up to a unique isomorphism.

Proof.

We first show the case when
\mathcal{A}
is connective.

Let
X
and
X^{\prime}
be two homotopy cartesian squares.
We first show fullness.
Let
f:LX\rightarrow LX^{\prime}
be a morphism in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Cosp},\mathcal{A})
.

From the adjunction

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{D}({\mathrm{Sq}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Cosp})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}
,
we have a morphism
g:X\rightarrow RLX^{\prime}
.

Since the object
X^{\prime}
is homotopy cartesian, by Lemma
3.16
,
the map
X\rightarrow RLX^{\prime}
induces a morphism
h:X\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}RLX^{\prime}\xleftarrow{\sim}X^{\prime}
, as the following diagram shows

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}RLX^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces RLX^{\prime}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}

By applying the functor
L
to the above diagram, we see that
L(h)=f
.
This shows the fullness.

Next we show faithfulness.
Let
h:X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
be a morphism between homotopy cartesian squares.
We have the following diagram in
\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sq})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}RLX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces RLX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}RLX^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces RLX^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces RL(h)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}

Therefore if the morphism
L(h)
is zero, then
h
is also zero.

For the general case, consider the following diagram of functors

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{rep}(k\mathrm{Sq},\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{rep}(k\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{D}(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}\otimes k(\mathrm{Sq}^{op}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes k(\mathrm{Sq}^{op}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{D}(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}\otimes k(\mathrm{Cosp}^{op}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes k(\mathrm{Cosp}^{op}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{rep}(k\mathrm{Cosp},\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{rep}(k\mathrm{Cosp},\mathcal{A})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G^{\prime}}

Let
X
and
X^{\prime}
be two objects in
\mathrm{rep}(k\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A})
which are homotopy cartesian.

We have a canonical isomorphism of triangle functors
L\circ H\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}H^{\prime}\circ L^{\prime}
.
Since the restriction functor
L
commutes with the truncation functors
\tau_{\leq 0}
on
\mathcal{D}(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}\otimes k(\mathrm{Sq}^{op}))
and on
\mathcal{D}(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}\otimes k\mathrm{Cosp}^{op})
, and since the functor
G
(resp.
G^{\prime}
) is a composition of
\tau_{\leq 0}
and
H
(resp.
H^{\prime}
), we have a natural isomorphism of functors
G^{\prime}\circ L^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\sim}L\circ G:\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{rep}(k\mathrm{Cosp},\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A})
.

Let
f:L^{\prime}X\rightarrow L^{\prime}X^{\prime}
be a morphism in
\mathrm{rep}(k\mathrm{Cosp},\mathcal{A})
.
The map
G^{\prime}(f):G^{\prime}L^{\prime}X\rightarrow G^{\prime}L^{\prime}S
then yields a canonical morphism
g:LGX\xrightarrow{\sim}LGX^{\prime}
.
From the connective case, there is a morphism
h^{\prime}:GX\rightarrow GX^{\prime}
such that
g=L(h^{\prime})
.
Since
G
is an equivalence of categories, there exists a morphism
h:X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
such that
h^{\prime}=G(h)
.
Since
G^{\prime}
is also an equivalence of categories, we see that
f=L^{\prime}(h)
.

Similarly, one shows that if a morphism
h:X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
is such that
L^{\prime}(h)=0
, then we have
h=0
.
∎

Remark 3.24

(Universal property of homotopy pullbacks)
.

Similarly, one can show that given a homotopy cartesian square
X^{\prime}
and an object
X
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
, if we have a map
\varphi:LX\rightarrow LX^{\prime}
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Cosp})
, then we have a canonical map
\theta:X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
such that
L(\theta)=\varphi
.

Consider an object
X\in\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sq})
as follows

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}

where
N
is acyclic.

Lemma 3.25
.

We have an isomorphism in
\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sq})
from
X
to

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\oplus N}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}f\\
-g\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}j{,}k{]}}

which restricts to
\mathrm{id}_{A}
and
\mathrm{id}_{C}
.

Remark 3.26
.

Therefore if an object
X
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A})
is such that
N
is acyclic, we will assume that
N
is actually the zero dg module.

Recall that we have the pair of duality functors

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{A})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{I}^{op},\mathcal{A}^{op})^{op}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{RHom}(-\text{,}\mathcal{A})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{RHom}(-\text{,}\mathcal{A})}

Then we can form the dual definitions of a homotopy cocartesian square with respect to
\mathcal{A}
and of a homotopy pushout of an object in
\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sp})
.

Definition 3.27
.

An object
X\in\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
given by the diagram
3.3.1
is a
homotopy

cocartesian square with respect to
\mathcal{A}
if the canonical map
\mathrm{Cone}((f,g)^{\intercal})\rightarrow X_{11}
induces an isomorphism in
\mathcal{D}(k)

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(X_{11},A^{\wedge})\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(\mathrm{Cone}((f,g)^{\intercal}),A^{\wedge})

for each
A
in
\mathcal{A}
.

Consider the adjunction
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sp})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sq})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}

induced by the inclusion
\mathrm{Sp}\rightarrow\mathrm{Sq}
.

Definition 3.28
.

An object
S
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sp})
is said to admit a homotopy pushout if there is a homotopy cartesian square
X
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A})
with an isomorphism
\varphi:S\rightarrow RX
in
\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sp})
. In this case, the pair
(X,\varphi)
is called a homotopy pushout of
S
. We will also abuse the notation and say that
X
is a homotopy pushout of
S
.

Let us give another way of presenting the duality between homotopy pushouts and homotopy pullbacks.
First we observe that
k\mathrm{Sq}
is quasi-equivalent to the cofibrant dg
k
-path category

\Lambda=\Lambda(\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1})
given by the differential graded quiver

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 2}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 3}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}

where
|f|=|j|=|l|=|g|=|k|=0
,
|h_{1}|=|h_{2}|=-1
,
d(h_{1})=l-kg
and
d(h_{2})=l-jf
, cf. the discussions after
Remark
5.38
.
Then objects in
\mathrm{rep}(\Lambda,\mathcal{A})
are isomorphic to objects whose terms are representable,
e.g. one can argue as in Lemma
3.41
.
Such objects canonically give objects in
\mathrm{rep}(\Lambda,\mathcal{A}^{op})
by simply reversing the arrows and
composing with the obvious isomorphism
\Lambda\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\Lambda^{op}
.
In such a way, one defines an object in
\mathrm{rep}(\Lambda,\mathcal{A})
to be a homotopy pushout if and only if the corresponding object in
\mathrm{rep}(\Lambda,\mathcal{A}^{op})
is a homotopy pullback.

Example 3.29
.

Let
A
be a finite-dimensional
k
-algebra.
Let
\mathcal{H}^{[-1,0]}(\mathrm{proj}\,A)
be the full subcategory of
\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{H}^{b}(\mathrm{proj}\,A)
consisting of two-term complexes
P^{-1}\to P^{0}
of finitely generated projective
A
-modules.
Let
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{C}^{b}_{dg}(\mathrm{proj}\,A)
be the canonical enhancement of

{\mathcal{H}}^{b}(\mathrm{proj}\,A)
and
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
its full dg subcategory on the objects
P^{-1}\to P^{0}
.
For an

-module

its

One can show that there exists a homotopy bicartesian square in

which is not homotopy bicartesian in

if and only if there exists an

satisfying the following properties

(1)

, and

(2)

, and

is an isomorphism.

Below, we will show by examples that there is no redundance in these conditions.
Suppose we are given such an

-module

.
Take a minimal projective presentation of

0\rightarrow P_{1}\rightarrow P_{0}\rightarrow M\rightarrow 0.

Then we have a left exact sequence of left

-modules:

Take a minimal projective presentation of

0\rightarrow Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0}\rightarrow N\rightarrow 0.

Then we have a left exact sequence of right
A
-modules:

0\rightarrow M\rightarrow Q_{0}^{*}\rightarrow Q_{1}^{*}.

Then the following square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(P_{1}\rightarrow P_{0})}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(0\rightarrow Q_{1}^{*})}

is homotopy bicartesian in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, but not in
\mathcal{A}
.

Note that conditions (1) and (3) together do not imply condition (2), as the following example shows.
Let

be the algebra given by the following quiver the relations

3.30.
An
A_{\infty}
-theoretic description

Our aim is to give a description of the homotopy
category of homotopy
3
-term complexes using the
A_{\infty}
-formalism.
We first recall some basic facts and notation for
A_{\infty}
-categories. Our standard references for
A_{\infty}
-categories are
[
82
,
83
,
84
,
95
]
. We follow the sign conventions of
[
50
]
. Note that we keep the assumption that
k
is a commutative ring.

Definition 3.31
.

An
A_{\infty}
-category
\mathcal{A}
is the datum of

—

a class of objects
\mathrm{obj}(\mathcal{A})
,

—

for all
A,B\in\mathcal{A}
, a
\mathbb{Z}
-graded
k
-module
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A,B)
, often denoted by
(A,B)
,

—

for all
n\geq 1
and all
A_{0}
, …,
A_{n}
, a graded map

m_{n}:(A_{n-1},A_{n})\otimes(A_{n-2},A_{n-1})\otimes\cdots\otimes(A_{0},A_{1})\rightarrow(A_{0},A_{n})

of degree
2-n

such that for each
n\geq 1
and all
A_{0},\ldots,A_{n}\in\mathcal{A}
, we have the identity

\sum(-1)^{r+st}m_{u}(\boldsymbol{1}^{\otimes r}\otimes m_{s}\otimes\boldsymbol{1}^{\otimes t})=0

of maps

(A_{n-1},A_{n})\otimes(A_{n-2},A_{n-1})\otimes\cdots\otimes(A_{0},A_{1})\rightarrow(A_{0},A_{n})

where the sum runs over all decompositions
n=r+s+t
and we put
u=r+1+t
.

Remark 3.32
.

The composition
m_{2}
induces an associative composition

\mu:H^{0}(\mathcal{A})(B,C)\otimes H^{0}(\mathcal{A})(A,B)\rightarrow H^{0}(\mathcal{A})(A,C)

for each triple of objects
(A,B,C)
in
\mathcal{A}
.

Definition 3.33
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be an
A_{\infty}
-category and
A\in\mathcal{A}
. A morphism
e_{A}\in\mathrm{Hom}^{0}_{\mathcal{A}}(A,A)
is a strict identity if we have

m_{2}(f,e_{A})=f\mbox{ and }m_{2}(e_{A},g)=g

whenever these make sense and

m_{n}(\ldots,e_{A},\ldots)=0

for all
n\neq 2
.
In particular,
e_{A}
is a cycle of the complex
(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A,A),m_{1})
.
Clearly, if
e_{A}
exists, it is unique.
The
A_{\infty}
-category
\mathcal{A}
has strict identities if there is a strict identity
e_{A}
for each object
A\in\mathcal{A}
.

Definition 3.34
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
be two
A_{\infty}
-categories. An
A_{\infty}
-functor
F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
is the datum of

—

a map
F:\mathrm{obj}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{obj}(\mathcal{B})
,

—

for all
n\geq 1
and all
A_{0}
, …,
A_{n}\in\mathcal{A}
a graded map

F_{n}:(A_{n-1},A_{n})\otimes(A_{n-2},A_{n-1})\otimes\cdots\otimes(A_{0},A_{1})\rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{B}}(FA_{0},FA_{n})

of degree
1-n

such that

\sum(-1)^{r+st}F_{u}(\boldsymbol{1}^{\otimes r}\otimes m_{s}\otimes\boldsymbol{1}^{\otimes t})=\sum(-1)^{s}m_{r}(F_{i_{1}}\otimes F_{i_{2}}\otimes\cdots\otimes F_{i_{r}})

where the first sum runs over all decompositions
n=r+s+t
, we put
u=r+1+t
, and the second sum runs over all
1\leq r\leq n
and all decompositions
n=i_{1}+\cdots+i_{r}
; the sign on the right hand side is given by

s=(r-1)(i_{1}-1)+(r-2)(i_{2}-1)+\cdots+2(i_{r-2}-1)+(i_{r-1}-1).

The
A_{\infty}
-functor
F
is strict if we have
F_{n}=0
for all
n\geq 2
. Clearly the above datum with
F_{n}=0
for
n\geq 2
defines a strict
A_{\infty}
-functor if and only if for each
k\geq 1
, we have

F_{1}m_{k}=m_{k}(F_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes F_{1}).

Definition 3.35
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
be two
A_{\infty}
-categories with strict identities. An
A_{\infty}
-functor
F
is strictly unital if

F_{1}(e_{A})=e_{FA}

and

F_{i}(\cdots\otimes e_{A}\otimes\cdots)=0

for all
i\geq 2
.

The following simple example, due to M. Kontsevich, shows that already between dg categories,
A_{\infty}
-functors are quite interesting.

Example 3.36

(
[
93
,
28
]
)
.

Let
I_{2}
be the
k
-category generated by the category
J_{2}
with
2
objects and precisely one morphism with any given source and target

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 2.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

We consider it as a dg category concentrated in degree 0. Let
\mathcal{A}
be a dg category and
X,Y
two objects in
\mathcal{A}
.

We will show that
X
and
Y
are homotopy equivalent if and only if there exists a strictly unital
A_{\infty}
-functor from
I_{2}
to
\mathcal{A}
such that
1
is sent to
X
and
2
is sent to
Y
.

Let
\mathcal{K}
be the Kontsevich dg category defined as the dg
k
-path category given by

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 2}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{2}}

where
|a|=|b|=0
,
|h_{1}|=-1=|h_{2}|
,
|r|=-2
and
d(a)=d(b)=0
,
d(h_{1})=1-ba
,
d(h_{2})=1-ab
,
d(r)=-ah_{1}+h_{2}a
.
By
[
28
, Corollary 3.7.3]
,
\mathcal{K}
is a cofibrant resolution of
I_{2}
.
In particular we have

(3.36.1)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{n}_{\mathcal{K}}(i,j)=0

for
i,j\in\{1,2\}
and
n\neq 0
.

Suppose
X
and
Y
are homotopy equivalent.
Then we have a homotopy equivalence
f:X\rightarrow Y
and a homotopy inverse
g:Y\rightarrow X
.
By definition there exist
\widetilde{h_{1}}:X\rightarrow X
and
\widetilde{h_{2}}:Y\rightarrow Y
of degree
-1
such that
d(\widetilde{h_{1}})=1-gf
and
d(\widetilde{h_{2}})=1-fg
.
Set
{h_{1}}=\widetilde{h_{1}}+g\widetilde{h_{2}}f-gf\widetilde{h_{1}}
and
{h_{2}}=\widetilde{h_{2}}
. Let
r=\widetilde{h_{2}}\widetilde{h_{2}}f-\widetilde{h_{2}}f\widetilde{h_{1}}
.
Then
d({h_{1}})=d(\widetilde{h_{1}})
and
-f{h_{1}}+{h_{2}}f=d(r)
.
Thus
(f,g,h_{1},h_{2},r)
defines a dg functor
G:\mathcal{K}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
.

Notice that
m_{i}
vanishes in
I_{2}
for
i\neq 2
and in
\mathcal{A}
for
i\geq 3
.
When
i=2
,
m_{2}
produces either identities or zeros in
I_{2}
.
Thus for an
A_{\infty}
-functor
F:I_{2}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
, the conditions become

\displaystyle d(F_{1}(a))

\displaystyle=0,d(F_{1}(b))=0

\displaystyle 1=F_{1}(b)F_{1}(a)+d(F_{2}(b,a)),1

\displaystyle=F_{1}(a)F_{1}(b)+d(F_{2}(a,b))

(3.36.2)

\displaystyle\sum(-1)^{r}F_{n-1}(\boldsymbol{1}^{\otimes r}\otimes m_{2}\otimes\boldsymbol{1}^{\otimes t})

\displaystyle=d\circ(F_{n})+\sum(-1)^{i_{1}-1}m_{2}(F_{i_{1}}\otimes F_{i_{2}})

where
n\geq 3
,
r+t=n-2
and
i_{1}+i_{2}=n
.
When acting on
(a_{1},\cdots,a_{n})
, the conditions become trivial for
n\geq 3
if some
a_{i}
is an identity.
When each
a_{i}
is non identity,
m_{2}
in each summand of the left hand side will produce an identity and hence becomes zero by
F_{n-1}
.
Thus we only need to take care of
F_{n}(a_{1},a_{2},\cdots,a_{n})
with
a_{i}\in\{a,b\}
and
a_{i}\neq a_{i+1}
.

We define an
A_{\infty}
-functor
F:I_{2}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
as follows: the value of
F_{n}
on a sequence
(a_{1},a_{2},\cdots,a_{n})
, where
a_{i}\in\{a,b\}
and
a_{i}\neq a_{i+1}
, is the image under the dg functor
G
of an element
\widetilde{F_{n}}(a_{1},a_{2},\cdots,a_{n})
, which is constructed by induction, in
\mathcal{K}(i,j)
with
(i,j)
depending on the sequence
(a_{1},a_{2},\cdots,a_{n})
.
More precisely

\displaystyle\widetilde{F_{1}}(a)

\displaystyle=a,\widetilde{F_{1}}(b)=b

\displaystyle\widetilde{F_{2}}(a,b)

\displaystyle=h_{2},\widetilde{F_{2}}(b,a)=h_{1}.

\displaystyle\widetilde{F_{3}}(a,b,a)=r.

By induction we have

(3.36.3)

\displaystyle\sum(-1)^{i_{1}}d\circ m_{2}(\widetilde{F_{i_{1}}}\otimes\widetilde{F_{i_{2}}})(a_{1},a_{2},\cdots,a_{n})=0.

where
(i_{1},i_{2})
runs through the pair such that
i_{1}+i_{2}=n
. Here
(\widetilde{F_{i_{1}}}\otimes\widetilde{F_{i_{2}}})(a_{1},a_{2},\cdots,a_{n})
is understood as
\widetilde{F_{i_{1}}}(a_{1},\cdots,a_{i_{1}})\otimes\widetilde{F_{i_{2}}}(a_{i_{1}+1},\cdots,a_{n})
.

By
3.36.1
, there exists an element
\widetilde{F_{n}}(a_{1},a_{2},\cdots,a_{n})\in\mathcal{K}(i,j)^{1-n}
whose coboundary is the cocycle

\sum(-1)^{i_{1}}\widetilde{F_{i_{1}}}(a_{1},\cdots,a_{i_{1}})\circ\widetilde{F_{i_{2}}}(a_{i_{1}+1},\cdots,a_{n})

which appears on the left hand side of
3.36.3
.

For example we may put

\widetilde{F_{3}}(b,a,b)=-brb+bh_{2}^{2}+h_{1}^{2}b-h_{1}bh_{2}.

Remark 3.37
.

The Kontsevich dg category
\mathcal{K}
is quasi-equivalent to the dg
k
-path category
\mathcal{C}
given by the differential graded quiver

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 2}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{\prime}}

where
|a|=|b|=|b^{\prime}|=0
,
|h_{1}|=-1=|h_{2}|
, and
d(a)=d(b)=d(b^{\prime})=0
,
d(h_{1})=1-ba
,
d(h_{2})=1-ab^{\prime}
.
A quasi-equivalence
F:\mathcal{K}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is given as follows: on the objects we have
F(1)=1
and
F(2)=2
and on the arrows we have
F(a)=a
,
F(b)=b^{\prime}
,
F(h_{2})=h_{2}
,

\displaystyle F(h_{1})

\displaystyle=h_{1}+b^{\prime}(h_{2}a-ah_{1})+(1-b^{\prime}a)(bh_{2}-h_{1}b^{\prime})a

\displaystyle F(r)

\displaystyle=h_{2}h_{2}a-h_{2}a(h_{1}+(bh_{2}-h_{1}b^{\prime})a).

We call this dg category the Cisinski dg category because it is the image of Cisinski’s interval
J
(cf.
[
23
, Definition 3.3.3]
) under the functor
\Lambda
(cf.
5.29.1
).

The datum of a dg functor
F:\mathcal{K}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
is equivalent to a morphism
\alpha:X_{1}\rightarrow X_{2}
closed of degree
0
in
\mathcal{A}
together with a contracting homotopy for
\mathrm{Cone}(\alpha^{\wedge}:X_{1}^{\wedge}\rightarrow X_{2}^{\wedge})
, while the datum of a dg functor
G:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
is equivalent a morphism
\alpha:X_{1}\rightarrow X_{2}
closed of degree
0
in
\mathcal{A}
together with null-homotopies of the maps
[0,\;1]^{\intercal}:X_{2}^{\wedge}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cone}(\alpha^{\wedge})
and
[1,\;0]:\mathrm{Cone}(\alpha^{\wedge})\rightarrow\Sigma X_{1}^{\wedge}
.

Let
\mathcal{B}
be a small
A_{\infty}
-category and
\mathcal{A}
an
A_{\infty}
-category.
It is known, cf.
[
93
]
, that there is a natural
A_{\infty}
-category
\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
of strictly unital
A_{\infty}
-functors between
\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{A}
.
It was constructed in
[
95
, 8.1.3]
using twists of
A_{\infty}
-structures.
Keller further developed an idea in
[
105
]
and interpreted it in
[
84
, 5.7]
as an internal
\mathrm{Hom}
-object in the tensor category of cocomplete augmented dg cocategories.
Note that when the target
\mathcal{A}
is a dg category, the
A_{\infty}
-category
\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
is again a dg category.
The reason is that we use the
m_{j}^{\mathcal{A}}
,
j\geq i
, to define the map
m_{i}
of the
A_{\infty}
-category

\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
and when
\mathcal{A}
is a dg category, then the
m_{j}^{\mathcal{A}}
vanish for all
j\geq 3
.

Example 3.38
.

The dg category
\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(k\mathrm{Mor},\mathcal{A})
is isomorphic to the dg morphism category
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})
introduced in
[
28
, 2.9]
. More precisely,
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})
has as objects the closed morphisms
f:A\rightarrow B
of degree 0 in
\mathcal{A}
. The morphism complex
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})((A,B,f),(A^{\prime},B^{\prime},f^{\prime}))
has as the degree
m
component the space of matrices

\begin{pmatrix}j&0\\
h&l\end{pmatrix}

where the morphisms
j:A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
,
l:B\rightarrow B^{\prime}
are of degree
m
and the morphism
h:A\rightarrow B^{\prime}
is of degree
m-1
. The differential
d
carries a morphism

\begin{pmatrix}j&0\\
h&l\end{pmatrix}

to

\begin{pmatrix}-d(j)&0\\
d(h)+f^{\prime}j-(-1)^{m}lf&d(l)\end{pmatrix}
.
The composition map is the multiplication of matrices.

Now let
\mathcal{A}
be a dg category and

be the dg

By definition, it has strictly unital

A strictly unital

-functor

Definition 3.39
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a dg category.
The homotopy category
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
of 3-term homotopy complexes (= 3-term
h
-complexes, or 3-term complexes up to homotopy) over
\mathcal{A}
is defined to be
H^{0}\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
where
\mathcal{B}
is the dg category
3.38.1
.
More precisely, its objects are given by diagrams
X
in
\mathcal{A}
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

where
|f|=|j|=0
,
|h|=-1
and
d(f)=0
,
d(j)=0
and
d(h)=-jf
.

Suppose
X^{\prime}
is given by the diagram with objects and morphisms with superscript a prime symbol.

A morphism from
X
to
X^{\prime}
is given by a homotopy equivalence class of 6-tuples
(h_{i},s_{j},t)
,
i=0,1,2
,
j=1,2
where

h_{i}:A_{i}\rightarrow A_{i}^{\prime},|h_{i}|=0,d(h_{i})=0,

s_{j}:A_{j-1}\rightarrow A_{j}^{\prime},|s_{j}|=-1,d(s_{1})=f^{\prime}h_{0}-h_{1}f,

(3.39.1)

d(s_{2})=j^{\prime}h_{1}-h_{2}j,

and

(3.39.2)

t:A_{0}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\prime},|t|=-2,d(t)=h_{2}\circ h-h^{\prime}\circ h_{0}-s_{2}\circ f-j^{\prime}\circ s_{1}.

Two 6-tuples
(h_{i},s_{j},t)
and
(h_{i}^{\prime},s_{j}^{\prime},t^{\prime})
are homotopy equivalent if there exists a 6-tuple
(h^{\prime\prime}_{i},s_{j}^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime})
such that

|h_{i}^{\prime\prime}|=-1,h_{i}-h_{i}^{\prime}=d(h_{i}^{\prime\prime}),

|s_{j}^{\prime\prime}|=-2,s_{1}-s_{1}^{\prime}=d(s_{1}^{\prime\prime})+f^{\prime}\circ h_{0}^{\prime\prime}-h_{1}^{\prime\prime}\circ f,

s_{2}-s_{2}^{\prime}=d(s_{2}^{\prime\prime})+j^{\prime}\circ h_{1}^{\prime\prime}-h_{2}^{\prime\prime}\circ j,

and

|t^{\prime\prime}|=-3,t-t^{\prime}=d(t^{\prime\prime})-j^{\prime}\circ s_{1}^{\prime\prime}+h^{\prime}\circ h_{0}^{\prime\prime}-s_{2}^{\prime\prime}\circ f+h_{2}^{\prime\prime}\circ h.

The composition of two morphisms given by homotopy equivalence classes of 6-tuples
(h_{i}^{\prime},s_{j}^{\prime},t^{\prime}):F\rightarrow F^{\prime}
and
(h_{i}^{\prime\prime},s_{j}^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}):F^{\prime}\rightarrow F^{\prime}
, is the morphism given by the 6-tuple
(\widetilde{h}_{i},\widetilde{s}_{j},\widetilde{t}):F\rightarrow F^{\prime\prime}
where

\displaystyle\widetilde{h}_{i}

\displaystyle=h_{i}^{\prime\prime}h_{i}^{\prime},

\displaystyle\widetilde{s}_{1}

\displaystyle=h_{1}^{\prime\prime}s_{1}^{\prime}+s_{1}^{\prime\prime}h_{0}^{\prime},

\displaystyle\widetilde{s}_{2}

\displaystyle=h_{2}^{\prime\prime}s_{2}^{\prime}+s_{2}^{\prime\prime}h_{1}^{\prime}

\displaystyle\widetilde{t}

\displaystyle=h_{2}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime}+t^{\prime\prime}h_{0}^{\prime}-s_{2}^{\prime\prime}s_{1}^{\prime}.

The identity morphism for
X
is given by the homotopy equivalence class of the 6-tuple
(h_{i},s_{j},t)
where

,
s_{j}=0
and
t=0
for

and

.

From the definition, we see that
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
is isomorphic to
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\tau_{\leq 0}(\mathcal{A}))
.
Thus we may assume
\mathcal{A}
is strictly connective when needed.

Clearly if a 6-tuple

Let
