Proposition 3.40

(
[
95
]
, Proposition 8.2.2.3)
.

Let
\theta:F\rightarrow F^{\prime}
be a morphism in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
given by the homotopy equivalence class of a 6-tuple
(h_{i},s_{j},t)
as above.
If
h_{i}
is a homotopy equivalence in
\mathcal{A}
for each
i=0,1,2
, then
\theta
is an isomorphism.

Proof.

We use the notations in the above discussion.
For each
F^{\prime\prime}
in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
, we have a morphism of graded-split short exact sequences of complexes over
k

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F^{\prime\prime},A_{2}^{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F^{\prime\prime},F)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F^{\prime\prime},U)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F^{\prime\prime},A_{2}^{\prime 2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F^{\prime\prime},F^{\prime})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F^{\prime\prime},U^{\prime})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma}

We want to show that the morphisms
\alpha
and
\gamma
are quasi-isomorphisms of complexes.
It is enough to show the following claim.

Claim: for each homotopy equivalence
A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}
, and for each
i=0
,
1
,
2
, the induced morphism

(F^{\prime\prime},A^{i})\rightarrow(F^{\prime\prime},A^{\prime i})

is a quasi-isomorphism of complexes.

To see this, we apply
\mathrm{Hom}(-,A^{i})
and
\mathrm{Hom}(-,A^{\prime i})
to the associated graded-split short exact sequences for
F^{\prime\prime}
and get morphisms of graded-split short exact sequences of complexes over
k

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces((A_{0}^{\prime\prime})^{0},A^{i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(U^{\prime\prime},A^{i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces((A_{1}^{\prime\prime})^{1},A^{i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces((A_{0}^{\prime\prime})^{0},A^{\prime i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(U^{\prime\prime},A^{\prime i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces((A_{1}^{\prime\prime})^{1},A^{\prime i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(U^{\prime\prime},A^{i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F^{\prime\prime},A^{i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces((A_{2}^{\prime\prime})^{2},A^{i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(U^{\prime\prime},A^{\prime i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F^{\prime\prime},A^{\prime i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces((A_{2}^{\prime\prime})^{2},A^{\prime i})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0.}

Now we observe that for any pair of objects
B
and
C
in
\mathcal{A}
, the complex
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})}(B^{i},C^{j})
is isomorphic to a shift of
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(B,C)
if
i\leq j
and is zero if
j>i
.
Since
A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
is a homotopy equivalence in
\mathcal{A}
, the above maps in blue are quasi-isomorphisms of complexes.
This implies that the morphism
(F^{\prime\prime},A^{i})\rightarrow(F^{\prime\prime},A^{\prime i})
is a quasi-isomorphism.
This proves the claim and hence the proposition.
∎

Denote by
\widetilde{\mathrm{Com}}
the dg path
k
-category of the quiver

(3.40.1)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 2}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

where
{|}a{|}=0
,
{|}b{|}=0
,
{|}c{|}=-1
, and
d(c)=ba
.

We identify objects in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes\widetilde{\mathrm{Com}}^{op})
with sequences

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

in
\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
where
f
and
j
are closed morphisms of degree 0 and
h
is a morphism of degree
-1
such that
d(h)=jf
.

Lemma 3.41
.

Each object in
\mathrm{rep}(\widetilde{\mathrm{Com}},\mathcal{A})
is isomorphic to an object of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\wedge}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\wedge}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{\wedge}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\wedge}}

where
A,B,C
are objects in
\mathcal{A}
, the maps
f
and
j
are of degree
0
, the map
h
is of degree
-1
and
d(h)=jf
.

Proof.

We observe that
\widetilde{\mathrm{Com}}
is a cofibrant dg category.
Recall that for dg categories
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
where
\mathcal{B}
is cofibrant, we have a canonical bijection
[
134
, Theorem 4.2]

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Hqe}}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{dgcat}}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})/\mathrm{htp}\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Iso}(\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}))

where the homotopy class of a dg functor
F:\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
is sent to the isomorphism class of the dg bimodule
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(-,F(-))
.
Thus each object in
\mathrm{rep}(\widetilde{\mathrm{Com}},\mathcal{A})
is isomorphic to an object given by a dg functor
\widetilde{\mathrm{Com}}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
.
∎

The following theorem is claimed by Kontsevich, modulo some results by Toën.
We give a direct proof in the special case where
\mathcal{B}
is the dg category
3.38.1
.

Theorem 3.42

(
[
21
]
cf. also
[
38
]
)
.

We have a canonical isomorphism

\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(-,-)\rightarrow\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(-,-)

of bifunctors
\mathrm{Hqe}_{k-\mathrm{cf}}^{op}\times\mathrm{Hqe}\rightarrow\mathrm{Hqe}
, where
\mathrm{Hqe}_{k-\mathrm{cf}}
is the
full subcategory of
\mathrm{Hqe}
whose objects are the dg categories whose morphism
complexes are cofibrant dg
k
-modules.

Corollary 3.43
.

Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be a full dg subcategory of
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
be a small dg category.
Let
F:\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}^{\prime})\rightarrow\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
be the functor induced by the inclusion
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
.
Then an object
X\in\mathrm{rep}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
lies in the essential image of
F
if and only if for each object
B
in
\mathcal{B}
,
X(-,B)
is quasi-isomorphic to a dg
\mathcal{A}
-module represented by an object in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

Proof of the Corollary.

Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime}
be the closure of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
under homotopy equivalences in
\mathcal{A}
. The inclusion of

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
into
\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime}
is a quasi-equivalence and therefore induces a quasi-equivalence in

\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B},?)
. By the above theorem, it also induces a quasi-equivalence in

\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},?)
. Thus, we may assume that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is stable under homotopy equivalences
in
\mathcal{A}
. Now the inclusion
\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}^{\prime})\to\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
is clearly an isomorphism
onto the full subcategory of
A_{\infty}
-functors whose values on objects lie in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
Thanks to the theorem, this implies the statement.
∎

Lemma 3.44
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a small dg category and
\mathcal{C}
be a dg category given by a differential graded quiver
Q
without relations and whose differential
d
is such that
Q
admits a finite filtration

F_{0}\subset F_{1}\subset F_{2}\subset\ldots\subset F_{N}=Q

such that all
F_{p}
have the same objects as
Q
, and the bimodule of arrows of
F_{0}
vanishes and
d(F_{p})
is contained in
kF_{p-1}
.
Then for each dg functor
F:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
, the associated dg
\mathcal{C}
-
\mathcal{A}
-bimodule
{}_{F}\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{A}}=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(-,F(-))
admits a cofibrant resolution

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ker}(p)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bigoplus_{i\in Q}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(-,F(i))\otimes\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(i,-)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(-,F(-))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

Proof.

Let
F:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
be a dg functor.
Then we have a short exact sequence of dg
\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{C}^{op}
-modules

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ker}(p)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bigoplus_{i\in Q}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(-,F(i))\otimes\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(i,-)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(-,F(-))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

where the dg module
\mathrm{ker}(p)
is isomorphic to

\bigoplus_{\alpha:i\rightarrow j\text{ in $Q$}}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(-,F(i))\otimes\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(j,-)\otimes k\alpha

as a graded module.
It has a finite increasing filtration

0\subset M_{0}\subset M_{1}\subset\ldots\subset M_{N}=\mathrm{ker}(p)

where

M_{k}=\bigoplus_{\alpha:i\rightarrow j\text{ in $F_{k}$}}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(-,F(i))\otimes\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(j,-)\otimes k\alpha.

The subquotient
M_{k+1}/M_{k}
is isomorphic to the shift of the representable dg bimodule

\bigoplus_{\alpha:i\rightarrow j\text{ in $F_{k+1}\backslash F_{k}$}}\Sigma^{|\alpha|}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(-,F(i))\otimes\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(j,-).

Thus
\mathrm{Cone}(u)
is a cofibrant resolution of the dg bimodule
{}_{F}\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{A}}
associated with the dg functor
F:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
.
∎

Proposition 3.45
.

Let
\mathcal{B}
be the dg category defined by
3.38.1
.
We have a canonical isomorphism
\mu:\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
in
\mathrm{Hqe}
.

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
be the dg category
\widetilde{\mathrm{Com}}
defined by
3.40.1
.
We have a quasi equivalence
\mathcal{B}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
.

We define a dg functor
\widetilde{\mu}:\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B}^{\prime},\mathcal{A})
as follows:

Let
F
be an object in
\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
with the corresponding diagram
3.38.2
.
Let

be the dg
\mathcal{B}^{\prime op}\otimes\mathcal{A}
module which corresponds to the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{0}^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}^{\wedge}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\wedge}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces-h^{\wedge}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\wedge}}

Denote by
X=2^{\wedge}\otimes A_{0}^{\wedge}
,
Y=1^{\wedge}\otimes A_{0}^{\wedge}\oplus 2^{\wedge}\otimes A_{1}^{\wedge}\oplus 2^{\wedge}\otimes\mathrm{Cone}(\mathrm{id}_{A_{0}^{\wedge}})
and
Z=0^{\wedge}\otimes A_{0}^{\wedge}\oplus 1^{\wedge}\otimes A_{1}^{\wedge}\oplus 2^{\wedge}\otimes A_{2}^{\wedge}
the cofibrant dg
\mathcal{B}^{\prime op}\otimes\mathcal{A}
-modules.
By Lemma
3.44
, we have an exact sequence of dg
\mathcal{B}^{\prime op}\otimes\mathcal{A}
-modules:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma}

where

\alpha^{\intercal}=\begin{bmatrix}b^{\wedge}\otimes\mathrm{id}&\mathrm{id}\otimes f^{\wedge}&1\otimes{[}0,1{]}^{\intercal}\end{bmatrix},

\beta=\begin{bmatrix}a^{\wedge}\otimes\mathrm{id}&0&-(ba)^{\wedge}\otimes{[}0,1{]}-c^{\wedge}\otimes{[}s^{-1},0{]}\\
-\mathrm{id}\otimes f^{\wedge}&b^{\wedge}\otimes\mathrm{id}&0\\
0&-\mathrm{id}\otimes j^{\wedge}&\mathrm{id}\otimes{[}-h^{\wedge}{,}(jf)^{\wedge}{]}\end{bmatrix}

and

is the obvious morphism.

The object

is sent by

to the totalization of the sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta}

So
\widetilde{\mu}(F)
is quasi-isomorphic to

.

Let
H:F\rightarrow F^{\prime}
be a morphism of degree
n
in
\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
given by the diagram
3.38.3
.

Recall that for a dg
\mathcal{A}
-module
M
,
s:M\rightarrow\Sigma M
is the graded map of degree
-1
which is
\mathrm{id}:{M^{n}}\rightarrow(\Sigma M)^{n-1}=M^{n}
on each degree
n
.
Clearly
d(s)=0
.

We have the following diagram in
\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\mathcal{B}^{\prime op}\otimes\mathcal{A})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta^{\prime}}

where

u=\mathrm{id}\otimes h_{0}^{\wedge},

v=(-1)^{n}\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{id}\otimes h_{0}^{\wedge}&0&0\\
0&\mathrm{id}\otimes h_{1}^{\wedge}&\mathrm{id}\otimes{[}s_{1}^{\wedge}\circ s^{-1},(f^{\prime}h_{0}-h_{1}f)^{\wedge}{]}\\
0&0&\mathrm{id}\otimes\begin{bmatrix}(-1)^{n}s\circ h_{0}^{\wedge}\circ s^{-1}\ \ \ 0\\
0\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ h_{0}^{\wedge}\end{bmatrix}\end{bmatrix},

w=\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{id}\otimes h_{0}^{\wedge}&0&0\\
0&\mathrm{id}\otimes h_{1}^{\wedge}&0\\

\mathrm{id}\otimes s_{1}^{\wedge}&0&-b^{\wedge}\otimes{[}0,s_{1}^{\wedge}{]}\\
0&\mathrm{id}\otimes s_{2}^{\wedge}&-\mathrm{id}\otimes{[}t^{\wedge},(s_{2}\circ f)^{\wedge}{]}\end{bmatrix}.

The morphism

is sent by the dg functor

to the morphism

\begin{bmatrix}u&0&0\\

We have that

\alpha^{\prime}u=(-1)^{n}v\alpha,

d(u)=\mathrm{id}\otimes(d(h_{0}))^{\wedge},

d(v)=(-1)^{n}\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{id}\otimes d(h_{0})^{\wedge}&0&0\\
0&\mathrm{id}\otimes d(h_{1})^{\wedge}&\mathrm{id}\otimes{[}s_{1}^{\prime\wedge}\circ s^{-1},(f^{\prime}d(h_{0})-d(h_{1})f)^{\wedge}{]}\\
0&0&\mathrm{id}\otimes\begin{bmatrix}(-1)^{n+1}s\circ(d(h_{0}))^{\wedge}\circ s^{-1}\ \ 0\\
0\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ d(h_{0})\end{bmatrix}\end{bmatrix},

d(w)=\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{id}\otimes d(h_{0})^{\wedge}&0&0\\
0&d(h_{1})^{\wedge}&0\\
0&0&\mathrm{id}\otimes d(h_{1})^{\wedge}\end{bmatrix},

d(r)+\beta^{\prime}v-(-1)^{n}w\beta=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\
\mathrm{id}\otimes s_{1}^{\prime\wedge}&0&-b^{\wedge}\otimes{[}0,s_{1}^{\prime\wedge}{]}\\
0&\mathrm{id}\otimes s_{2}^{\prime\wedge}&-\mathrm{id}\otimes{[}t^{\prime\wedge},(s_{2}^{\prime}\circ f)^{\wedge}{]}\end{bmatrix}

where

s_{1}^{\prime}=d(s_{1})+(-1)^{n+1}f^{\prime}h_{0}+(-1)^{n}h_{1}f,

s_{2}^{\prime}=d(s_{2})+(-1)^{n+1}j^{\prime}h_{1}+(-1)^{n}h_{2}j,

t^{\prime}=d(t)+(-1)^{n}j^{\prime}s_{1}+h^{\prime}h_{0}+(-1)^{n}s_{2}f+(-1)^{n+1}h_{2}h.

So the functor
\widetilde{\mu}:\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{B}^{\prime},\mathcal{A})
is indeed a dg functor.

By Lemma
3.41
, the functor
\widetilde{\mu}
is quasi-dense.

To show the quasi-full faithfulness, we may assume that the dg category
\mathcal{A}
contains a zero object.
We adopt the notations used in the discussions before Proposition
3.40
.
In particular, the object
U\in\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
corresponds to the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

And we have graded-split short exact sequences in
\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}^{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{0}^{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0,}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0.}

Thus it suffices to show that
\widetilde{\mu}
induces quasi-isomorphisms between objects of the form

where
A\in\mathcal{A}
and

.

This can be checked using the fact that
\widetilde{\mu}(F)
is a cofibrant resolution of

.
∎

modulo
\mathcal{A}\otimes\{01\}
and hence a localization functor, i.e. the restriction functor along
\mathrm{id}\otimes G^{op}
is fully faithful.

Let
\mathcal{S}
be the right orthogonal of the objects
(A,01)^{\wedge}
in
\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sq})
, where
A
runs through objects in
\mathcal{A}
.
More precisely,
\mathcal{S}
is the full triangulated subcategory of
\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sq})
consisting of squares

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}

where
N
is an acyclic dg
\mathcal{A}
-module.

Lemma 3.46
.

F
is a quasi-equivalence and
G
induces an equivalence
\mathcal{S}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes\widetilde{\mathrm{Sq}}^{op})
.

Proof.

It is enough to show that
F
induces a quasi-isomorphism of complexes

\mathrm{Hom}_{\widetilde{\mathrm{Com}}}(0,2)\rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\widetilde{\mathrm{Sq}}}(00,11).

On the left hand side, the complex is given by

\cdots\rightarrow 0\rightarrow k\cdot c\xrightarrow{\sim}k\cdot(ba)\rightarrow 0\rightarrow\cdots

which is contractible. On the right hand side, the complex is given by

\cdots\rightarrow k\cdot(lh^{3}g)\xrightarrow{\sim}k\cdot(lh^{2}g)\xrightarrow{0}k\cdot(lhg)\xrightarrow{\sim}k\cdot(lg)\rightarrow 0\rightarrow\cdots

which is also contractible. Thus
F
is a quasi-equivalence.
∎

As a consequence of Lemma
3.46
, we have a fully faithful functor

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes\widetilde{\mathrm{Com}}^{op})}

which sends an object

)

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

to

)

and Lemma

.

Corollary 3.47
.

Assume the dg category
\mathcal{A}
contains a contractible object, e.g.
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is an additive category.
Each object

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}

in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
, where

is acyclic, is isomorphic in
\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Sq})
to an object of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces IA^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\wedge}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\wedge}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\wedge}}

Remark 3.48
.

If
X
and
Z
are already representable dg modules,
then the isomorphism can be chosen such that when restricted to both ends of the squares, the morphisms are identities in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
.

Recall that the homotopy category
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
of 3-term h-complexes over
\mathcal{A}
is defined to be
H^{0}(\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}))
where
\mathcal{B}
is the dg category defined by
3.38.1
.
Then we have a fully faithful functor

F:\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{rep}(\widetilde{\mathrm{Com}},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})

sending a 3-term h-complex over
\mathcal{A}

(3.48.1)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

where
|f|=|j|=0
,
|h|=-1
and
d(f)=0
,
d(j)=0
and
d(h)=-jf
, to the following object in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})

(3.48.2)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{0}^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces IA_{0}^{\wedge}\;\;}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\;\;A_{2}^{\wedge}\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\wedge}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\wedge}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}-h^{\wedge}{,}-d(h^{\wedge}){]}}

Definition 3.49
.

A 3-term h-complex over
\mathcal{A}
given by
3.48.1
is a homotopy (resp. left, resp. right) short exact sequence if the corresponding object
3.48.2
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
is homotopy bicartesian (resp. cartesian, resp. cocartesian).

Let
\mathcal{C}_{dg}^{\leq 0}(k)
be the full dg subcategory of
\mathcal{C}_{dg}(k)
consisting of complexes concentrated in non-positive degrees.
Consider a sequence in
\mathcal{C}_{dg}^{\leq 0}(k)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

where
|f|=|j|=0
,
|h|=-1
and
d(f)=0
,
d(j)=0
and
d(h)=-jf
.
It is a
homotopy left exact sequence
and we say that it is a
homotopy kernel
of
j:V\rightarrow W
, provided that the canonical morphism

U\xrightarrow{[f\;,h]^{\intercal}}\tau_{\leq 0}\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(j)

is a quasi-isomorphism of complexes, or equivalently, for each
n\leq 0
and each pair of elements
(v,w)\in Z^{n}V\times W^{n-1}
such that
d(w)=-j(v)
, there exists an element
u\in Z^{n}U
, unique up to a coboundary, such that there exists a pair of elements
(v^{\prime},w^{\prime})\in V^{n-1}\times W^{n-2}
satisfying
v-f(u)=d(v^{\prime})
,
w-h(u)=-d(w^{\prime})-j(v^{\prime})
.
Then we have

Lemma 3.50
.

A 3-term h-complex given by
3.48.1
is a homotopy left (resp. right) exact sequence if and only if for each object
A
in
\mathcal{A}
, the corresponding 3-term h-complex over
\mathcal{C}_{dg}^{\leq 0}(k)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}(A,A_{0})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}(A,A_{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}(A,A_{2}),}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}{(}A{,}f{)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}{(}A{,}h{)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}{(}A{,}j{)}}

resp.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}(A_{2},A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}(A_{1},A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}(A_{0},A)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}{(}j{,}A{)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}{(}h{,}A{)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}{(}f{,}A{)}}

is a homotopy left exact sequence.
It is a homotopy short exact sequence if and only if both of the above sequences are homotopy left exact.

Recall that for a dg category
\mathcal{A}
, we denote by
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
its pretriangulated hull.
We observe that the dg category
\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
can be seen a non-full dg subcategory of
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
via the dg functor
\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
. On objects
\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}
sends an
A_{\infty}
-functor
F:\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
which corresponds to the diagram
3.38.2
, to the formal sum
(\Sigma^{2}A_{0}\oplus\Sigma A_{1}\oplus A_{0},q)
where
q
is the matrix

\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\
-f&0&0\\
h&-j&0\end{bmatrix}.

Let
d(q)
be the matrix with
d(q)_{ij}=d(q_{ij})
.
Clearly
d(q)+q^{2}=0
.
The dg functor
\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}
sends a morphism which corresponds to the diagram
3.38.3
, to the matrix

\begin{bmatrix}h_{0}&0&0\\
(-1)^{n-1}s_{1}&(-1)^{n}h_{1}&0\\
t&s_{2}&h_{2}\end{bmatrix}.

Since the dg functor
\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}
is not full,
the induced functor
H^{0}(\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}):\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{A})
is neither full nor faithful in general.

For two objects
F
and
F^{\prime}
in
\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
, we use
(F,F^{\prime})
to indicate the morphism complex in
\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
and use
\mathcal{A}(F,F^{\prime})
to indicate the morphism complex in
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
of the objects
\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}(F)
and
\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}(F^{\prime})
.
In the following, we will describe the functor
\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
in more detail.
We assume the dg category
\mathcal{A}
contains a zero object.
Note that
\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}(A_{0}^{0})=\Sigma^{2}A_{0}^{\wedge}
and
\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}(A_{1}^{1})=\Sigma A_{1}^{\wedge}
.

Let
V^{\prime}
and
W
be the following objects in
\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0,}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

Let
M
be the complex

(\Sigma^{2}\mathcal{A}(A_{2}^{\prime},A_{0})\oplus\Sigma\mathcal{A}(A_{1}^{\prime},A_{0})\oplus\Sigma\mathcal{A}(A_{2}^{\prime},A_{1}),d)

where

is of degree

and

and

.

We have the following commutative diagrams in

, which relates the complex

with
\mathcal{A}(F^{\prime},F)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}(A_{1}^{\prime},\Sigma^{-2}A_{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma^{2}(V^{\prime},W)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta}

where

,

and the action of

on the degree

\gamma(\begin{bmatrix}h_{0}^{\prime}&s_{1}&h_{1}\\

t&s_{2}&h_{2}^{\prime}\end{bmatrix})=\begin{bmatrix}h_{1}&s_{1}&(-1)^{n+1}s_{2}\end{bmatrix}.

Let
\mathrm{Filt}_{3}(\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A}))
be the dg category with objects the twisted objects
(Y=\oplus_{i\in I}\Sigma^{n_{i}}Y_{i}^{\wedge},d)
with a 3-step filtration

such that

are dg submodules.
Then we have a localization dg functor
\mathrm{Filt}_{3}(\mathrm{pretr}\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})

which sends an object

to

.
It admits a fully faithful left adjoint
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{Filt}_{3}(\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A}))
which sends a dg module

to

.
Then the totalization dg functor
\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
is the composition of a fully faithful funtor

and the localization dg functor
\mathrm{Filt}_{3}(\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A}))\rightarrow\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
.
Indeed, for each object

, the dg module
\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}(F)
has a natural filtration given by

i(F)=(\mathrm{Tot}_{3}(\mathcal{A}),A_{2}^{\wedge}\subseteq\mathrm{Cone}(j^{\wedge}:A_{1}^{\wedge}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\wedge})\subseteq\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathcal{A}}(F)).

4.
Basic diagram lemmas

4.1.
Homotopy kernels and cokernels

Recall the morphism category
\mathrm{Mor}
defined in subsection
3.2

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}

and the dg category

defined in

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

Definition 4.2
.

By homotopy kernel of an object
j:B\rightarrow C
in
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})
(cf. Example
3.38
), we mean a homotopy left exact squence
X
(cf. Definition
3.49
)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

Sometimes we say
f:A\rightarrow B
or
A
is the homotopy kernel of
j
.

Dually we define the homotopy cokernel of an object in
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})
.

Remark 4.3
.

Assume the dg category
\mathcal{A}
contains a zero object.
An object
f:A\rightarrow B
in
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})
is a homotopy monomorphism if its homotopy kernel is zero, or equivalently, for each
A^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}
, the morphism
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},A)\rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},B)
induces an isomorphism in each negative degree cohomology and an injection in degree zero cohomology. Dually we have the notion of homotopy epimorphism.

A homotopy kernel need not be the homotopy kernel of its homotopy cokernel (if they exist).
Also, a homotopy kernel need not be a homotopy monomorphism.

An object
f:A\rightarrow B
in
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})
is a homotopy monomorphism if and only if the object in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\wedge}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\wedge}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\wedge}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\wedge}}

is a homotopy cartesian square.

In the above definition, we have that
\mathrm{Res}^{\prime}(X)=j
.
Compare Definition
4.2
with Definition
3.21
.
The two definitions are compatible with each other, due to the following observation:

Lemma 4.4
.

Let

Recall that

is defined as

is the dg category defined by

Let us recall the universal property of homotopy left exact sequences.
Suppose we have 3-term h-complexes

and

being homotopy left exact.

extends uniquely to a morphism

in

such that

.
Indeed, we have the following

Lemma 4.5
.

Suppose we have 3-term h-complexes

in
\mathcal{A}
,

,

, of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{i}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j_{i}}

where
X_{2}
is homotopy left exact. Then any morphism in

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}

\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{1}}

Proof.

Put

and

. Then the pair

Since

of degree

such that there exists a pair

where

is a morphism from

to

of degree

,

and

. So the 6-tuple

to

in

∎

Let

be an object in

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

the associated object

in the category

.

.
Then a homotopy kernel of the object

can be identified with a homotopy pullback of the cospan

, the homotopy kernel of an object in

4.6.
Restriction of morphisms in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})

Let
\overline{\mathrm{Sq}}
be the dg
k
-path category of the following graded quiver

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 00}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 01}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 10}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 11}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}

where
f
,
g
,
j
and
k
are closed morphisms of degree
0
and
h
is a morphism
of degree
-1
such that
d(h)=kg-jf
.
The obvious dg functor
\overline{\mathrm{Sq}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Sq}
is a quasi-equivalance and induces an equivalence of categories
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{rep}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})
.
We will transport the definitions and results in the previous sections to objects in
\mathrm{rep}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})
.
One reason for working with this category is that objects in
\mathrm{rep}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})
are isomorphic to objects given by dg functors
F:\overline{\mathrm{Sq}}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
, because the dg category
\overline{\mathrm{Sq}}
is cofibrant.

If we take a span (resp. cospan) of representable dg modules, if its homotopy pushout (resp. pullback) exists, we can assume the homotopy pushout (resp. pullback) restricts to the original span (resp. cospan), and is
not merely isomorphic to it.

Let
f:A\rightarrow B
and
f^{\prime}:A^{\prime}\rightarrow B^{\prime}
be two objects in
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})
.
Then a morphism
\eta:f\rightarrow f^{\prime}
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
gives rise to a class of objects in
\mathrm{rep}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}

which are isomorphic to each other: two homotopic morphisms from
f
to
f^{\prime}
give rise to homotopic dg functors
\overline{\mathrm{Sq}}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}
in the sense of
[
131
, Remark 2.0.12]
.

Lemma 4.7
.

We have a quasi-equivalence

\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Mor}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})).

In particular, we have an epivalence

\mathrm{rep}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Mor},H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))).

Proof.

Recall that we have quasi-equivalences
k\overline{\mathrm{Sq}}\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}k\mathrm{Mor}\otimes k\mathrm{Mor}
and
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(k\mathrm{Mor},\mathcal{A})
.
Then for any small dg category
\mathcal{B}
, we have canonical bijections

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hqe}(\mathcal{B},\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A}))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hqe}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}}\otimes\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hqe}(k\mathrm{Mor}\otimes k\mathrm{Mor}\otimes\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hqe}(\mathcal{B},\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(k\mathrm{Mor},\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})).

Therefore we have a quasi-equivalence

\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(k\mathrm{Mor},\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})).

Thus we have an epivalence

\mathrm{rep}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{rep}(k\mathrm{Mor},\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Dia}}\mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Mor},H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))).

∎

Recall the restriction functors
\mathrm{Res},\mathrm{Res}^{\prime}:\mathrm{Fun}_{\infty}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})
defined before Definition
4.2
.
Suppose we have a morphism

in

of the form

Definition 4.8
.

As above, let

be a morphism in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
.
We call

to

Similarly, we call

to

We have a morphism from the sequence in blue to the mapping triangle of
v
as follows

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V_{3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma V_{3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V_{3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cone}(v)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma V_{3}\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}0\;\;0\\
h_{1}\;\;0\\
-s_{2}\;\;1\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}0\;\;0\;\;0\\
1\;\;0\;\;0\\
0\;\;1\;\;0\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\theta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}0{,}1{]^{\intercal}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}1{,}0{]}}

By direct inspection, we see that
\mathrm{Cone}(v)
is isomorphic to the mapping cone of

\mathrm{Cone}(\mathrm{id}_{\Sigma^{-1}A_{1}})\rightarrow W.

The map
\theta
is the canonical inclusion from
W
to this cone.
One checks directly that the rightmost square commutes and the middle square commutes up to homotopy.

Now we see that the composition of the canonical maps
A_{0}\xrightarrow{[f,h_{0},s_{1}]^{\intercal}}V_{3}
and
v:V_{3}\rightarrow V
is homotopic to the canonical map
A_{0}\rightarrow V
.

(a) Since
X^{\prime}
is homotopy left exact, the map
u^{\prime}:A_{0}^{\prime}\rightarrow V^{\prime}
induces a quasi-isomorphism

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A,\Sigma^{-i}A_{0}^{\prime})\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A,\Sigma^{-i}V^{\prime})

for each
A^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}
.
Thus the induced map

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}(A^{\prime},V_{3})\rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}(A^{\prime},V)

is a quasi-isomorphism for each
A\in\mathcal{A}
.

So
X
is homotopy left exact if and only if
X^{\prime\prime}
is homotopy cartesian.

(b) Put
U_{3}=\mathrm{Cone}((f,h_{0})^{\intercal})
.

Since
X^{\prime\prime}
is homotopy cocartesian, the canonical map
U_{3}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\prime}
induces a quasi-isomorphism

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A_{1}^{\prime},A^{\prime})\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(U_{3},A^{\prime})

for each
A^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}
. This implies that the canonical map
U\rightarrow U^{\prime}
induces a quasi-isomorphism

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(U^{\prime},A^{\prime})\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(U,A^{\prime})

for each
A^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}
. From the rightmost square, we infer that
X
is homotopy right exact if and only if so is
X^{\prime}
.
∎

Corollary 4.10
.

Suppose we have the following diagram in
\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
with lower square being homotopy cartesian and the upper square an object in
\mathrm{rep}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})
.
Then the outer square (i.e. the square on the right hand side) is homotopy cartesian if and only if so is the upper square.

Suppose we have a homotopy pullback square

Corollary 4.11
.

Keep the notations as above.
If we have homotopy pullback squares
X_{2}
and
X_{3}
, then there exists a pair

such that

is also homotopy pullback and that the composition of
X_{1}
and
X_{2}
is homotopic to
X_{3}
viewed as morphisms in
Z^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
.

Consider the morphism

(h,-j,0):M=\mathrm{Cone}(A\xrightarrow{[f,\alpha]^{\intercal}}B\oplus A^{\prime})\rightarrow C.

Since
X^{\prime\prime}
is the homotopy pushout of
S
, we have a morphism
j^{\prime}:B^{\prime}\rightarrow C
such that there exists a graded morphism
(-t,s_{2},h^{\prime}):M\rightarrow C
of degree
-1
such that

d(-t,s_{2},h^{\prime})=(-j^{\prime}s_{1}+h,-j+j^{\prime}h_{1},-j^{\prime}f^{\prime}).

So we have

(-d(t)-h^{\prime}\alpha-s_{2}f,d(s_{2}),d(h^{\prime}))=(-j^{\prime}s_{1}+h,-j+j^{\prime}h_{1},-j^{\prime}f^{\prime}).

Thus we have a morphism
\mu:X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
of the form
4.13.1
where
X^{\prime}
is the 3-term h-complex on the second row.

By Proposition
4.9
, we deduce that
X^{\prime}
is homotopy right exact and that if both
X
and
X^{\prime}
are homotopy short exact sequences, then
X^{\prime\prime}
is homotopy bicartesian.
∎

The following is a direct consequence of Lemma
4.4
and Proposition
4.13
.

We still denote by
X
the associated morphism from
f:A\rightarrow B
to
k:C\rightarrow D
given by the homotopy cartesian square
X
. Then there exists a morphism
\beta:f^{\prime}\rightarrow f
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
such that
X\circ\beta=\alpha
and that
\beta
restricts to
\mathrm{id}_{B}
.

Proof.

Consider the morphism

A^{\prime}\xrightarrow{[f^{\prime},-g^{\prime},s^{\prime}]^{\intercal}}M=\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(B\oplus C\xrightarrow{[j,k]}D).

Since
X
is homotopy cartesian, we have a morphism
r:A^{\prime}\rightarrow A
such that there exists a graded morphism
[u,v,w]^{\intercal}:A^{\prime}\rightarrow M
of degree
-1
such that

d([u,v,w]^{\intercal})=[f,-g,s]^{\intercal}\circ r-[f^{\prime},-g^{\prime},s^{\prime}]^{\intercal}.

So we have
d(u)=fr-f^{\prime}
,
d(v)=g^{\prime}-gr
and
d(w)=-ju-kv+s^{\prime}-sr
.

We have the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}

So we have a morphism
\beta:f^{\prime}\rightarrow f
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
as follows

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

such that the composition of
\beta
with
X
is homotopic to
\alpha
.
∎

If the cospan
L

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}

admits a homotopy pullback, then we have the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{\prime\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{\prime\prime\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\prime}j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\prime}}

where

a)

The left bottom square is a homotopy pullback square.

b)

The sequence on the leftmost column is a homotopy left exact sequence.

c)

The sequence in the middle row is a homotopy left exact sequence which is homotopy short exact if the homotopy pullback of the cospan
L
is homotopy short exact.

d)

The 6-tuple
(\mathrm{id}_{A},w,f^{\prime},s^{\prime},s,t)
is a morphism from the 3-term h-complex in the first column to that in the second column in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
.

e)

We have
h^{\prime\prime\prime}=j^{\prime}s+h^{\prime}v
and the 6-tuple
(v,j,\mathrm{id}_{D},s,0,0)
is a morphism from the 3-term h-complex in the second row to that in the bottom row in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
.

Since the diagram functor
\mathrm{Dia}:H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))\to\mathrm{Mor}(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}))
is an epivalence,
an object
f:A\to B
of
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})
is a homotopy equivalence if and only if
this holds for any object
f^{\prime}:A^{\prime}\to B^{\prime}
such that
\mathrm{Dia}(f)
and
\mathrm{Dia}(f^{\prime})
are
isomorphic in
\mathrm{Mor}(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}))
.
It is direct to verify the following lemma.

of
\mathrm{rep}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})
which is homotopy cartesian.
If the morphism
j
is a homotopy equivalence, then so is the morphism
g
.

5.
Exact dg categories

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a dg category over
k
which is
additive
, i.e.
H^{0}{\mathcal{A}}
is additive.
For convenience, we will assume that
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is an additive category.

For an object
f:A\rightarrow B
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Mor})
, denote by
[f]
its isomorphism class and by
\overline{f}
the corresponding morphism in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
, i.e. the corresponding object in
\mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Mor},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}))
.

Recall that by Lemma
3.12
, the diagram functor
\mathrm{Dia}:\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{Mor})\rightarrow\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}))
is an epivalence.
It restricts to an epivalence
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))\rightarrow\mathrm{Mor}(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}))
.
Therefore if a property of objects in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
is stable under isomorphisms, we will also say that the corresponding objects in
\mathrm{Mor}(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}))
have the same property.
We emphasize that if the object
f:A\rightarrow B
is isomorphic to
f^{\prime}:A^{\prime}\rightarrow B^{\prime}
and
g:B\rightarrow C
is isomorphic to
g^{\prime}:B^{\prime}\rightarrow C^{\prime}
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
, it is not necessarily true that
gf

is isomorphic to
g^{\prime}f^{\prime}
.
But this will not cause confusion because in what follows, we consider objects in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
up to isomorphism.
For example, when we say “compositions of deflations are deflations”,
it means that
gf
is a deflation whenever
g
and
f
are deflations and then
g^{\prime}f^{\prime}
is also a deflation,
although
g^{\prime}f^{\prime}
and
gf
may not be isomorphic.

Definition 5.1
.

An exact structure on
\mathcal{A}
is a class
\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
stable under isomorphisms, consisting of homotopy short exact sequences (called conflations)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

where
i
is called an inflation and
p
is called a deflation, such that the following axioms are satisfied

Ex0

\mathrm{id}_{0}
is a deflation.

Ex1

Compositions of deflations are deflations.

Ex2

Given a deflation
p:B\rightarrow C
and any map
c:C^{\prime}\rightarrow C
in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
, the object

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

admits a homotopy pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

and
{p^{\prime}}
is also a deflation.

\mathrm{Ex}2^{op}

Given an inflation
i:A\rightarrow B
and any map
a:A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
, the object

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}

admits a homotopy pushout

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{\prime}}

and
{i^{\prime}}
is also an inflation.

We call
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
or simply
\mathcal{A}
an exact dg category.

Definition 5.2
.

Let
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
and
(\mathcal{A}^{\prime},\mathcal{S}^{\prime})
be exact dg categories.
A morphism
F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
in
\mathrm{Hqe}
is exact if the induced functor
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
sends objects in
\mathcal{S}
to objects in
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
.
We denote by
\mathrm{Hqe}_{ex}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
the subset of
\mathrm{Hqe}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
consisiting of exact morphisms.

Remark 5.3
.

Note that the class
\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
is stable under isomorphisms.
Let
\overline{\imath}
be a morphism in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.
If a representative
i
of
\overline{\imath}
is an inflation, then any representative in

\overline{\imath}
is also an inflation.
Thus, being an inflation is a property of the morphism
\overline{\imath}
.
We have an even stronger property: If we view
\overline{\imath}:A_{0}\rightarrow A_{1}
as an
object in
\mathrm{Mor}(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}))
, then being an inflation is stable under isomorphisms in
\mathrm{Mor}(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}))
, cf. Lemma
4.4
.

In the setting of Axiom
{\mathrm{Ex}}2
, since the homotopy pullback is unique up to a unique isomorphism
in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
, by Lemma
3.12
, the object
{j^{\prime}}
is unique up to a canonical isomorphism
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
.

Remark 5.4
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be additive dg categories.

a)

By Lemma
3.20
and its dual, the exact dg structures on
\mathcal{A}
are in bijection with the exact structures on
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}
.

b)

Let
F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be a quasi-equivalence of dg categories.
Then
F
induces an equivalence of categories
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
which
preserves and reflects the property of being homotopy short exact.
Thus, the quasi-equivalence
F
induces a bijection between the class of exact dg structures
on
\mathcal{A}
and that on
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

For two objects
C
and
A
in
\mathcal{A}
, consider the set of ‘equivalence classes of extensions’

\mathbb{E}(C,A)
(resp.
\mathbb{E}^{\prime}(FC,FA)
), to be defined in Definition
5.12
, which is associated with the exact structure on
\mathcal{A}
(resp.
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
).
The quasi-equivalence
F
induces a bijection between
\mathbb{E}(C,A)
and
\mathbb{E}^{\prime}(C,A)
, cf. Lemma
5.13
.

c)

Let
\mathcal{A}
be an exact dg category and
\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
be the inclusion of
\mathcal{A}
into its pretriangulated hull.
Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be the additive closure of
\mathcal{A}
in
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
.
Since
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is an additive category, the inclusion of
\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a quasi-equivalence.
By b), we may replace
\mathcal{A}
by
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and assume that the dg category
\mathcal{A}
is such that
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is an additive category.

Note that an object
f:A\rightarrow B
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
is a deflation (resp. an inflation) if and only if it admits a homotopy kernel (resp. homotopy cokernel) (cf. Definition
4.2
) which is a conflation. Observe that homotopy equivalences are both inflations and deflations by axioms
Ex0, Ex2 and Ex
2^{op}
.

Example 5.5
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be an additive category which we consider as a dg category concentrated in degree 0.

Let
A
,
B
and
C
be objects in
\mathcal{A}
and consider a 3-term h-complex
X
in
\mathcal{A}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

Since
\mathcal{A}
is concentrated in degree zero, the homotopy
h
is zero.
By Example
3.18
, the 3-term h-complex
X
is a homotopy short exact sequence if and only if the corresponding sequence
0\rightarrow A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{j}C\rightarrow 0
is a kernel-cokernel pair in the additive category
\mathcal{A}
.
Also, two kernel-cokernel pairs are isomorphic (resp. equivalent) if and only if the corresponding homotopy short exact sequences are isomorphic (resp. equivalent).

By
[
78
, Appendix A]
, the axioms of a Quillen exact structure on
\mathcal{A}
correspond to the axioms of an exact dg structure on
\mathcal{A}
.
Therefore, to endow an additive category
\mathcal{A}
with a Quillen exact structure is the same as to endow
\mathcal{A}
with an exact dg structure.

Example 5.6
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a pretriangulated dg category.
By Remark
5.4
, we may assume that the dg category
\mathcal{A}
is strictly pretriangulated.
Then each morphism
f:A\rightarrow B
admits a homotopy cokernel

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cone}(f).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

Dually, each morphism admits a homotopy kernel.
It is not hard to check that the class of all homotopy short exact sequences in
\mathcal{A}
defines an exact structure on
\mathcal{A}
.
If not stated otherwise, we always consider this maximal exact structure on a pretriangulated dg category.

Example-Definition 5.7
.

A full dg subcategory
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
of an exact dg category
\mathcal{A}
is extension-closed provided that for each conflation in
\mathcal{A}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C,}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

if
A
and
C
belong to
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, then so does
B
.

Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be an extension-closed subcategory of an exact dg category
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
.
Let
X
be a conflation in
\mathcal{A}
with all terms in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
Then
X
can be seen as a 3-term h-complex in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
By Remark
3.15
, the object
X
is a homotopy short exact sequence in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

We have an inclusion functor
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})\hookrightarrow\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
.
Let
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
be the class of objects in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
whose image in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
belongs to
\mathcal{S}
.
We show that the class
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
defines an exact dg structure on
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
Axiom
{\mathrm{Ex}}0
is direct to check.
Axiom
{\mathrm{Ex}}1
follows from Lemma
4.16
and the fact that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is extension-closed in
\mathcal{A}
.
Consider the span
S
of a morphism in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
along an inflation in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
It admits a homotopy pushout in
\mathcal{A}
, and by Proposition
4.13
,
the homotopy pushout
X
is an extension of objects in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and hence remains an object in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
Again by Proposition
4.13
, the pushout of the inflation in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is an inflation in
\mathcal{A}
and
the conflation that this inflation belongs to is in
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
.
Thus Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}2^{op}
is satisfied.
Dually, one checks Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}2
.

Example 5.8
.

We consider a special case of
[
72
, 1.2]
where the torsion pair
\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{X}\perp\mathcal{Y}
is a t-structure.
Let
\mathcal{T}
be an algebraic triangulated category and
\mathcal{S}
a thick subcategory with a t-structure
\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{X}\perp\mathcal{Y}
.
Assume that
\mathcal{T}
has torsion pairs
\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{X}\perp\mathcal{X}^{\perp}={{}^{\perp}\mathcal{Y}}\perp\mathcal{Y}
where
(-)^{\perp}
and
{}^{\perp}(-)
both denote the Hom orthogonal.
Put
\mathcal{Z}=\mathcal{X}^{\perp}\cap{{}^{\perp}\Sigma\mathcal{Y}}
and
\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{T}/\mathcal{S}
.
So we have a sequence of functors
\mathcal{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{T}\xrightarrow{\pi}\mathcal{T}/\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{U}
.
By
[
72
, Theorem 1.1]
, we have that the above composition is an equivalence of
k
-categories
F:\mathcal{Z}\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathcal{U}
.
Indeed, the triangulated structure on
\mathcal{Z}
is canonical and does not depend on the categories
\mathcal{X}
and
\mathcal{Y}
, once we fix a dg enhancement for
\mathcal{T}
.
We denote the dg enhancements of the above categories by adding a subscript
dg
to the notations of the corresponding categories.
In particular, we have that
\mathcal{U}_{dg}
is the dg quotient
\mathcal{T}_{dg}/\mathcal{S}_{dg}
.
Claim: the composition of dg functors
\mathcal{Z}_{dg}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{T}_{dg}\rightarrow\mathcal{U}_{dg}
induces a quasi-equivalence
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{Z}_{dg}\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{U}_{dg}
.
Indeed, let
Z
be an object in
\mathcal{Z}
. Then
\Sigma^{-1}Z
is in the subcategory
\Sigma^{-1}\mathcal{X}^{\perp}\cap{{}^{\perp}\mathcal{Y}}\subseteq\Sigma^{-1}\mathcal{X}^{\perp}\cap{{}^{\perp}\Sigma\mathcal{Y}}
.
We take the triangle of
\Sigma^{-1}Z
associated with the t-structure
\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{X}\perp\mathcal{X}^{\perp}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V\rightarrow\Sigma^{-1}Z\rightarrow Z^{\prime}\rightarrow\Sigma V.}

We see that
Z^{\prime}
is in
\mathcal{Z}
and
F(Z^{\prime})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\Sigma^{-1}F(Z)
.
For
i\geq 0
and
W\in\mathcal{Z}
, we have

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{T}}(Z^{\prime},\Sigma^{-i}W)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{T}}(Z,\Sigma^{-i+1}W).

Therefore by induction we have

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{T}}(Z,\Sigma^{-i+1}W)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{U}}(F(Z),\Sigma^{-i+1}F(W))

for
i\geq 0
.
Since
\mathcal{U}_{dg}
is pretriangulated, we have that
\mathcal{Z}_{dg}
is an exact dg category with conflations given by all homotopy short exact sequences in
\mathcal{Z}_{dg}
.
Note that in general
\mathcal{Z}_{dg}
is not a pretriangulated dg category.

The following diagram lemma is useful.
It is a direct consequence of Lemma
4.15
and Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}2
(or
\mathrm{Ex}2^{op}
).

be a morphism in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
.

(resp.

to

(resp.

).

\alpha
can be written as a composition

and

\overline{a}:A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
and

, and the morphism
\gamma
restricts to
\mathrm{id}_{A^{\prime}}

\overline{c}:C\rightarrow C^{\prime}
.

Remark 5.10
.

If we use the biadditive bifunctor
\mathbb{E}
which is to be defined in
5.15
, then we have
[X^{\prime}]\in\mathbb{E}(C,A^{\prime})
and the morphism
\beta
(resp.
\gamma
) shows that
[\widetilde{X}]=\overline{a}_{*}[X]
(resp.
[\widetilde{X}]=\overline{c}^{*}[X^{\prime}]
).

Combining Lemma
5.9
and Lemma
4.17
, we have

Corollary 5.11
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be an exact dg category.
If a morphism
\alpha:X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
of conflations restricts to homotopy equivalences on both ends, it restricts to a homotopy equivalence between the middle terms.

\theta:X_{1}\rightarrow X_{2}
in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
is called an equivalence if it restricts to
\mathrm{id}_{A}
and
\mathrm{id}_{C}
.

, an equivalence of conflations is necessarily an isomorphism in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
.
For a conflation, we denote by
[X]
the equivalence class to which
X
belongs.

We define
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}(C,A)
to be the set of equivalence classes of conflations

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

with fixed ends
A
and
C
.
When there is no risk of confusion, we will simply denote it by
\mathbb{E}(C,A)
.

Lemma 5.13
.

Let
F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be a quasi-equivalence of dg categories.
Suppose
\mathcal{A}
is an exact dg category.
Equip
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
with the induced exact structure from the quasi-equivalence
F
.
For two objects
C
,
A
in
\mathcal{A}
, consider the sets
\mathbb{E}(C,A)
(resp.
\mathbb{E}^{\prime}(FC,FA)
), which is associated with the exact structure on
\mathcal{A}
(resp.
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
).
The quasi-equivalence
F
induces a bijection

\mathbb{E}(C,A)\rightarrow\mathbb{E}^{\prime}(FC,FA).

Proof.

It is direct to check that the above map is an injection.
We show that it is a surjection.
For an object
X\in\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
, we denote by
FX
the object in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
induced by
F
.

Let
[X^{\prime}]
be an element in
\mathbb{E}^{\prime}(FC,FA)
.
Suppose
X^{\prime}
is of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FA}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FC\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\prime}}

Since
F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a quasi-equivalence, we have a homotopy equivalence
FB\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}B^{\prime}
for some
B\in\mathcal{A}
.
Hence we have an isomorphism in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime}))
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FB}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FC}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FC\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F{(}j{)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\prime}}

By Lemma
4.4
, we may assume
B^{\prime}=FB
and
j^{\prime}=F(j)
for some
j:B\rightarrow C
in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.
The morphism
j:B\rightarrow C
is a deflation.
Suppose its homotopy kernel
Y
is of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{h}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

Then we have an isomorphism
\theta:X^{\prime}\rightarrow FY
in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
which restricts to the identity of
j^{\prime}:FB\rightarrow FC
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime}))
.
Let
\overline{a^{\prime}}:FA^{\prime}\rightarrow FA
be the restriction of
\theta
to
FA
.
Then we have a morphism
a:A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
such that
F(a)
is a homotopy inverse of
a^{\prime}
.
We have an isomorphism in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime}))
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f=\widetilde{f}a}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{f}}

By Lemma
4.4
, we infer that
X^{\prime}
is equivalent to
FX
where
X
is of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

∎

Proposition 5.14
.

Suppose
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
is an exact dg category.
The following statements hold:

a)

The diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\oplus B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}1\ 0{]}^{\intercal}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}0\ 1{]}}

is a conflation for
A,B\in\mathcal{A}
.

b)

If a morphism
g:B\rightarrow C
in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
admits a homotopy kernel and for some
h:B^{\prime}\rightarrow B
the composition
gh:B^{\prime}\rightarrow C
is a deflation, then
g
is a deflation.

b)
{}^{\text{op}}

If a morphism
f:A\rightarrow B
admits a homotopy cokernel and for some
e:B\rightarrow B^{\prime}
the composition
ef:A\rightarrow B^{\prime}
is an inflation, then
f
is an inflation.

c)

The direct sum of two conflations is a conflation.

d)

Axiom
{\mathrm{Ex}1}^{op}
holds.

Observe that the morphism
B_{1}\oplus B_{2}\xrightarrow{r}B_{1}\oplus C_{2}
is a homotopy pullback of the deflation
j_{2}:B_{2}\rightarrow C_{2}
along
B_{1}\oplus C_{2}\rightarrow C_{2}
and hence is a deflation.
Similarly, the morphism
B_{1}\oplus C_{2}\xrightarrow{s}C_{1}\oplus C_{2}
is also a deflation.
So the composition
B_{1}\oplus B_{2}\rightarrow C_{1}\oplus C_{2}
is a deflation.
This proves Statement c).

It remains to prove Axiom
{\mathrm{Ex}1}^{op}
and then one proves b)
op
dually.

Let
f:A\rightarrow B
be an inflation with the homotopy cokernel given by

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

Let
f^{\prime}:B\rightarrow B^{\prime}
be another inflation.
Our aim is to show that the morphism
f^{\prime}f
is also an inflation.

By Axiom
{\mathrm{Ex}2}^{op}
, the span

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

admits a homotopy pushout

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{j}}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{j^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f^{\prime\prime}}}

which is homotopy bicartesian.
Thus by the dual of Claim 1,
the morphism
[{j^{\prime}},{f^{\prime\prime}}]:{B^{\prime}}\oplus{C}\rightarrow{C^{\prime}}
is a deflation.
By the dual of Corollary
4.14
, the morphism
{j^{\prime}}
admits a homotopy kernel which is isomorphic to
f^{\prime}f:A\rightarrow B^{\prime}
.

By Axiom
{\mathrm{Ex}1}
, the morphism
[{j^{\prime}},{f^{\prime\prime}}]\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\
0&{j}\end{bmatrix}
is a deflation.
By the above diagram, the morphism
{j^{\prime}}[1,{f^{\prime}}]
is homotopic to it and hence is also a deflation.
So by Statement b), the morphism
{j^{\prime}}
is a deflation.
Hence the morphism
f^{\prime}f
is an inflation.
This proves Statement d).
∎

By the universal property of homotopy pushouts, cf. Remark
3.24
, there is a unique morphism
\mu
in
\mathrm{rep}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})
from
S_{1}
to
S_{2}
which restricts to
\mathrm{id}_{L}
.
We still denote by
S_{i}
the morphism in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
from
f
to
f_{i}
given by the square
S_{i}
for
i=1
,
2
.
By Lemma
4.7
, the morphism
\mu:S_{1}\rightarrow S_{2}
yields morphisms
\mathrm{id}_{f}
,
S_{1}
,
S_{2}
and a morphism
\alpha
from
f_{1}:A^{\prime}\rightarrow B_{1}
to
f_{2}:A^{\prime}\rightarrow B_{2}
which restricts to
\mathrm{id}_{A^{\prime}}
and such that we have
\alpha\circ S_{1}=S_{2}\circ\mathrm{id}_{f}
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
.
By the universal property of homotopy pushouts, the morphism
\alpha
induces a morphism
\theta_{3}:X_{1}\rightarrow X_{2}
in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
such that we have
\theta_{3}\circ\theta_{1}=\theta_{2}
.
Then the morphism
\theta_{3}
is an equivalence between
X_{1}
and
X_{2}
.
Since
\theta_{3}
is necessarily an isomorphism by Corollary
5.11
, we have that the morphism
\alpha:S_{1}\rightarrow S_{2}
is an isomorphism.
So we have

Lemma 5.16
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be an exact dg category.
Suppose we have a morphism
\alpha:X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
of conflations in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
given by the diagram
4.7.1
.
If the morphism
h_{2}:A_{2}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\prime}
is a homotopy equivalence, then the left square is homotopy bicartesian.

Proposition 5.17
.

The operation
\overline{a}:A\rightarrow A^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{a}_{*}:\mathbb{E}(C,A)\rightarrow\mathbb{E}(C,A^{\prime})
,
where an element
[X]
is sent to
\overline{a}_{*}[X]{\coloneqq}[X^{\prime}]
which is specified by the above mentioned property,
together with its dual operation
\overline{c}:C^{\prime}\rightarrow C\mapsto\overline{c}^{*}:\mathbb{E}(C,A)\rightarrow\mathbb{E}(C^{\prime},A)
,
makes
\mathbb{E}:H^{0}(\mathcal{A})^{op}\times H^{0}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{Set}
into a bifunctor.

Remark 5.18
.

In section
6.16
, we will prove that
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
carries a canonical extriangulated structure in the
sense of Nakaoka–Palu
[
111
]
whose extension bifunctor is
\mathbb{E}

By the definition of
[X_{2}]
, we have a homotopy cartesian square which gives rise to a morphism
\alpha
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
from
j_{2}:E_{2}\rightarrow C^{\prime}
to
j_{1}:E_{1}\rightarrow C
.
We also have a morphism
\beta
from
j_{3}:E_{3}\rightarrow C^{\prime}
to
j_{1}:E_{1}\rightarrow C^{\prime}
.
By Lemma
4.15
, we have a morphism
\gamma
from
j_{3}:E_{3}\rightarrow C^{\prime}
to
j_{2}:E_{2}\rightarrow C^{\prime}
which restricts to
\mathrm{id}_{C^{\prime}}
and such that
\alpha\circ\gamma=\beta
.
The associated diagram in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
is as follows:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E_{3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{f_{3}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\jmath_{3}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{c}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\jmath}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\jmath_{1}}}

By universal property of the homotopy pullbacks (cf. Remark
3.24
), the morphism
\gamma
induces a morphism from
X_{3}
to
X_{2}
.
It clearly restricts to
\overline{a}:A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
.
Therefore
\overline{a}_{*}[X_{3}]=[X_{2}]
.
∎

Our next aim is to show that
\mathbb{E}(C,A)
is an abelian group for each pair
(C,A)
of objects in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
such that
\mathbb{E}:H^{0}(\mathcal{A})^{op}\times H^{0}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{Ab}
is a biadditive bifunctor.
We start by describing the addition operation on
\mathbb{E}(C,A)
.

Let
[X]
and
[X^{\prime}]
be two elements in
\mathbb{E}(C,A)
given by the diagram
5.12.1
.
Put
\overline{a}=[1\ 1]:A\oplus A\rightarrow A
and
\overline{c}=[1\ 1]^{\intercal}:C\rightarrow C\oplus C
. Recall from Proposition
c)
that the direct sum
X\oplus X^{\prime}
is also a conflation.
Then the sum
[X]+[X^{\prime}]
is defined to be
\overline{c}^{*}\overline{a}_{*}[X\oplus X^{\prime}]
.

Lemma 5.19
.

The above addition operation is well-defined, associative and commutative and that the equivalence class of

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\oplus C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}1\\
0\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}0{,}1{]}}

is a zero element.

Proof.

It is direct to check the well-definedness and commutativity.
To show that the above conflation is a zero element, observe that we have the following morphism in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\oplus A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\oplus C\oplus B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C\oplus C}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}0\\
1\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}0{,}\;j{,}\;1{]^{\intercal}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}1{,}\;1{]^{\intercal}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\prime}}

where
f^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\
0&0\\
0&f\end{bmatrix}
,
j^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\
0&0&j\end{bmatrix}
,
h^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\
0&h\end{bmatrix}
,
s=[0,\;h,\;0]^{\intercal}
.

To show the associativity, observe that we have the equality

\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\
0&1\\
0&1\end{bmatrix}\circ\begin{bmatrix}1\\
1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\
1&0\\
0&1\end{bmatrix}\circ\begin{bmatrix}1\\
1\end{bmatrix}:A\rightarrow A\oplus A\oplus A.

∎

Conflations in the equivalence class of zero elements are called
splitting
.

.

The following statements are equivalent:

1)

X
is a splitting conflation.

2)

\overline{f}
is a split monomorphism in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.

2)
{}^{\text{op}}

\overline{\jmath}
is a split epimorphism in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.

Proof.

The implication
1)\Rightarrow 2)
follows from Corollary
5.11
.

We show
2)\Rightarrow 1)
.

Suppose
\overline{f}
is a split monomorphism in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.
Then we have an isomorphism from
A\rightarrow A\oplus C^{\prime}
to
f:A\rightarrow B
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
, which restricts to
\mathrm{id}_{A}
.
So their homotopy cokernels are isomorphic and hence
C^{\prime}
is homotopy equivalent to
C
.
So we have an isomorphism in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
from
f^{\prime}=(1\ 0)^{\intercal}:A\rightarrow A\oplus C
to
f:A\rightarrow B
which restricts to
\mathrm{id}_{A}
.
Then it induces an isomorphism
\alpha
in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\oplus C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}1{,}0{]^{\intercal}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}0\ 1{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

where we have omitted the diagonal morphisms and
h_{0}
is homotopic to
\mathrm{id}_{A}
.
Let
c
be a homotopy inverse of
h_{2}
.
Then the morphism
c
gives rise to a morphism
\beta

Then
[-X]
, where
-X
is of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces-f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces-h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

is an inverse of
[X]
under the addition defined above. So this addition makes
\mathbb{E}(C,A)
into an abelian group.

Proof.

It is direct to check that the element
[-X]
is well-defined.
The following diagram in
\mathcal{A}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\oplus A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\oplus B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C\oplus C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}-1\\
1\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}1\\
1\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}1\\
1\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\prime}}

where the diagonal morphisms are zero and where
f^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}-f&0\\
0&f\end{bmatrix}
,
j^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}j&0\\
0&j\end{bmatrix}
and
h^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}-h&0\\
0&h\end{bmatrix}
, gives a morphism
\alpha:X\rightarrow-X\oplus X
in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
.
We apply Lemma
5.9
to the morphism
\alpha
.

Put
a=(1\ 1):A\oplus A\rightarrow A
,
a^{\prime}=(-1\ 1)^{\intercal}:A\rightarrow A\oplus A
and
c=(1\ 1)^{\intercal}:C\rightarrow C\oplus C
.

Then we have
\alpha=\gamma\circ\beta
where
\beta:X\rightarrow\widetilde{X}
,
\gamma:\widetilde{X}\rightarrow-X\oplus X
and
[\widetilde{X}]=\overline{a^{\prime}}_{*}[X]=\overline{c}^{*}[-X\oplus X]
.

So we have

[X]+[-X]=\overline{a}_{*}\overline{c}^{*}[-X\oplus X]=\overline{a}_{*}[\widetilde{X}]=\overline{a}_{*}\overline{a^{\prime}}_{*}[X]=0_{*}[X]=0.

This shows that
[-X]
is an additive inverse of
[X]
.

∎

Proposition 5.23
.

The bifunctor
\mathbb{E}
is a biadditive bifunctor from
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})^{op}\times H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
to the category
\mathrm{Ab}
of abelian groups.

Proof.

Let
X_{i}
,
i=1
,
2
, be a conflation of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j_{i}}

and
\overline{b}:A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
a morphism in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.

Put
a=(1\ 1):A\oplus A\rightarrow A
,
a^{\prime}=(1\ 1):A^{\prime}\oplus A^{\prime}\rightarrow A^{\prime}
,
c=(1\ 1)^{\intercal}:C\rightarrow C\oplus C
and
d=\begin{bmatrix}b&0\\
0&b\end{bmatrix}:A\oplus A\rightarrow A^{\prime}\oplus A^{\prime}
.

Put
[\widetilde{X_{i}}]=\overline{b}_{*}[X_{i}]
,
i=1,2
.
Then we have
d_{*}[X_{1}\oplus X_{2}]=[\widetilde{X_{1}}\oplus\widetilde{X_{2}}]
.

So we have

\displaystyle\overline{b}_{*}([X_{1}]+[X_{2}])

\displaystyle=\overline{b}_{*}\overline{a}_{*}\overline{c}^{*}[X_{1}\oplus X_{2}]=\overline{a}^{\prime}_{*}\overline{d}_{*}\overline{c}^{*}[X_{1}\oplus X_{2}]

\displaystyle=\overline{a}^{\prime}_{*}\overline{c}^{*}\overline{d}_{*}[X_{1}\oplus X_{2}]=\overline{a}^{\prime}_{*}\overline{c}^{*}[\widetilde{X_{1}}\oplus\widetilde{X_{2}}]

\displaystyle=\widetilde{X_{1}}+\widetilde{X_{2}}=\overline{b}_{*}[X_{1}]+\overline{b}_{*}[X_{2}].

So the map
\overline{b}_{*}
is a morphism of abelian groups.

\displaystyle(\overline{b}_{1}+\overline{b}_{2})_{*}[X]

\displaystyle=\overline{a}^{\prime}_{*}\overline{d}^{\prime}_{*}\overline{a}^{\prime\prime}_{*}[X]=\overline{a}^{\prime}_{*}\overline{d}^{\prime}_{*}\overline{c}^{*}[X\oplus X]

\displaystyle=\overline{a}^{\prime}_{*}\overline{c}^{*}\overline{d}^{\prime}_{*}[X\oplus X]=\overline{a}^{\prime}_{*}\overline{c}^{*}[Y_{1}\oplus Y_{2}]

\displaystyle=Y_{1}+Y_{2}=(\overline{b}_{1})_{*}[X]+(\overline{b}_{2})_{*}[X].

This together with its dual, shows that the bifunctor

For two elements
