5.25.
DG nerve of an exact dg category

In this subsection, we link our notion of exact dg category to Barwick’s notion of exact

\infty
-category
[
8
]
. Standard references for
\infty
-categories are
[
104
,
101
,
23
,
94
,
102
]
.

One of the aims of this section is to prove the following theorem. The construction of
the dg nerve will be recalled in
5.29.1
and the notion of an exact structure on an
\infty
-category
in Definition
5.43
. The notion of exact structure on a dg category is given in Definition
5.1
.

Theorem 5.26
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a dg category such that
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is an additive category.
Then there is a bijection between the class of exact structures on the dg category
\mathcal{A}
and the class of
exact structures on the
\infty
-category
N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.
Moreover, if
\mathcal{A}
is a pretriangulated dg category endowed with the maximal exact structure
(given by all homotopy short exact sequences), then its dg nerve is a stable
\infty
-category
endowed with the maximal exact structure (where each morphism is both an inflation and a deflation).

This extends in particular a theorem by Faonte
[
39
]
, who showed that
if a dg category is pretriangulated, then its dg nerve is a stable
\infty
-category.

We begin by recalling some basic definitions concerning simplicial sets. We follow the treatment in
[
66
]
.
The
simplicial
category
\Delta
is the full subcategory of the category
\mathrm{cat}
of small categories consisting of the totally ordered sets

[n]=\{0,1,\cdots,n\}

for
n\geq 0
.
The simplicial category
\Delta
is generated by the injective morphisms
d^{i}:[n-1]\rightarrow[n]
for
n\geq 1
and
0\leq i\leq n
, where the image of
d^{i}
does not include
i
, and the surjective morphisms

s^{i}:[n]\rightarrow[n-1]
for
0\leq i\leq n-1
, where
s^{i}
identifies
i
and
i+1
.
It is not hard to check that these satisfy the following relations called cosimplicial identities

—

d^{j}d^{i}=d^{i}d^{j-1}
for
i<j
,

—

s^{j}d^{i}=\begin{cases}d^{i}s^{j-1},&(i<j)\\
\mathrm{id},&(i=j\ \text{or}\ j+1)\\
d^{i-1}s^{j},&(i>j+1)\end{cases}

—

s^{j}s^{i}=s^{i-1}s^{j}
for
i>j
.

Moreover, one can show that the category
\Delta
has a presentation given by these generators
and relations, cf.
[
41
, II.2.2]
.
For a category
\mathcal{C}
, the category of
simplicial objects
in
\mathcal{C}
is the
category
\mathrm{Fun}(\Delta^{op},\mathcal{C})
of
\mathcal{C}
-valued presheaves on
\Delta
.
The most important examples are the category
\mathrm{sSet}
of simplicial sets and the
category
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
of simplicial
k
-modules.

For
n\geq 0
, we have the
standard
n
-simplex

\Delta^{n}
defined as the functor
represented by the object
[n]
. For a simplicial set
X
and an integer
n\geq 0
, we write

X_{n}
for the set
X([n])
of
n
-simplices of
X
. Notice that by the Yoneda lemma,
this set identifies with

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{sSet}}(\Delta^{n},X).

Thus, an
n
-simplex
x
of
X
can be viewed as a morphism
x:\Delta^{n}\rightarrow X
.
For a morphism
d^{i}:[n-1]\rightarrow[n]
in
\Delta
, by abuse of notation, we put
d_{i}=X(d^{i}):X_{n}\rightarrow X_{n-1}
, which is a
face map
.
Similarly for a morphism
s^{j}:[n]\rightarrow[n-1]
, we put
s_{j}=X(s^{j}):X_{n-1}\rightarrow X_{n}
, which is a
degeneracy map
.
The set
\pi_{0}(X)
of
connected components
of
X
is defined as the coequalizer of the double arrow

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(X_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{0}).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d_{0}}

This extends to a functor

\pi_{0}:\mathrm{sSet}\rightarrow\mathrm{Set},\;\;X\mapsto\pi_{0}(X).

It admits a right adjoint

\mathrm{const}:\mathrm{Set}\rightarrow\mathrm{sSet},\;\;A\mapsto\mathrm{const}(A)

where
\mathrm{const}(A)
is the constant functor
\Delta^{op}\rightarrow\mathrm{Set}
with value
A
.
So we have the following adjunction

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{sSet}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Set}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{const}}

where
\pi_{0}
is the left adjoint.

The inclusion functor
\Delta\rightarrow\mathrm{cat}
extends to a unique colimit-preserving functor

h(-):\mathrm{sSet}\rightarrow\mathrm{cat}

which associates to each simplicial set
X
its
homotopy category

hX
. It can be described
as the path category of the quiver
(X_{0},X_{1},d_{1},d_{0})
modulo the relations given
by

d_{1}(h)\sim d_{0}(h)\circ d_{2}(h)

for all elements
h\in X_{2}
.
The
nerve functor

N(-):\mathrm{cat}\rightarrow\mathrm{sSet}
is right adjoint to
h(-)
.
More explicitly, for a small category
\mathcal{C}
we have

N(\mathcal{C})_{n}=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{cat}}([n],\mathcal{C})

for each
n\geq 0
. For any
n\geq 0
, the
boundary
of the standard
n
-simplex is

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\partial\Delta^{n}=\bigcup_{E}\Delta^{E}\subset\Delta^{n}}

where
E
runs through the proper full subcategories of
[n]
and
\Delta^{E}
is the nerve
N(E)
.
Similarly, for integers
n\geq 1
and
0\leq k\leq n
, the
k
-th
horn
of
\Delta^{n}
is

\Lambda^{n}_{k}=\bigcup_{k\in E}\Delta^{E}\subset\Delta^{n}

where
E
runs through proper full subcategories of
[n]
which contain the object
k
.
Obviously, we have
\Lambda^{n}_{k}\subsetneq\partial\Delta^{n}\subsetneq\Delta^{n}
.

A simplicial set
X
is an
\infty
-category
provided each map
\Lambda^{n}_{k}\rightarrow X
can be lifted to a map
\Delta^{n}\rightarrow X
along
\Lambda^{n}_{k}\rightarrow\Delta^{n}
whenever
n\geq 2
and
0<k<n
.
It is a
Kan complex
if the same is true whenever
n\geq 2
and
0\leq k\leq n
.

For two simplicial sets
X
and
Y
, their
product

X\times Y
is defined by
(X\times Y)_{n}=X_{n}\times Y_{n}
.
The
mapping
simplicial set
\mathrm{Map}(X,Y)
is defined by putting

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{sSet}}(\Delta^{n},\mathrm{Map}(X,Y))\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{sSet}}(\Delta^{n}\times X,Y)

for each
n\geq 0
.
The simplicial set
\mathrm{Map}(X,Y)
is an
\infty
-category (resp. Kan complex) whenever
Y
is.

Let
\mathcal{E}
be an
\infty
-category.
An element
x\in\mathcal{E}_{0}
is called an
object
or a
vertex
of
\mathcal{E}
.
An element
f\in\mathcal{E}_{1}
is called a
morphism
or an
arrow
of
\mathcal{E}
.
Put
x=d_{1}(f)
and
y=d_{0}(f)
.
We write
f
as
f:x\rightarrow y
and say that
f
is a
morphism from
x
to
y
.
A morphism
f:x\rightarrow y
is an
isomorphism
if it becomes an isomorphism in the homotopy category
h(\mathcal{E})
and in this case, we say that
x
is
isomorphic
to
y
as objects of the
\infty
-category
\mathcal{E}
.
Let
\sigma
be a
2
-simplex in
\mathcal{E}
. Put
f=d_{2}(\sigma)
,
g=d_{0}(\sigma)
and
h=d_{1}(\sigma)
.
Then
\sigma
corresponds to a diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}

which identifies
h
with the
composition

g\circ f
and we shall write
g\circ f\sim h
.
The homotopy category
h\mathcal{E}
can be described alternatively as follows (cf.
[
14
]
, also
[
23
]
): let us fix two objects
x
and
y
in
\mathcal{E}
. We define the following four relations on the set of morphisms of
\mathcal{E}
from
x
to
y
:

f\sim_{1}g
if
f1_{x}\sim g
;

f\sim_{2}g
if
1_{y}f\sim g
;

f\sim_{3}g
if
g1_{x}\sim f
;

f\sim_{4}g
if
1_{y}g\sim f
;

It is a standard result that the above four relations are equal and that they are equivalence relations on the set of morphisms from
x
to
y
in
\mathcal{E}
.

For two objects
x
and
y
in
\mathcal{E}
, put

\mathrm{Hom}_{h^{\prime}\mathcal{E}}(x,y)=\{\text{morphisms from }x\text{ to }y\}/\sim_{1}.

Given a morphism
f:x\rightarrow y
in
\mathcal{E}
, we write
[f]
for its equivalence class in
\mathrm{Hom}_{h^{\prime}\mathcal{E}}(x,y)
.
For any triple of objects
(x,y,z)
in
\mathcal{E}
, the composition map is given by

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}_{h^{\prime}\mathcal{E}}(y,z)\times\mathrm{Hom}_{h^{\prime}\mathcal{E}}(x,y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}_{h^{\prime}\mathcal{E}}(x,z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces({[}g{]},{[}f{]})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}g{]}\circ{[}f{]}}

where
[g]\circ[f]=[h]
whenever
gf\sim h
.
It is standard that this map is well-defined and that the above produces a category
h^{\prime}\mathcal{E}
.
By the universal property of
h\mathcal{E}
, there exists a functor
h\mathcal{E}\rightarrow h^{\prime}\mathcal{E}
which is the
identity on the set of objects.
It is standard that this functor is fully faithful and thus we have a canonical isomorphism of categories
h\mathcal{E}\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}h^{\prime}\mathcal{E}
.

Let
f:X\rightarrow Y
be a morphism of simplicial sets.
It is a
weak homotopy equivalence
provided the induced map
\pi_{0}\mathrm{Map}(Y,K)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\pi_{0}\mathrm{Map}(X,K)
is a bijection for each Kan complex
K
.
The category
\mathrm{sSet}
carries the
Kan-Quillen model structure
whose weak equivalences are the weak homotopy equivalences and whose cofibrations are the injections of simplicial sets.
Fibrations in the Kan-Quillen model structure are called
Kan fibrations
.
The fibrant objects in the Kan-Quillen model structure are exactly the Kan complexes.

The triple
(\mathrm{sSet},\times,\Delta^{0})
is a closed symmetric monoidal model category with the Kan-Quillen model structure, where the internal Hom is given by
\mathrm{Map}
.
A
simplicial category
is a category enriched over
\mathrm{sSet}
.
A simplicial category
\mathcal{C}
is
fibrant
if for each pair
(X,Y)
of objects in
\mathcal{C}
, the Hom simplicial set
\mathcal{C}(X,Y)
is fibrant, i.e. a Kan complex.

Let
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
be two
\infty
-categories. A morphism
f:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
of
\infty
-categories is an
equivalence of
\infty
-categories
if there exists a morphism
g:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
such that
gf
is isomorphic to
\mathrm{id_{\mathcal{C}}}
in the
\infty
-category
\mathrm{Map}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C})
and
fg
is isomorphic to
\mathrm{id_{\mathcal{D}}}
in
\mathrm{Map}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D})
.
The induced functor
h(f):h(\mathcal{C})\rightarrow h(\mathcal{D})
of an equivalence of
\infty
-categories
f:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is in particular an equivalence of categories.

A morphism
f:X\rightarrow Y
of simplicial sets is a
categorical equivalence
provided the induced morphism

\mathrm{Map}(Y,\mathcal{C})\rightarrow\mathrm{Map}(X,\mathcal{C})

is an equivalence of
\infty
-categories for each
\infty
-category
\mathcal{C}
.

\mathrm{sSet}
carries the
Joyal model structure
whose weak equivalences are the
categorical equivalences and whose cofibrations are the injections of simplicial sets.
The fibrant objects in the Joyal model structure are exactly the
\infty
-categories and
the categorical equivalences between
\infty
-categories are exactly the equivalences of
\infty
-categories.
We will write
\mathrm{sSet}_{Quillen}
or
\mathrm{sSet}_{Joyal}
when we want to stress the model structure we are using.
Let
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
be two
\infty
-categories and
f:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
a morphism in
\mathrm{Ho}(\mathrm{sSet}_{Joyal})
.
The morphism
f
yields an isomorphism class of functors
h(\mathcal{C})\rightarrow h(\mathcal{D})
.
In the special case of
\mathcal{C}=\Delta^{0}
, we obtain a canonical bijection

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ho}(\mathrm{sSet}_{Joyal})}(\Delta^{0},\mathcal{D})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Iso}(h(\mathcal{D})).

The triple
(\mathrm{sSet},\times,\Delta^{0})
is a closed symmetric monoidal model category with the Joyal model structure, where the internal Hom is given by
\mathrm{Map}
, cf.
[
76
, Theorem 6.12]
.

Let
K
be a Kan complex and
x,y\in K_{0}
two 0-simplices.
Define
x
to be
homotopic
to
y
, written
x\sim y
, if and only if there is a 1-simplex
z\in K_{1}
such that
d_{1}z=x
and
d_{0}z=y
.
One checks that homotopy of vertices is an equivalence relation and that
\pi_{0}K=K_{0}/\sim
.
If
v
is a vertex of
K
, then one defines
\pi_{0}(K,v)
to be the pointed set
\pi_{0}X
with basepoint the equivalence class
[v]
of
v
.
Let
n>0
and
v\in K_{0}
.
For a simplicial set
X
, we will denote the map
X\rightarrow\Delta^{0}\xrightarrow{v}K
by
v
and refer to it as the
constant map with value
v
.
For example when
X=\Delta^{n}
, we will still denote by
v
the corresponding
n
-simplex in
K
.
Let
F
be the pullback of the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Map}(\Delta^{n},K)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Delta^{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Map}(\partial\Delta^{n},K).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}

It is clear that
F
is a Kan complex. The pointed set
\pi_{0}(F,v)
carries a canonical
group structure, which is abelian for
n\geq 2
. It is called the

nth homotopy group

\pi_{n}(K,v)
of
K
at
v
.

By Whitehead’s theorem, a morphism
f:K\rightarrow K^{\prime}
of Kan complexes is a weak homotopy equivalence if and only if it satisfies the following conditions:

(a)

The map of sets
\pi_{0}(f):\pi_{0}(K)\rightarrow\pi_{0}(K^{\prime})
is a bijection;

(b)

For each vertex
x\in K
with image
y=f(x)\in K^{\prime}
and each
n\geq 1
, the map of homotopy groups
\pi_{n}(f):\pi_{n}(K,x)\rightarrow\pi_{n}(K^{\prime},y)
is an isomorphism.

For each simplicial set
K
, we have the free simplicial
k
-module
FK
generated by
K
so that
(FK)_{n}
is the free
k
-module generated by the set
K_{n}
for each
n\geq 0
and the structure maps are extended from those of
K
by
k
-linearity.
This determines the
free functor

F:\mathrm{sSet}\rightarrow\mathrm{sMod}\,k
.
Let
U
be the forgetful functor
\mathrm{sMod}\,k\rightarrow\mathrm{sSet}
.
For a simplicial
k
-module
X
, the
underlying simplicial set
of
X
is
U(X)
.
Then we have the adjunction

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{sSet}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{sMod}\,k}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U}

where
F
is the left adjoint.

In order to relate dg categories with
\infty
-categories, we need the
Dold-Kan correspondence
(
[
26
]
) as a key ingredient. Note that we are working with cochain complexes.
We denote by
\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
the category of nonpositively graded cochain complexes.

Let
X
be a simplicial
k
-module.
Put

C^{-n}(X)=X_{n}

and

d^{-n}=\sum_{0\leq i\leq n}(-1)^{i}d_{i}:C^{-n}(X)\rightarrow C^{-n+1}(X)

for
n\geq 0
.
The
unnormalized cochain complex

C^{*}(X)
is given by

\cdots\rightarrow C^{-n}(X)\xrightarrow{d^{-n}}C^{-n+1}(X)\rightarrow\cdots C^{-2}(X)\xrightarrow{d^{-2}}C^{-1}(X)\xrightarrow{d^{-1}}C^{0}(X)\rightarrow 0\rightarrow\cdots.

For each
n\geq 0
, put

N^{-n}(X)=\bigcap_{1\leq i\leq n}\mathrm{ker}(d_{i})\subseteq C^{-n}(X)=X_{n}.

The map
d^{-n}
carries
N^{-n}(X)
into
N^{-n+1}(X)
and therefore we obtain the
normalized cochain complex

N^{*}(X)

\cdots\rightarrow N^{-n}(X)\xrightarrow{d^{-n}}N^{-n+1}(X)\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow N^{-2}(X)\xrightarrow{d^{-2}}N^{-1}(X)\xrightarrow{d^{-1}}N^{0}(X)\rightarrow 0\rightarrow\cdots\ .

The assignment
X\mapsto N^{*}(X)
determines the
normalized cochain complex functor

N:\mathrm{sMod}\,k\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
.

Theorem 5.27

(
[
26
]
)
.

The normalized cochain complex functor
N:\mathrm{sMod}\,k\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
is an equivalence of categories.

Its quasi-inverse is the
Dold-Kan construction

DK:\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}\rightarrow\mathrm{sMod}\,k
:
A concrete description of
DK
can be found in
[
101
, Construction 1.2.3.5]
.
The construction of the functor
DK
remains valid if we replace
\mathrm{Mod}\,k
by any additive category and it is an equivalence of categories if the additive category has split retractions (i.e. it is weakly idempotent complete).
In our case, for a complex
V\in\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
, we identify the
k
-module
DK(V)_{n}
with

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{sMod}\,k}(N(F(\Delta^{n})),V)

where
F(\Delta^{n})
is the free simplicial
k
-module generated by
\Delta^{n}
.

The category
\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
carries the
projective model structure
(cf.
[
123
]
and
[
51
, Theorem 1.5]
) such that

—

the weak equivalences are the quasi-isomorphisms of complexes;

—

the cofibrations are the monomorphisms with componentwise projective cokernel;

—

the fibrations are the morphisms which are epimorphisms in strictly negative degrees.

By the Dold-Kan correspondence, this induces a model structure on
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
which is called the
projective model structure
.

Let
f:X\rightarrow Y
be a morphism in
\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
.
We will need the following explicit factorization of
f
into a trivial cofibration followed by a fibration.
For a
k
-module
M
and any
n\leq-1
, denote by
D^{n}(M)
the following complex

\dots\rightarrow 0\rightarrow M^{n}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}M^{n+1}\rightarrow 0\rightarrow\dots

where
M^{n}=M
is in degree
n
and
M^{n+1}=M
is in degree
n+1
.
For each
n\leq-1
, let
u^{n}:Q^{n}\to Y^{n}
be a surjective morphism with projective
Q^{n}
.
Let
P(Y)
be the following contractible complex

\bigoplus_{n\leq-1}D^{n}(Q^{n}).

For each
n\leq-1
, the surjective map
u^{n}:Q^{n}\rightarrow Y^{n}
induces a map
s^{n}:D^{n}(Q^{n})\rightarrow Y
which is surjective in degree
n
.
Let
v:P(Y)\rightarrow Y
be the morphism given by the
s^{n}
,
n\leq-1
.
Clearly
v
is surjective in each strictly negative degree.
Then we have the following factorization of
f

(5.27.1)

X\xrightarrow{g=\begin{bmatrix}1\\
0\end{bmatrix}}X\oplus P(Y)\xrightarrow{h=\begin{bmatrix}f\;\;v\end{bmatrix}}Y.

Here the morphism
g
is a trivial cofibration and
h
is a fibration.
Note that for a complex
Q\in\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
which is componentwise projective, each null-homotopic map
Q\rightarrow Y
factors through the map
v:P(Y)\rightarrow Y
.

Let
f:X\rightarrow Y
be a morphism of simplicial
k
-modules.
By
[
101
, Proposition 1.3.2.11]
, the map
U(f)
is a Kan fibration if and only if the map
N(f)
is a fibration in the projective model structure of
\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
.
In particular, the underlying simplicial set of a simplicial
k
-module is a Kan complex.

For a simplicial
k
-module
X
, the additive operation
X\times X\rightarrow X
,
(x,y)\in X_{n}\times X_{n}\mapsto x+y\in X_{n}
induces a map
\pi_{n}(X,0)\times\pi_{n}(X,0)\rightarrow\pi_{n}(X,0)
for each
n\geq 0
.
This gives an abelian group structure on
\pi_{n}(X,0)
.
The Eckmann-Hilton argument shows that it agrees with the usual group structure on
\pi_{n}(X,0)
for
n>0
.
An element
[\alpha]\in\pi_{n}(X,0)
is an equivalence class of maps
\alpha:\Delta^{n}\rightarrow X
such that
d_{i}(\alpha)=0
for
i=0,\dots,n
.
Such maps
\alpha:\Delta^{n}\rightarrow X
are in bijection with elements in
Z^{-n}N^{*}(X)
.
Unwinding the definition of the equivalence relation, we see that two such maps
\alpha,\beta:\Delta^{n}\rightarrow X
are equivalent if and only if the corresponding elements in
Z^{-n}N^{*}(X)
are cohomologous.
Therefore
\pi_{n}(X,0)
can be identified with
H^{-n}N^{*}(X)
.
Fix a vertex
x\in X_{0}
.
The morphism
\theta_{x}:X\rightarrow X
of simplicial sets, defined by sending
y\in X_{n}
to
x+y\in X_{n}
, induces an isomorphism of pointed sets
\pi_{n}(X,0)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\pi_{n}(X,x)
for
n>0
.

Let
f:X\rightarrow Y
be a morphism of simplicial
k
-modules.
By the above discussions, the map
U(f)
between the underlying simplicial sets
is a weak homotopy equivalence if and only if
N(f):N^{*}(X)\rightarrow N^{*}(Y)
is a weak equivalence in the projective model structure.
Thus, the projective model structure on
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
is the
right transferred model structure

(cf.
[
24
, Section 3]
) from
\mathrm{sSet}_{Quillen}
along
U
.
In particular,
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
is cofibrantly generated and the adjunction

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{sSet}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{sMod}\,k}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U}

is a Quillen adjunction, cf.
[
30
, 9.1]
.

Let
\mathcal{I}
be a small category and
F:\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
a functor.
Since
\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{sMod}\,k
is a simplicial model category (
[
51
, Theorem 4.13]
), one has the local definition of homotopy limits of
F
(
[
128
, Definition 8.2]
).

In general, one also has a nice global definition of homotopy limits of
F
since
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
is a
combinatorial model category
in the sense of Jeff Smith (cf. also
[
104
, A.2.6]
),
and the global and local definitions of homotopy limits coincide (
[
128
, Theorem 8.5]
).

We recall the global definition of homotopy limits and will use it for computation.
We follow Lurie’s treatment as in
[
104
, A.2.8]
.
Let
\mathcal{I}
be a small category and
\mathrm{const}:\mathrm{sMod}\,k\rightarrow\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathrm{sMod}\,k)
the functor sending an object
X\in\mathrm{sMod}\,k
to the constant functor
\mathrm{const}(X):\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathrm{sMod}\,k
with value
X
.
It has a right adjoint
\lim:\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathrm{sMod}\,k)\rightarrow\mathrm{sMod}\,k
sending a functor

F:\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathrm{sMod}\,k
to
\lim F
. Thus we have the following adjunction

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{sMod}\,k}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathrm{sMod}\,k).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{const}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lim}

Since
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
is combinatorial,
\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathrm{sMod}\,k)
carries the
injective model structure
, where

—

A morphism
\alpha:F\rightarrow G
is a weak equivalence if and only if for each
i\in\mathcal{I}
, the map
\alpha_{i}:F(i)\rightarrow G(i)
is a weak equivalence in
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
.

—

A morphism
\alpha:F\rightarrow G
is a cofibration if and only if for each
i\in\mathcal{I}
, the map
\alpha_{i}:F(i)\rightarrow G(i)
is a cofibration in
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
(with the projective model structure).

It follows that
\mathrm{const}:\mathrm{sMod}\,k\rightarrow\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathrm{sMod}\,k)
is a left Quillen functor with respect to the injective model structure on
\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathrm{sMod}\,k)
.
Let
F:\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathrm{sMod}\,k
be an object in
\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathrm{sMod}\,k)
and
A
an object in
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
.
Let
\alpha:\mathrm{const}(A)\rightarrow F
be a natural transformation and
\beta:A\rightarrow\lim F
the corresponding morphism in
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
.
Then
\alpha

exhibits
A
as a homotopy limit of
F
if for some weak equivalence
F\rightarrow F^{\prime}
where
F^{\prime}
is fibrant in
\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathrm{sMod}\,k)
, the composite map
A\rightarrow\lim F\rightarrow\lim F^{\prime}
is a weak equivalence in
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
.

Note that
\mathrm{sSet}_{Quillen}
is also combinatorial.
It is immediate that the right Quillen functor
U:\mathrm{sMod}\,k\rightarrow\mathrm{sSet}
is compatible with homotopy limits.

Example 5.28
.

Let
\mathcal{I}
be the cospan category
\mathrm{Cosp}
defined in subsection
3.2
.
Then an object
F
in
\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}

is fibrant in the injective model structure if and only if both
j
and
k
are fibrations in
\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
.

Thus using the factorization in
5.27.1
, we obtain a fibrant replacement

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y\oplus P(Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\oplus P(Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}j\;\;v\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}k\;\;v\end{bmatrix}}

By diagram chase, we see that the pullback of this diagram is quasi-isomorphic to

\tau_{\leq 0}\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(X\oplus Y\xrightarrow{[k,\;j]}Z).

Take a cofibrant replacement
r:Q\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(X\oplus Y\xrightarrow{[k,j]}Z)
.
Then any null-homotopic map
Q\rightarrow Z
factors through
v:P(Z)\rightarrow Z
.
Thus we obtain a commutative diagram in
\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\oplus P(Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z\mathrlap{.}}

Let
F^{\prime}
be the cospan obtained from the above diagram by restriction.
Then we have a weak equivalence
F\rightarrow F^{\prime}
in
\mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Cosp},\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0})
and the above diagram exhibits
Q
as a homotopy pullback of
F^{\prime}
.

Therefore, a commutative diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}

is homotopy pullback if and only if the canonical map

U\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(X\oplus Y\xrightarrow{[k,\;j]}Z)

is a quasi-isomorphism of connective complexes.

Let
\mathrm{Cat}_{\Delta}
be the category of simplicial categories, i.e. categories which are enriched over
\mathrm{sSet}
.
There is a Quillen equivalence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{sSet}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cat}_{\Delta}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}(-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}

relating Bergner’s model structure on
\mathrm{Cat}_{\Delta}
with
\mathrm{sSet}_{Joyal}
, cf.
[
104
, 1.1.5]
and
[
29
]
for an explicit description of the mapping spaces in
\mathcal{C}(S)
for a general simplicial set
S
.
The functor
N:\mathrm{Cat}_{\Delta}\rightarrow\mathrm{sSet}
is called the
simplicial nerve functor
or
homotopy coherent nerve functor
.
An ordinary category
\mathcal{B}
can be considered as a simplicial category via the functor
\mathrm{const}:\mathrm{Set}\rightarrow\mathrm{sSet}
.
Then the simplicial nerve of
\mathcal{B}
agrees with the ordinary nerve of
\mathcal{B}
.

Example 5.29
.

The simplicial category
\mathcal{C}(\Delta^{2})
has the elements of
\{0,1,2\}
as objects.
The mapping spaces
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}(\Delta^{2})}(0,1)
and
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}(\Delta^{2})}(1,2)
are isomorphic to
\Delta^{0}
.
The mapping space
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}(\Delta^{2})}(0,2)
is isomorphic to
\Delta^{1}
.
The composition map

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}(\Delta^{2})}(1,2)\times\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}(\Delta^{2})}(0,1)\rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}(\Delta^{2})}(0,2)

can be identified with the map
1:\Delta^{0}\rightarrow\Delta^{1}
.

In analogy with the nerve functor
N
taking a small category to an
\infty
-category, there
is a
dg nerve functor
N_{dg}
which turns a small dg category into an
\infty
-category.
A construction is given by Lurie in
[
101
, Construction 1.3.1.6]
using an explicit description of
the
n
-simplices due to Hinich and Schechtman
[
64
, Appendix A2.2]
.
The dg nerve is proved in
[
101
, Proposition 1.3.1.20]
to be a right Quillen functor
in a Quillen adjunction given by a cosimplicial object in
\mathrm{dgcat}
.
The cosimplicial object is made explicit in
[
124
, Section 6]
: it takes
the poset
[n]
to the cobar-bar construction of the associated
k
-category
k[n]
.
To make the Quillen adjunction more precise,
let us endow
\mathrm{dgcat}
with the Dwyer-Kan model structure and

\mathrm{sSet}
with the Joyal model structure. Then the Quillen adjunction is (cf.
[
101
]
)

(5.29.1)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{sSet}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{dgcat}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Lambda}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N_{dg}}

where
N_{dg}
is the right Quillen functor.
In particular, as each small dg category is fibrant in the Dwyer-Kan model structure, the
dg nerve sends quasi-equivalences to equivalences of
\infty
-categories.

Let us describe the functor
\Lambda
in more detail.
For a standard
n
-simplex
\Delta^{n}
, the dg category

\Lambda(\Delta^{n})
is defined as follows: let
Q^{(n)}
be the
graded quiver with vertex set
[n]
and for each chain
I=\{i<p_{1}<\cdots<p_{l}<j\}
with
l\geq 0
an arrow

I:i\rightarrow j

of degree
l
. Then
\Lambda(\Delta^{n})
is the dg
k
-category whose underlying graded category is the free graded
k
-category generated by
Q^{(n)}
with differential given by

d(I)=\sum_{1\leq m\leq l}(-1)^{l-m}(I\backslash\{p_{m}\}-\{p_{m}<\cdots<p_{l}<j\}\circ\{i<p_{1}<\cdots<p_{m}\})

on each chain
I=\{i<p_{1}<\cdots<p_{l}<j\}
.

For a morphism
\sigma:[m]\rightarrow[n]
in
\Delta
, the dg functor
\Lambda(\Delta^{\sigma}):\Lambda(\Delta^{m})\rightarrow\Lambda(\Delta^{n})
is given by

f_{\sigma}(I)=\begin{cases}\sigma(I)&\text{if }\sigma|_{I}\text{ is injective,}\\
\mathrm{id}_{p}&\text{if }I=\{i<j\}\text{ and }\sigma(i)=\sigma(j)=p,\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

We now construct a natural dg functor (cf.
[
95
]
)

\theta_{m,n}:\Lambda(\Delta^{m}\times\Delta^{n})\rightarrow\Lambda(\Delta^{m})\otimes\Lambda(\Delta^{n}).

A
chain
of a finite ordered set is a totally ordered finite subset.
Recall that we have the following presentation of
\Delta^{m}\times\Delta^{n}
(
[
41
, Chapter 2, 5.5]
)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{1\leq i<j\leq\left(\begin{smallmatrix}m+n\\
m\end{smallmatrix}\right)}\Delta^{n_{c{(i)}\cap c{(j)}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{1\leq i\leq\left(\begin{smallmatrix}m+n\\
n\end{smallmatrix}\right)}\Delta^{n_{c{(i)}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Delta^{m}\times\Delta^{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}

where each
c(i)
is a maximal chain of the ordered set
[m]\times[n]
and
n_{c(i)}=m+n
is the length of the chain
c(i)
for each
i
.
The maximal chain
c(i)
corresponds to an
(m,n)
-shuffle, i.e. a strictly increasing map of ordered sets
\sigma^{(i)}:[m+n]\rightarrow[m]\times[n]
.
The chain
c(i)\cap c(j)
corresponds to the equalizer
\mathrm{Eq}_{i,j}
of the maps
\sigma^{(i)}
and
\sigma^{(j)}
.
The maps
u
and
v
then correspond to the inclusion of

\mathrm{Eq}_{i,j}
into
[m+n]
.

For an
(m,n)
-shuffle
\sigma:[m+n]\rightarrow[m]\times[n]
, put
\sigma_{-}:[m+n]\rightarrow[m]
and
\sigma_{+}:[m+n]\rightarrow[n]
the components of
\sigma
, i.e.
\sigma(j)=(\sigma_{-}(j),\sigma_{+}(j))
for
0\leq j\leq m+n
.

Now for each
1\leq i\leq\left(\begin{smallmatrix}m+n\\
n\end{smallmatrix}\right)
define

F_{c(i)}:\Lambda(\Delta^{n_{c(i)}})\rightarrow\Lambda(\Delta^{m})\otimes\Lambda(\Delta^{n})

to be the dg functor given by
\Lambda(\sigma^{(i)}_{-})
and
\Lambda(\sigma^{(i)}_{+})
.
Then by definition
(F_{c(i)})_{1\leq i\leq\left(\begin{smallmatrix}m+n\\
n\end{smallmatrix}\right)}
induces a dg functor

\theta_{m,n}:\Lambda(\Delta^{m}\times\Delta^{n})\rightarrow\Lambda(\Delta^{m})\otimes\Lambda(\Delta^{n}).

It extends by colimit to

\theta_{X,Y}:\Lambda(X\times Y)\rightarrow\Lambda(X)\otimes\Lambda(Y)

for simplicial sets
X
and
Y
.

Proposition 5.30
.

For any pair of simplicial sets
(X,Y)
, the above dg functor
\theta_{X,Y}
is a quasi-equivalence.

This can be proved using the fact that the coherent nerve commutes with products (up to categorical
weak equivalence), which is proved in
[
104
, Corollary 2.2.5.6]
.
We give a direct proof after Lemma
5.36
.
The key ingredient is to express each
\infty
-category as the localization of the nerve of an ordinary category by a subcategory, cf.
[
23
, Proposition 7.3.15]
.

Since right adjoints of monoidal functors preserve internal Homs, we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 5.31

(
[
65
]
, Lemma 5.1)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a small dg category and
X
a simplicial set.
We have an equivalence of
\infty
-categories

\varphi_{X,\mathcal{A}}:N_{dg}(\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\Lambda(X),\mathcal{A}))\rightarrow\mathrm{Map}(X,N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})).

In particular, we have an equivalence of categories

\delta_{X,\mathcal{A}}:\mathrm{rep}(\Lambda(X),\mathcal{A})\rightarrow h(\mathrm{Map}(X,N_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))).

Proof.

Let
Y
be a simplicial set.
Put
\mathcal{H}=\mathrm{Ho}(\mathrm{sSet}_{Joyal})
.
Then by adjunction we have

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{H}}(Y,\mathrm{Map}(X,N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{H}}(Y\times X,N_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Hqe}}(\Lambda(Y\times X),\mathcal{A})

\displaystyle\xleftarrow{\mathrm{Hom}(\theta_{X,Y},\mathcal{A})}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Hqe}}(\Lambda(X)\otimes\Lambda(Y),\mathcal{A})

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Hqe}}(\Lambda(Y),\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\Lambda(X),\mathcal{A}))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{H}}(Y,N_{dg}\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\Lambda(X),\mathcal{A})).

Thus we have a natural isomorphism in
\mathrm{Ho}(\mathrm{sSet}_{Joyal})

N_{dg}(\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\Lambda(X),\mathcal{A}))\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Map}(X,N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})).

∎

We have the following diagram of functors

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k\mbox{-}\mathrm{cat}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{dgcat}_{k}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{cat}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\infty\mbox{-}\mathrm{cat}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N_{dg}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k(-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Lambda}

where
k(-)
is the
k
-linearization functor and
F
is the forgetful functor.
For a
k
-category
\mathcal{C}
, we have an isomorphism of
\infty
-categories
N(F(\mathcal{C}))\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}N_{dg}(\mathcal{C})
.
For a small category
\mathcal{I}
, we have a natural morphism
N(\mathcal{I})\rightarrow N_{dg}(k(\mathcal{I}))
which induces a canonical dg functor
\Lambda(N(\mathcal{I}))\rightarrow k(\mathcal{I})
.

Lemma 5.32
.

The canonical dg functor
\Lambda(N(\mathcal{I}))\rightarrow k\mathcal{I}
is a quasi-equivalence for each small category
\mathcal{I}
.

Proof.

We first consider the special case when
\mathcal{I}
is the path category
P(Q)
of a quiver
Q
.
Recall that
N(\mathcal{I})
is the colimit of the functor
\Delta(N(\mathcal{I}))\rightarrow\mathrm{sSet}
sending
(\Delta^{n},x:\Delta^{n}\rightarrow N(I))
to
\Delta^{n}
(cf.
[
66
, Lemma 3.13]
).
Notice that the full subcategory
\mathcal{J}
of
\Delta(N(\mathcal{I}))
consisting of
n
-simplices of
N(\mathcal{I})

(i_{0}\xrightarrow{\alpha_{0}}i_{1}\xrightarrow{\alpha_{1}}\ldots\xrightarrow{\alpha_{n-1}}i_{n})

where
\alpha_{j}
is an arrow in
Q
for
0\leq j\leq n-1
, is a cofinal subcategory.
Notice also that the morphisms
(\Delta^{n},p)\rightarrow(\Delta^{m},q)
in
\mathcal{J}
are induced by inclusions of paths, i.e.
q
is a part of
p
as a path. Therefore
\Lambda(N(\mathcal{I}))
is the colimit

\mathrm{colim}_{p:\Delta^{n}\rightarrow N(\mathcal{I})}\Lambda(\Delta^{n})

where
p
runs through the paths in
Q
and
n
is the length of
p
.

For any pair of objects
(i,j)
, let
\mathcal{S}_{i,j}
be the set of paths from
i
to
j
. Let
\Lambda^{\prime}
be the dg category whose set of objects is
Q_{0}
and the Hom complex
\mathrm{Hom}_{\Lambda^{\prime}}(i,j)
is given by the complex

\bigoplus_{p\in\mathcal{S}_{i,j}}\mathrm{Hom}_{\Lambda(\Delta^{m})}(0,m)

where
m
is the length of the path
p
.
The composition map

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hom}_{\Lambda(\Delta^{m})}(0,m)\otimes\mathrm{Hom}_{\Lambda(\Delta^{n})}(0,n)\rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\Lambda(\Delta^{m+n})}(0,m+n)

where
m
is the length of a path
p:i\rightarrow j
and
n
is the length of a path
q:j\rightarrow k
, is induced by the composition in the dg category
\Lambda(\Delta^{m+n})
through the morphisms
\sigma:\Delta^{m}\rightarrow\Delta^{m+n}
and
\delta:\Delta^{n}\rightarrow\Delta^{m+n}
, where
\sigma(l)=l
for
0\leq l\leq m
and
\delta(s)=s+m
for
0\leq s\leq n
.

For each path

p:i=p_{0}\rightarrow p_{1}\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow p_{n-1}\rightarrow j=p_{n}

of length
n
, we have a canonical dg functor
\Lambda(\Delta^{n})\rightarrow\Lambda^{\prime}
which sends the object
i
to
p_{i}
for each
0\leq i\leq n
and such that for each pair of objects
(u<v)
in
\Lambda(\Delta^{n})
, the morphism of Hom complexes

\mathrm{Hom}_{\Lambda(\Delta^{n})}(u,v)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hom}_{\Lambda(\Delta^{v-u})}(0,v-u)\rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\Lambda^{\prime}}(p_{u},p_{v}),\\

is the inclusion into the component given by the path

p_{u}\rightarrow p_{u+1}\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow p_{v}.

These dg functors are compatible with morphisms in
\mathcal{J}
.
Therefore we have a canonical dg functor
\Lambda(N(\mathcal{I}))\rightarrow\Lambda^{\prime}
which is full and faithful and which is the identity on objects.
Note that the canonical dg functor
\Lambda(\Delta^{n})\rightarrow k[n]
is a quasi-equivalence.
Therefore the complex
\mathrm{Hom}_{\Lambda(N(\mathcal{I}))}(i,j)
is quasi-isomorphic to
k\mathcal{S}_{i,j}
for each pair
(i,j)
and
\Lambda(N(\mathcal{I}))
is quasi-equivalent to
k\mathcal{I}
.

Now we show the case when
\mathcal{I}
is a general small category.
We consider the adjunction

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Quiv}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{cat}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P(-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(-)}

where the right adjoint
F(-)
is the forgetful functor.
This defines a comonad (cf.
[
107
, Chapter VI, Definition 1]
)
(C=PF,\varepsilon,P\eta F)
in the category
\mathrm{cat}
, where
\eta:\mathrm{id}\rightarrow FP
is the unit of the adjunction and
\varepsilon:PF\rightarrow\mathrm{id}
is the counit.
By
[
141
, 8.6.4]
, for each small category
\mathcal{I}
we have a simplicial object
C(\mathcal{I})
in the category
\mathrm{cat}

where
C(\mathcal{I})_{n}=(C)^{n+1}(\mathcal{I})
together with a morphism
C(\mathcal{I})_{0}=PF(\mathcal{I})\rightarrow\mathcal{I}
given by the counit, which serves as an augmentation.

We apply the
k
-linearization functor
k(-)
and the functor
\Lambda\circ N(-)
to the augmented simplicial object
C(\mathcal{I})
.
By the above, we have that the canonical dg functor
\Lambda N(C(\mathcal{I})_{n})\rightarrow k(C(\mathcal{I})_{n})
is a quasi-equivalence for each
n\geq 0
.
Therefore the canonical dg functor
\Lambda N(\mathcal{I})\rightarrow k(\mathcal{I})
is also a quasi-equivalence.
∎

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a simplicial set and
\mathcal{W}\subset\mathcal{C}
a simplicial subset. Given an
\infty
-category
\mathcal{D}
, we write
\mathrm{Map}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})
for the full subcategory of
\mathrm{Map}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})
which consists of functors
f:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
such that, for any map
u:x\rightarrow y
in
\mathcal{W}
, the induced map
f(u):f(x)\rightarrow f(y)
is invertible in
\mathcal{D}
. In other words, there is a pull-back square of the following form, induced by the opertation of restriction along
\mathcal{W}\subset\mathcal{C}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Map}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Map}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Map}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{W},\mathcal{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Map}(\mathcal{W},\mathcal{D}).}

Definition 5.33

(
[
23
]
, Definition 7.1.2.)
.

A localization of
\mathcal{C}
by
\mathcal{W}
is a functor
\gamma:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{W}^{-1}\mathcal{C}
such that

(i)

\mathcal{W}^{-1}\mathcal{C}
is an
\infty
-category;

(ii)

the functor
\gamma
sends the morphisms of
\mathcal{W}
to invertible morphisms in
\mathcal{W}^{-1}\mathcal{C}
;

(iii)

for any
\infty
-category
\mathcal{D}
, composing with
\gamma
induces an equivalences of
\infty
-categories of the form

(5.33.1)

\mathrm{Map}(\mathcal{W}^{-1}\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\rightarrow\mathrm{Map}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}).

By
[
23
, Proposition 7.1.3]
, the localization of
\mathcal{C}
by
\mathcal{W}
always exists and is essentially unique.
By taking the isomorphism classes of objects of the associated homotopy categories of the
\infty
-categories in
5.33.1
, we see that a localization
\gamma:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{W}^{-1}\mathcal{C}
induces a bijection

\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})

where
\mathcal{H}=\mathrm{Ho}(\mathrm{sSet}_{Joyal})
and
\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})
is the subset of the set of morphisms
\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
in
\mathcal{H}
whose induced functor
h(\mathcal{C})\rightarrow h(\mathcal{D})
send morphisms in
\mathcal{W}
to isomorphisms in
h(\mathcal{D})
.

Definition 5.34

(
[
134
,
135
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a dg category and
S
a subset of morphisms in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.
A morphism
\theta:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow L_{S}\mathcal{A}
in
\mathrm{Hqe}
is a localization of
\mathcal{A}
along
S
if for any
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Hqe}
, the induced morphism

\theta^{*}:\mathrm{Hqe}(L_{S}\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}^{\prime})\rightarrow\mathrm{Hqe}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}^{\prime})

is a bijection onto the subset
\mathrm{Hqe}_{S}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
whose elements are the morphisms
\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
whose induced functor
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow H^{0}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
sends all morphisms in
S
to isomorphisms in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
.

For any dg category
\mathcal{A}
and any set of morphisms
S
in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
, a localization
\mathcal{A}\rightarrow L_{S}(\mathcal{A})
exists in
\mathrm{Hqe}
, cf.
[
135
, 4.3, Proposition 3]
.

Lemma 5.35
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a simplicial set and
\mathcal{W}\subset\mathcal{C}
a simplicial subset.
Let
S\subseteq H^{0}(\Lambda(\mathcal{C}))\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}h(N_{dg}\Lambda(\mathcal{C}))
be the set of morphisms given by the morphisms in
\mathcal{W}
via the canonical functor
\mathcal{C}\rightarrow N_{dg}\Lambda(\mathcal{C})
.
Then we have a canonical quasi-equivalence of dg categories

\Lambda(\mathcal{W}^{-1}\mathcal{C})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}L_{S}\Lambda(\mathcal{C}).

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{B}
be any dg category. Put
\mathcal{H}=\mathrm{Ho}(\mathrm{sSet}_{Joyal})
.
Then we have

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hqe}(\Lambda(\mathcal{W}^{-1}\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{B})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{W}^{-1}\mathcal{C},N_{dg}(\mathcal{B}))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{C},N_{dg}(\mathcal{B}))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hqe}_{S}(\Lambda(\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{B}).

∎

Lemma 5.36

(
[
135
]
, Exercise 25)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}_{1}
and
\mathcal{A}_{2}
be cofibrant dg categories and
S_{1}\subset H^{0}(\mathcal{A}_{1})
and
S_{2}\subset H^{0}(\mathcal{A}_{2})
be two sets of morphisms which contain all the identities. Then we have a canonical quasi-equivalence of dg categories

L_{S_{1}\otimes S_{2}}(\mathcal{A}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{A}_{2})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}L_{S_{1}}\mathcal{A}_{1}\otimes L_{S_{2}}\mathcal{A}_{2}.

Proof.

The subset
S_{1}\otimes S_{2}\subset H^{0}(\mathcal{A}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{A}_{2})
consists of homotopy equivalence classes of
f\otimes g
where
\overline{f}\in S_{1}
and
\overline{g}\in S_{2}
. This is independent of the choice of the representatives
f
and
g
.
Let
\mathcal{B}
be any dg category.
We have

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hqe}(L_{S_{1}\otimes S_{2}}(\mathcal{A}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{A}_{2}),\mathcal{B})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hqe}_{S_{1}\otimes S_{2}}(\mathcal{A}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{A}_{2},\mathcal{B})

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hqe}_{S_{1}}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}_{2},\mathcal{B})_{S_{2}})

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hqe}(L_{S_{1}}\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(L_{S_{2}}\mathcal{A}_{2},\mathcal{B}))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hqe}(L_{S_{1}}\mathcal{A}_{1}\otimes L_{S_{2}}\mathcal{A}_{2},\mathcal{B})

where
\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}_{2},\mathcal{B})_{S_{2}}
is the full dg subcategory of
\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}_{2},\mathcal{B})
consisting of morphisms
\mathcal{A}_{2}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
in
\mathrm{Hqe}
sending morphisms in
S_{2}
to isomorphisms in
H^{0}(\mathcal{B})
.
∎

Similarly, for
\infty
-categories
\mathcal{C}_{1}
and
\mathcal{C}_{2}
, and simplicial subsets
\mathcal{W}_{1}\subset\mathcal{C}_{1}
and
\mathcal{W}_{2}\subset\mathcal{C}_{2}
both of which contain all the identities, we have a canonical equivalence of
\infty
-categories

(\mathcal{W}_{1}\times\mathcal{W}_{2})^{-1}(\mathcal{C}_{1}\times\mathcal{C}_{2})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathcal{W}_{1}^{-1}\mathcal{C}_{1}\times\mathcal{W}_{2}^{-1}\mathcal{C}_{2}.

Proof of Proposition
5.30
.

We may suppose that
X
and
Y
are
\infty
-categories.
By
[
23
, Proposition 7.3.15]
, the
\infty
-category
X
(resp.
Y
) is the localization of the nerve
N(\mathcal{I})
(resp.
N(\mathcal{J})
) of an ordinary category
\mathcal{I}
(resp.
\mathcal{J}
) by a certain simplicial subset
\mathcal{W}\subset N(\mathcal{I})
(resp.
\mathcal{W}^{\prime}\subset N(\mathcal{J})
).

Let
S\subset H^{0}(\Lambda(N(\mathcal{I})))
(resp.
S^{\prime}\subset H^{0}(\Lambda(N(\mathcal{J})))
) be the set of morphisms given by the morphisms in
\mathcal{W}
(resp.
\mathcal{W}^{\prime}
).
Then we have

\displaystyle\Lambda(X\times Y)\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle\Lambda(\mathcal{W}^{-1}N(\mathcal{I})\times W^{\prime-1}N(\mathcal{J}))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle\Lambda((\mathcal{W}\times\mathcal{W}^{\prime})^{-1}N(\mathcal{I})\times N(\mathcal{J}))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow[\sim]{\mathrm{Lemma}\penalty\ \ref{lem:localizationinftydg}}

\displaystyle L_{S\otimes S^{\prime}}\Lambda(N(\mathcal{I})\times N(\mathcal{J}))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow[\sim]{\mathrm{Lemma}\penalty\ \ref{lem:Lambdaklinearization}}

\displaystyle L_{S\otimes S^{\prime}}(k\mathcal{I}\otimes k\mathcal{J})

\displaystyle\xrightarrow[\sim]{\mathrm{Lemma}\penalty\ \ref{lem:dglocalizationtensor}}

\displaystyle L_{S}(k\mathcal{I})\otimes L_{S^{\prime}}(k\mathcal{J})

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle L_{S}(\Lambda(N(\mathcal{I})))\otimes L_{S^{\prime}}(\Lambda(N(\mathcal{J})))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle\Lambda(\mathcal{W}^{-1}N(\mathcal{I}))\otimes\Lambda(\mathcal{W}^{\prime-1}N(\mathcal{J}))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}

\displaystyle\Lambda(X)\otimes\Lambda(Y).

∎

Lemma 5.37
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{A}
is a connective additive dg category and that
S
is a set of morphisms in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
which admits a calculus of left fractions in the sense of
[
41
, Chapter 1, 2.2]
.
Then we have an equivalence of
k
-categories
H^{0}(L_{S}\mathcal{A})\rightarrow H^{0}(\mathcal{A})[S^{-1}]
.

Proof.

We assume that
\mathcal{A}
is cofibrant and strictly connective.
The dg functor
\mathcal{A}\rightarrow H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is universal among morphisms in
\mathrm{Hqe}
from
\mathcal{A}
to dg categories concentrated in degree 0.
Indeed, it follows from the fact that each morphism
\mathcal{B}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}_{2}
in
\mathrm{Hqe}
between dg categories concentrated in degree zero is given by a dg functor
F:\mathcal{B}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}_{2}
.
Note that two dg functors
F,G:\mathcal{B}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}_{2}
give rise to the same morphism in
\mathrm{Hqe}
if and only if they are isomorphic as
k
-linear functors.

Let
\theta:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow L_{S}{\mathcal{A}}
be the localization morphism in
\mathrm{Hqe}
.
By
[
41
, Chapter 1, 3.3]
, the category
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})[S^{-1}]
is additive and the localization functor
u:H^{0}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow H^{0}(\mathcal{A})[S^{-1}]
is an additive functor.
We have the following diagram in
\mathrm{Hqe}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{S}\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}(\mathcal{A})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}(L_{S}\mathcal{A})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}(\mathcal{A})[S^{-1}]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\theta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}(\theta)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}

where
p
and
q
are the projection dg functors.
By the universal property of
\theta
, there exists a morphism
t:L_{S}\mathcal{A}\rightarrow H^{0}(\mathcal{A})[S^{-1}]
such that
t\theta=up
.
By the universal property of
q
, there exists a morphism
r:H^{0}(L_{S}\mathcal{A})\rightarrow H^{0}(\mathcal{A})[S^{-1}]
such that
rq=t
.
By the universal property of
u
, there exists a functor
s:H^{0}(\mathcal{A})[S^{-1}]\rightarrow H^{0}(L_{S}\mathcal{A})
such that
su=H^{0}(\theta)
.
We view
s
as a morphism in
\mathrm{Hqe}
.
Then we have
rsup=rsH^{0}(\theta)=rq\theta=t\theta=up
. It follows that
rsu=u
in
\mathrm{Hqe}
, or equivalently
rsu
is isomorphic to
u
as
k
-linear functors. Therefore
rs
is isomorphic to
\mathrm{id}
as
k
-linear functors, or equivalently as dg functors. Hence
rs=\mathrm{id}
in
\mathrm{Hqe}
.
Similarly we have
srq\theta=st\theta=sup=H^{0}(\theta)p=q\theta
and hence
sr=\mathrm{id}
in
\mathrm{Hqe}
.
∎

Remark 5.38
.

By Corollary
5.31
, we define an
\mathcal{I}
-indexed diagram in
\mathcal{A}
to be an object in
\mathrm{rep}(k(\mathcal{I}),\mathcal{A})
and use it to define homotopy limits in
\mathcal{A}
.
The case for homotopy colimits is completely dual.
For a small category
\mathcal{I}
, let
\mathcal{I}^{\vartriangleleft}
be the join of
*
and
\mathcal{I}
, i.e. the category obtained from
\mathcal{I}
by adding a new object
*
together with a unique map from
*
to each object in
\mathcal{I}
.

to

and similarly for

and

.
Let
M
be an object in
\mathrm{rep}(k\mathcal{I}^{\vartriangleleft},\mathcal{A})
.
Then
M
corresponds to a morphism
F^{*}H^{*}M\rightarrow G^{*}M
in
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}\otimes k(\mathcal{I}^{\vartriangleleft})^{op})
.
By adunction, we have a morphism
H^{*}M\rightarrow F_{*}G^{*}M
.

Let
N
be an object in
\mathrm{rep}(k\mathcal{I},\mathcal{A})
. Then a pair
(M,\theta)
, where
M
is an object in
\mathrm{rep}(k\mathcal{I}^{\vartriangleleft},\mathcal{A})
and
\theta:G^{*}M\rightarrow N
is an isomorphism in
\mathrm{rep}(k\mathcal{I},\mathcal{A})
, is called the homotopy limit of
N
if for each object
A\in\mathcal{A}
, the canonical map

H^{*}M\rightarrow F_{*}G^{*}M\xrightarrow{F_{*}(\theta)}F_{*}N
in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
induces a quasi-isomorphism of complexes

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\wedge},H^{*}M)\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\wedge},F_{*}N).

We are mainly concerned with the case when
X=\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1}
.
The dg category
\Lambda(X)
is the dg
k
-path category given by the graded quiver

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 2}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 3}

,

,

and

.

Lemma 5.39
.

Let
X
be an object of the form (
5.38.1
) where
h_{1}
and
h_{2}
vanish.
Then
X
is a homotopy pullback square if and only if the corresponding object
X^{\prime}
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
is homotopy cartesian in the sense of Definition
3.14
.

We will prove the lemma after Theorem
5.41
below.

To compute homotopy pullbacks/pushouts in the
\infty
-category
N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
, we will need a homotopy equivalent description of the dg nerve functor, which we denote by
N^{big}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
, following
[
39
]
.

The category
\mathrm{sMod}\,k
is a monoidal category with tensor products given by componentwise tensor product of
k
-modules.
We denote this tensor product by
(X,Y)\mapsto X\boxtimes Y
.
The Dold-Kan construction
DK
is a right-lax monoidal functor (in the sense of
[
104
, Definition A.1.3.5]
).
The truncation functor
\tau_{\leq 0}:\mathcal{C}(k)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
and the forgetful functor
F:\mathrm{sMod}\,k\rightarrow\mathrm{sSet}
are also right-lax monoidal.
Thus, by
[
104
, Remark A.1.4.3]
, from a dg
k
-category
\mathcal{A}
, one can produce a simplicial category
s(\mathcal{A})
having the same objects as
\mathcal{A}
and where the simplicial set of morphisms from
x
to
y
is the
underlying simplicial set of the Dold–Kan construction applied to the truncation
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}(x,y)
.
Notice that
s(\mathcal{A})
is locally fibrant in the sense that,
for each pair of objects
x,y
in
\mathcal{A}
, the mapping space
s(\mathcal{A})(x,y)
is a Kan complex.
This implies that
s(\mathcal{A})
is also fibrant as a simplicial category by
[
13
, Theorem 1.1]
.
By
[
104
, Proposition 1.1.5.10]
, the
simplicial nerve
of
s(\mathcal{A})
denoted by

N^{big}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})=N(s(\mathcal{A}))

is an
\infty
-category.

Proposition 5.40

(
[
101
]
, Proposition 1.3.1.17)
.

There is a canonical equivalence of
\infty
-categories
\theta:N^{big}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.

In general, for complexes
U,V\in\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
, the simplicial
k
-module map

DK(U)\boxtimes DK(V)\rightarrow DK(U\otimes V),

which defines the right-lax monoidal structure of the functor
DK
, is not very explicit.
But it is explicit at the level of
0
-simplices and this is enough for our purposes: it sends

f\boxtimes g
to
f\otimes g
.
Also the
k
-module
DK(V)_{1}
can be identified with
V^{-1}\oplus V^{0}
and
DK(V)_{0}
can be identified with
V^{0}
.
The maps
d_{0},d_{1}:DK(V)_{1}\rightarrow DK(V)_{0}
are then identified with maps

d_{0}:(h,k)\mapsto d(h)+k,\;\;d_{1}:(h,k)\mapsto k

where
h\in V^{-1}
and
k\in V^{0}
.
A
2
-simplex of
N^{big}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
can be identified with a simplicial functor
\mathcal{C}(\Delta^{2})\rightarrow s(\mathcal{A})
, which in turn can be identified with a diagram in
\mathcal{A}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

where the morphisms
f
,
g
and
k
are closed of degree
0
, the map
h:A\rightarrow C
is of degree
-1
and
d(h)+k=g\circ f
.

Theorem 5.41

(
[
104
]
, Theorem 4.2.4.1)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{J}
be fibrant simplicial categories and
F:\mathcal{J}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be a simplicial functor.
Suppose we are given an object
C\in\mathcal{C}
and a compatible family of maps
\{\eta_{I}:F(I)\rightarrow C\}_{I\in\mathcal{J}}
.
The following conditions are equivalent:

(1)

The maps
\eta_{I}
exhibit
C
as a homotopy colimit of the diagram
F
.

(2)

Let
f:N(\mathcal{J})\rightarrow N(\mathcal{C})
be the simplicial nerve of
F
and
\overline{f}:N(\mathcal{J})^{\vartriangleright}\rightarrow N(\mathcal{C})
the extension of
f
determined by the maps
\{\eta_{I}\}
.
Then
\overline{f}
is a colimit diagram in
N(\mathcal{C})
.

Then the object
X
restricts to a cospan and this gives rise to a simplicial functor
F:\mathcal{J}\rightarrow s(\mathcal{A})
where
s(\mathcal{A})
is the simplicial category described before Proposition
5.40
.
Since we have
kg=jf
in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
, the morphisms
f:A\rightarrow B
,
g:A\rightarrow C
and
kg:A\rightarrow D
form a compatible family of maps.
Note that
N(\mathcal{J})^{\vartriangleleft}=\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1}
and that
X
is the extension of
N(F)
determined by the family of maps
\{f,\;g,\;kg\}
.
By Theorem
5.41
, the object
X
is a homotopy pullback diagram in
N(s(\mathcal{A}))=N_{dg}^{big}(\mathcal{A})
if and only if for each object
A^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}
, the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(DK(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},A)))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(DK(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},B)))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(DK(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},C)))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(DK(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},D)))}

is homotopy pullback in
\mathrm{sSet}_{Quillen}
.
Note that here we are using the fact that the homotopies
h_{1}
and
h_{2}
in
X
are both zero so that we could apply Theorem
5.41
.
Since both functors
U
and
DK
are right Quillen functors which preserve and reflect weak equivalences, this is equivalent to the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},B)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},C)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},D)}

being homotopy pullback in
\mathcal{C}(k)^{\leq 0}
.
By Example
5.28
, this is equivalent to saying that the map

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},A)\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}((\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},B)\oplus\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},C))\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},D))

is an isomorphism in
\mathcal{D}(k)
.
The complex on the right hand side is quasi-isomorphic to

\tau_{\leq 0}\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},B)\oplus\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},C)\rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime},D))

which is further isomorphic to

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\prime\wedge},\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(B^{\wedge}\oplus C^{\wedge}\rightarrow D^{\wedge})).

Thus
X
is homotopy cartesian in
N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
if and only if the canonical map

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\prime\wedge},A^{\wedge})\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{RHom}(A^{\prime\wedge},\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(B^{\wedge}\oplus C^{\wedge}\rightarrow D^{\wedge}))

is an isomorphism in
\mathcal{D}(k)
for each
A^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}
, i.e. the corresponding object
X^{\prime}
in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq})
is homotopy cartesian in the sense of Definition
3.14
.
∎

Remark 5.42
.

Similarly, for a family of objects
\{A_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}
in
\mathcal{A}
, the homotopy coproduct
is an object
A\in\mathcal{A}
with morphisms
A_{i}\rightarrow A
in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
such that the induced morphism of complexes

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}(A,B)\to\tau_{\leq 0}\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\mathcal{A}(A_{i},B)

is a quasi-isomorphism of complexes for each
B\in\mathcal{A}
.
In particular, if the morphisms
A_{i}\rightarrow A
in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
yield a direct sum in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
, then they form a homotopy coproduct. The dual assertion also holds.

The notion of exact
\infty
-category was introduced by Barwick in
[
8
]
as a homotopy-theoretic
generalization of Quillen’s notion of exact category. Here we adopt a reformulation of Barwick’s
axioms due to Jasso.
Recall that an
\infty
-category that admits finite products and finite coproducts is defined to be
additive
if its homotopy
category is additive, cf.
[
8
, Definition 2.2]
, also
[
49
, Definition 2.6]
.

Definition 5.43
.

Let
\mathcal{E}
be an additive
\infty
-category.
An exact structure on
\mathcal{E}
is a class
\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathrm{Map}(\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1},\mathcal{E})
stable under isomorphisms, consisting of bicartesian squares (called admissible sequences)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

where
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
is called an inflation and
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
is called a deflation, such that the following axioms are satisfied

E0

For any
x\in\mathcal{E}
,
1_{x}:x\rightarrow x
is both an inflation and a deflation.

E1

Compositions of deflations (resp. inflations) are deflations (resp. inflations).

E2

Given a deflation
p:y\rightarrow z
and any map
g:z^{\prime}\rightarrow z
in
\mathcal{E}
, there exists a homotopy pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{y^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{z^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

and
{q}
is also a deflation;

E
2^{op}

Given an inflation
i:x\rightarrow y
and any map
f:x\rightarrow x^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{E}
, there exists a homotopy pushout

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{x}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{x^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{y^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

and
{j}
is also an inflation.

Recall that a
subcategory
of an
\infty
-category
\mathcal{E}
is a simplicial subset
\mathcal{E}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{E}
such that for some subcategory

h(\mathcal{E})^{\prime}
of the homotopy category
h(\mathcal{E})
, the square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{E}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N(h\mathcal{E})^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N(h\mathcal{E})}

is a pullback diagram of simplicial sets, cf.
[
104
, 1.2.11]
.

Lemma 5.44
.

The above definition of exact
\infty
-category is equivalent to Barwick’s.
More precisely, the assignment sending an exact structure
\mathcal{S}
to the pair of subcategories
(\mathcal{E}_{{\dagger}},\mathcal{E}^{{\dagger}})
, where
\mathcal{E}_{{\dagger}}
is the subcategory of inflations and
\mathcal{E}^{{\dagger}}
is the subcategory of deflations, gives a bijection between the class of exact structures in the sense of Definition
5.43
and the class of exact structures in the sense of Barwick
[
8
, Definition 3.1]
.

Proof.

To show that the pair
(\mathcal{E}_{{\dagger}},\mathcal{E}^{{\dagger}})
forms an exact structure in the sense of Barwick,
we need to show that in a homotopy pullback square
X
in
\mathcal{E}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{y^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{z^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

where
p
is a deflation and
g
is an inflation, the square is homotopy bicartesian and the morphism
h
is an inflation.
By Axiom
\rm{E}2
, the morphism
q
is also a deflation and hence the homotopy fiber of
q
is homotopy bicartesian.
So the above square
X
is homotopy bicartesian.
The homotopy cofiber of
h
is a composition of
p
and the homotopy cofiber of
g
and hence is a deflation.
Therefore the morphism
h
is an inflation.

Conversely, suppose we are given a pair of full subcategories
(\mathcal{E}_{{\dagger}},\mathcal{E}^{{\dagger}})
defining an exact structure in the sense of Barwick.
We call morphisms in
\mathcal{E}_{{\dagger}}
(resp.
\mathcal{E}^{{\dagger}}
) inflations (resp. deflations).
Consider a square in
\mathcal{E}

(5.44.1)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

If
i
is an inflation and the square is a pushout, then by Barwick’s axioms, the square is homotopy bicartesian and
p
is a deflation since the morphism
x\rightarrow 0
is a deflation.
Dually, if
p
is a deflation and the square is a pullback, then the square is homotopy bicartesian and
i
is an inflation since the morphism
0\rightarrow z
is an inflation.
So the class
\mathcal{S}
of homotopy bicartesian squares (
5.44.1
), where
i
is an inflation and
p
is a deflation, defines an exact structure on
\mathcal{E}
in the sense of Definition
5.43
.
∎

Proof of Theorem
5.26
.

The
\infty
-category
N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
is an additive
\infty
-category if and only if
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is an additive category.
From now on, we may assume that
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is an additive category.
Note that the dg nerve functor
N_{dg}
sends quasi-equivalences to equivalences of
\infty
-categories and
that there is a bijection between the classes of exact
\infty
-structures on two equivalent exact
\infty
-categories.
The inclusion of
\mathcal{A}
into its additive closure
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
in
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
is a quasi-equivalence.
Hence we may replace
\mathcal{A}
by
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and assume that
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is additive and that
\mathcal{A}
has contractible pre-covers and contractible pre-envelopes.
Then any object in
\mathrm{Map}(\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1},N_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))
is isomorphic to an object of the form in Lemma
5.39

and similarly for objects in
\mathrm{rep}_{dg}(\Lambda(\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1}),\mathcal{A})
.

By Corollary
5.31
and Lemma
5.39
, the equivalence of categories

\delta=\delta_{\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1},\mathcal{A}}:\mathrm{rep}(\Lambda(\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1}),\mathcal{A})\rightarrow h(\mathrm{Map}(\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1},N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})))

induces a bijection between the classes of homotopy pullback squares.
Dually, it induces a bijection between the classes of homotopy pushout squares and hence also a bijection between the classes of homotopy bicartesian squares.

Recall that we have a fully faithful functor
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{rep}(\Lambda(\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1}),\mathcal{A})
. Its composition with
\delta
sends a 3-term h-complex

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

to the object in
\mathrm{Map}(\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1},N_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces IA}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}-h{,}\;-d(h){]}}

where
i:A\rightarrow IA=\mathrm{Cone}(\mathrm{id}_{A})
is the canonical inclusion.

Let
\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
be an exact dg structure on
\mathcal{A}
and let
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathrm{Map}(\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1},N_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))
be the corresponding class of objects which is closed under isomorphisms.
By the above discussion, the class
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
consists of homotopy bicartesian squares.
Let us check the axioms
\rm{E0}
–
\rm{E2}^{op}
for the class
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
.
Note that a morphism in
N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
is identified with a morphism in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
and that the class of inflations in
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
is stable under isomorphisms in
\mathrm{Map}(\Delta^{1},N_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))
.
Axiom E0 follows from Proposition
5.14
.
Suppose we have inflations
f:A\rightarrow B
and
g:B\rightarrow C
and a
2
-simplex

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

in
N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
where
j-gf=d(h)
.
If we view
f
and
g
as objects in
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})
, then they are inflations in
\mathcal{S}
and so is
gf
.
Since
j
is isomorphic to
gf
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
, the morphism
j
is also an inflation in
\mathcal{S}
and hence is an inflation in
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
by definition.
This proves that inflations are stable under compositions in
N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.
Dually one proves that deflations are stable under compositions and this shows Axiom
\rm{E1}
.
Suppose we are in the context of Axiom
\rm{E2}
.
So we have a deflation
j:B\rightarrow C
in
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
and a morphism
g:C^{\prime}\rightarrow C
in
N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.
Then the morphism
j
is also an inflation in
\mathcal{S}
.
Thus by Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}2
for the class
\mathcal{S}
, the cospan

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

admits a homotopy pullback and the homotopy pullback of
j
remains a deflation.
Thus the image of this homotopy pullback in
\mathrm{Map}(\Delta^{1}\times\Delta^{1},N_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))
under the functor
\delta
provides the required homotopy pullback. This proves Axiom
\rm{E2}
.
Dually one shows Axiom
\rm{E2}^{op}
for
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
.
Therefore the class
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
defines an exact
\infty
-structure on
N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.

Similarly, we show that the class
\mathcal{S}
defines an exact dg structure on
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
if it corresponds to a class
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
which defines an exact
\infty
-structure on
N_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.
∎

6.
Embedding theorem for connective exact dg categories

Throughout this section, let
\mathcal{A}
be an exact dg category.
By Remark
5.4
, we may assume that
\mathcal{A}
has cofibrant Hom complexes.
One of the main aims of this section is to show the following theorem.

Theorem 6.1
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be an exact dg category.
There exists a universal exact morphism
F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
in
\mathrm{Hqe}
from
\mathcal{A}
to a pretriangulated dg category
\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.

If
\mathcal{A}
is connective, this morphism satisfies:

1)

It induces a quasi-equivalence from
\tau_{\leq 0}{\mathcal{A}}
to
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
for an extension-closed dg subcategory
\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
of
\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.

2)

It induces a natural bijection
\mathbb{E}(C,A)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Ext}^{1}_{\mathcal{D}^{b}(\mathcal{A})}(FC,FA)
for each pair of objects
C,A
in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
where
\mathcal{D}^{b}(\mathcal{A})=H^{0}(\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))
.

We call
\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
the bounded dg derived category of
\mathcal{A}
.

Example 6.2
.

If
\mathcal{A}
is a Quillen exact category, then
\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
is quasi-equivalent to the canonical dg enhancement of the bounded derived category of
\mathcal{A}
, whence the name.

Remark 6.3
.

The analogous theorem for exact
\infty
-categories in the sense of Barwick is
due to Klemenc
[
91
]
.

Construction of the universal morphism

\mathcal{N}
be the full triangulated subcategory of

of conflations

We show that

is universal.
Let
G:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
be an exact morphism in
\mathrm{Hqe}
from
\mathcal{A}
to a pretriangulated dg category
\mathcal{B}
.
By the universal property of
\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
, there exists a unique morphism from
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
to
\mathcal{B}
in
\mathrm{Hqe}
which extends
G
.
Since
G
is an exact morphism,
H^{0}(G)
sends the totalization
N
of
X
to a zero object in
H^{0}(\mathcal{B})
.
By the universal property of Drinfeld dg quotient
[
131
]
, there exists a unique morphism in

\mathrm{Hqe}
from
\mathrm{pretr}(A)/\mathcal{N}_{dg}
to
\mathcal{B}
.
∎

Denote by
\mathcal{H}
the heart of the canonical t-structure
(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\leq 0},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\geq 0})
, cf. Lemma
3.4
. We denote by
H^{0}:\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
the associated homological functor.

Lemma 6.6
.

A 3-term h-complex

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

is exact if and only if its totalization
N
lies in
\mathcal{H}
. In this case, the totalization
N
is the cokernel of
H^{0}(B^{\wedge})\xrightarrow{H^{0}(j^{\wedge})}H^{0}(C^{\wedge})
in
\mathcal{H}
.

Proof.

Consider the diagram (

★

‣
6.4
).
For
A^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}
and
i\leq 0
, we have

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})}(A^{\prime\wedge},\Sigma^{i}A)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})}(A^{\prime\wedge},\Sigma^{i}V)

and so we have
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})}(A^{\prime\wedge},\Sigma^{i-1}N)=0
and hence
N\in\mathcal{D}^{\geq 0}
.

Since representable dg modules lie in
\mathcal{D}^{\leq 0}
, it is clear from the construction that
N\in\mathcal{D}^{\leq 0}
.
Therefore we have
N\in\mathcal{H}
.

From the rightmost column of the diagram (

★

‣
6.4
), we have
H^{1}(V)\xrightarrow{\sim}N
.

From the second row we have an exact sequence where we omit the symbol
{\wedge}
for representable dg modules.

Remark 6.7
.

We have an exact sequence in
\mathcal{H}:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}(B)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}(C)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}(\overline{\jmath})}

where, with the notations of (

★

‣
6.4
), the image of
H^{0}(j)
is
H^{0}(U)
.
Using the extriangulated category
(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
defined in subsection
6.16
, this is equivalent to saying that
N
is the defect (cf. Definition
6.58
) of the conflation

A\xrightarrow{\overline{f}}B\xrightarrow{\overline{\jmath}}C

in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.

Definition 6.8
.

Let
\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{H}
be the essential image of
\mathcal{N}
under the homological functor
H^{0}:\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
.
An object in
\mathcal{H}
is defective, if it is the cokernel of a map

H^{0}(B)\xrightarrow{H^{0}(\overline{\jmath})}H^{0}(C)\>,\;

where
j
is a deflation, or equivalently if it is the totalization of some conflation.

Let
X_{i}
,
i=1,2
, be homotopy short exact sequences

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j_{i}}

and
\alpha:X_{1}\rightarrow X_{2}
a morphism of
{\mathcal{H}}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
. Let

X_{3}
be the object

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}

of
\mathrm{rep}(\overline{\mathrm{Sq}},\mathcal{A})
obtained by restricting a representative of
\alpha
.
Notice that by Lemma
4.7
, up to (non canonical) isomorphism,
the object
X_{3}
is independent of the choice of representative.
Suppose that
\alpha
restricts to an isomorphism
C_{1}\rightarrow C_{2}
in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.
Then
X_{3}
is homotopy cartesian by Proposition
4.9
.
Let
N_{i}
be the totalization of
X_{i}
for
i=1
,
2
,
3
.

Lemma 6.9
.

a)

There exists a triangle in
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})

N_{3}\rightarrow N_{1}\rightarrow N_{2}\rightarrow\Sigma N_{3}

b)

If
X_{1}
is a conflation, the triangle in a) induces a short exact sequence in
\mathcal{H}

0\rightarrow N_{3}\rightarrow N_{1}\xrightarrow{g}N_{2}\rightarrow 0

where
g
is the morphism induced by
\alpha
.

Notice that if
X_{1}
is a conflation, then
X_{2}
is a conflation by the dual of Proposition
5.14
b)
and hence
X_{3}
is homotopy bicartesian by Lemma
5.16
.

6.10.
The canonical t-structure on the category
\mathcal{N}

In the rest of this section, we keep the assumption that
\mathcal{A}
is connective. In this case, we have

—

The left aisle
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\leq 0}
is formed by those dg modules whose cohomology is concentrated in non-positive degrees.

—

The heart
\mathcal{H}
of the t-structure
(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\leq 0},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\geq 0})
is equivalent to
\mathrm{Mod}\,H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
and the cohomological functor
H^{0}
sends a dg module
M
to
H^{0}(M):A\mapsto H^{0}(M(A))
.

—

In particular
H^{0}
is fully faithful on the full subcategory of quasi-representable dg modules and
H^{0}(M)
is projective in the heart for each quasi-representable dg module
M
.

Recall that a full subcategory of an abelian category is
wide
if it is stable under extensions,
kernels and cokernels. In particular, each wide subcategory is abelian and its inclusion is fully
faithful and fully exact.

Lemma 6.11
.

The full subcategory of
\mathcal{H}
, consisting of defective objects (cf. Definition
6.8
), is a wide subcategoy.

Corollary 6.12
.

An object in
\mathcal{H}
lies in
\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}
(cf. Definition
6.8
) if and only if it is defective. The t-structure
(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\leq 0},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})^{\geq 0})
on
\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A})
restricts to a bounded t-structure on
\mathcal{N}
.

Proof of the Corollary.

Let
\mathcal{N}^{\prime}
be the full subcategory of
\mathcal{N}
consisting of objects
N
such that
H^{i}(N)
is defective for each
i\in\mathbb{Z}
and only finitely many of them are nonzero.
By Lemma
6.11
, this is a triangulated subcategory of
\mathcal{N}
. It certainly contains totalizations of conflations and thus is equal to
\mathcal{N}
.
Therefore the objects
N
in
\mathcal{N}
have the property that
H^{i}(N)
is defective for each
i\in\mathbb{Z}
and only finitely many of them is nonzero.
∎

Proof of Lemma
6.11
.

Denote by
\overline{\mathcal{N}}
the full subcategory of
\mathcal{H}
consisting of defective objects. Consider a
three-term complex

(6.12.1)

\displaystyle P\rightarrow Q\rightarrow R

in
\mathrm{Mod}\,H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
which is exact in the middle.

We first show that
\overline{\mathcal{N}}
is closed under extensions.
Assume the sequence
6.12.1
is a short exact sequence with
P
and
R
defective.
Suppose
P
and
R
are totalizations of
X_{1}
and
X_{2}
respectively, where

,

, is of the form

Remark 6.13
.

The proof of Lemma
6.11
only uses the axioms
{\mathrm{Ex}0}
,
{\mathrm{Ex}1}
and
{\mathrm{Ex}2}
and Proposition
5.14

(b)
.
So a similar result holds for a left exact dg category, cf. Definition
7.1
.

Example 6.14
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{A}
is an idempotent complete Quillen exact category endowed with the associated exact dg structure. We claim that then
\mathcal{N}
is the category
\mathrm{Ac}^{b}(\mathcal{A})
of acyclic complexes over
\mathcal{A}
, cf.
[
114
]
, and that the t-structure given in Corollary
6.12
is the one described in [loc. cit.].
Indeed, as usual, we identify
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
with
\mathcal{C}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
. Then the totalization of a conflation which corresponds to the following sequence in
\mathcal{A}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

is identified with the complex

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

where
A
is in degree 0.
By definition,
\mathcal{N}
is the full triangulated subcategory of
\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{A})
generated by the totalizations of conflations.
So
\mathcal{N}
is identified with
\rm{Ac}^{b}(\mathcal{A})
.
By Corollary
6.12
, we have

\mathcal{N}^{\leq 0}=\{N\in\mathcal{N}{|}H^{i}N=0\text{ for i $\geq 1$}\}

and

\mathcal{N}^{\geq 0}=\{N\in\mathcal{N}{|}H^{i}N=0\text{ for i $\leq-1$}\}

It is clear that
\rm{Ac}^{b}(\mathcal{A})^{\leq 2}
is contained in
\mathcal{N}^{\leq 0}
and
\rm{Ac}^{b}(\mathcal{A})^{\geq 2}
is contained in
\mathcal{N}^{\geq 0}
. Thus the two t-structures coincide.

The following lemma is standard.

Lemma 6.15

(
[
72
]
, Lemma 3.3)
.

Let
T
be a triangulated category with a thick subcategory
\mathcal{S}
.
Suppose that
\mathcal{S}
admits a torsion pair (
[
73
, Definition 2.2]
)
\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})
.
Put
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{X}\cap\Sigma^{-1}\mathcal{Y}
.
Then for any
A\in{{}^{\perp}\mathcal{Y}}
and
B\in\Sigma^{-1}\mathcal{X}^{\perp}
, where the symbol
⟂
stands for the Hom orthogonal, the canonical map

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{T}/[\mathcal{P}]}(A,B)\rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{T}/\mathcal{S}}(A,B)

is a bijection.

In the above lemma, we have
\mathcal{P}=0
when
\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})
is in particular a t-structure.

Proof of Theorem
6.1
.

By construction, the dg category

.
