Since the essential image of the inclusion
\tau_{\leq 0}{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{C})
is extension-closed, the conclusion follows immediately.
∎

Corollary 6.52
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
be small connective exact dg categories. Let
\mathcal{C}
be a small exact dg category.
Then we have the following natural bijection

\mathrm{Hqe}_{ex}(\mathcal{A}\boxtimes\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hqe}_{ex}(\mathcal{A},\mathrm{rep}_{dg}^{ex}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})).

Proof.

The required bijection follows from the following composition of bijections

\mathrm{Hqe}_{ex}(\mathcal{A}\boxtimes\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hqe}_{biexact}(\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\mathrm{Hqe}_{ex}(\mathcal{A},\mathrm{rep}_{dg}^{ex}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})).

∎

Corollary 6.53
.

Keep the same assumptions as above.
We have the following quasi-equivalence of exact dg categories

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{rep}^{ex}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}\boxtimes\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{rep}^{ex}_{dg}(\mathcal{A},\mathrm{rep}_{dg}^{ex}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})).

6.54.
Subcategories, closed subbifunctors and exact dg substructures

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
be an extriangulated category.

Definition 6.55

(
[
111
]
, Definition 2.17)
.

Let
\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{C}
be a full additive subcategory, closed under isomorphisms.
The subcategory
\mathcal{D}
is extension-closed if, for any conflation

A\rightarrow B\rightarrow C

which satisfies
A,C\in\mathcal{D}
, we have
B\in\mathcal{D}
.

Definition 6.56

(
[
63
]
, Lemma 3.15)
.

Let
\mathbb{F}\subseteq\mathbb{E}
be an additive subbifunctor. The following are equivalent.

(1)

\mathbb{F}
is closed on the right, i.e. for any
\mathfrak{s}|_{\mathbb{F}}
-conflation
A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{j}C
, the sequence

\mathbb{F}(-,C)\xRightarrow{f_{*}}\mathbb{F}(-,B)\xRightarrow{j_{*}}\mathbb{F}(-,A)

is exact.

(2)

\mathbb{F}
is closed on the left, i.e. for any
\mathfrak{s}|_{\mathbb{F}}
-conflation
A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{j}C
, the sequence

\mathbb{F}(A,-)\xRightarrow{j^{*}}\mathbb{F}(B,-)\xRightarrow{f^{*}}\mathbb{F}(C,-)

is exact.

Thus, we simply say
\mathbb{F}\subseteq\mathbb{E}
is closed, if either of the conditions is satisfied.

Proposition 6.57

(
[
63
]
, Proposition 3.16)
.

For any additive subbifunctor
\mathbb{F}\subseteq\mathbb{E}
, the following are equivalent.

(1)

(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{F},\mathfrak{s}|_{\mathbb{F}})
is extriangulated.

(2)

\mathfrak{s}|_{\mathbb{F}}
-inflations are closed under composition.

(3)

\mathfrak{s}|_{\mathbb{F}}
-deflations are closed under composition.

(4)

\mathbb{F}
is closed.

Definition 6.58

(
[
117
]
, Definition 2.4)
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
be a small extriangulated category.
Let
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)
be an
\mathbb{E}
-extension.
Take a realization
A\xrightarrow{x}B\xrightarrow{y}C
of
\delta

and define
\widetilde{\delta}
to be the cokernel of
\mathcal{C}(?,y):\mathcal{C}(?,B)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(?,C)
in
\mathrm{Mod}\,\mathcal{C}
.
The functor
\widetilde{\delta}
is called the defect of
\delta
,
or the defect of an
\mathfrak{s}
-conflation
A\xrightarrow{x}B\xrightarrow{y}C
.
We denote by
\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{E}
the subcategory of
\mathrm{Mod}\,\mathcal{C}
consisting of
\mathcal{C}
-modules which are isomorphic to defects of some
\mathfrak{s}
-conflations.

Remark 6.59
.

Suppose we have an
\mathbb{E}
-extension
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)
and a morphism
c:C^{\prime}\rightarrow C
in
\mathcal{C}
.
By Lemma
A.6
, we have the following diagram

(6.59.1)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\oplus C^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c^{*}(\delta)=\theta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}1\\
0\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}g\\
v\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}y{,}\,-c{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u_{*}(\delta)=\mu}

A diagram chasing shows that there is a short exact sequence of defects

0\rightarrow\widetilde{\theta}\rightarrow\widetilde{\delta}\rightarrow\widetilde{\mu}\rightarrow 0

Theorem 6.60

(
[
33
]
, Theorem B)
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
be a small extriangulated category.
Then the map
\mathbb{F}\mapsto\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{F}
defines an isomorphism between the following posets, where the poset structures are given by inclusion.

(1)

The poset of closed subbifunctors of
\mathbb{E}
.

(2)

The poset of Serre subcategories of
\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{E}
.

Theorem 6.61
.

Let
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
be an exact dg category and
(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
the associated algebraic extriangulated category. The following posets, where the poset structures are given by inclusion, are isomorphic.

(1)

The poset of exact substructures of
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
.

(2)

The poset of closed subbifunctors of
\mathbb{E}
.

(3)

The poset of Serre subcategories of
\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{E}
.

Proof.

The isomorphism between items (2) and (3) is given by Theorem
6.60
.
We show the isomorphism between items (1) and (2).

Let
\mathbb{F}\subset\mathbb{E}
be a closed subbifunctor.
Let
\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{F}}\subseteq\mathcal{S}
be the class of conflations
X

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

whose equivalence class
[X]\in\mathbb{F}(C,A)\subseteq\mathbb{E}(C,A)
.
We first show that the class
\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{F}}
is closed under isomorphisms.
Let
X
be a conflation in
\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{F}}
and
\alpha:X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
an isomorphism in
\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
.
Then
X^{\prime}
is a conflation in
\mathcal{S}
.
By Lemma
5.9
, the isomorphism
\alpha
factorises as the composition of isomorphisms
X\rightarrow\widetilde{X}
and
\widetilde{X}\rightarrow X^{\prime}
and
[\widetilde{X}]=\overline{a}_{*}[X]=\overline{c}^{*}[X^{\prime}]
for some isomorphisms
\overline{a}
and
\overline{c}
in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.
So we have
[X^{\prime}]=(\overline{c}^{-1})^{*}\overline{a}_{*}[X]
and
X^{\prime}
also belongs to
\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{F}}
.

Since
\mathbb{F}
is an additive subbifunctor, Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}0
for
\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{F}}
is satisfied.

By Proposition
6.57
,
\mathfrak{s}|_{\mathbb{F}}
-deflations are closed under compositions.
Since we have showed
\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{F}}
is closed under isomorphisms, deflations are closed under compositions.
Thus Axiom
{\mathrm{Ex}1}
is satisfied.

Suppose we are in the context of Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}2
.
So we have a cospan

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

where
p:B\rightarrow C
is a deflation in
\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{F}}
.
Put
[X^{\prime}]=\overline{c}^{*}[X]
.
The morphism from
X^{\prime}
to
X
then restricts to the homotopy pullback of the above cospan.
Since
X^{\prime}
also belongs to
\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{F}}
, the homotopy pullback of
p
is also a deflation in
\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{F}}
.
Thus Axiom
{\mathrm{Ex}2}
is satisfied.
Dually, one shows Axiom
{\mathrm{Ex}2^{op}}
for
\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{F}}
.

Let
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{S}
be an exact dg substructure.
Let
(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{F}_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}},\mathfrak{s}^{\prime})
be the corresponding extriangulated structure.
The inclusion
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{S}
induces a natural transformation of additive bifunctors
\mathbb{F}_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}\rightarrow\mathbb{E}
which is compatible with the realizations
\mathfrak{s}
and
\mathfrak{s}^{\prime}
.
By Proposition
5.20
, the natural transformation
\mathbb{F}_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}\rightarrow\mathbb{E}
is an inclusion and thus defines a closed subbifunctor of
\mathbb{E}
by Proposition
6.57
.

It is direct to check that the maps
\mathbb{F}\mapsto\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{F}}
and
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\mapsto\mathbb{F}_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}
are inverse to each other.
∎

Corollary 6.62
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
be an algebraic extriangulated category.
Let
\mathbb{F}\subset\mathbb{E}
be a closed subbifunctor.
Then the extriangulated category
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{F},\mathfrak{s}|_{\mathbb{F}})
is still an algebraic extriangulated category.

Remark 6.63
.

We have an injection

\{\text{Exact dg structures on $\mathcal{A}$}\}\to\{\text{Extriangulated structures on $H^{0}(\mathcal{A})$}\}.

This map is in general not a surjection.
For example, when
\mathcal{A}
is concentrated in degree
0
,
then the exact dg structures on
\mathcal{A}
are exactly the Quillen exact structures on
\mathcal{A}
.
But
\mathcal{A}
may have nontrivial extriangulated structures, e.g. if
\mathcal{A}
is an algebraic triangulated category.

Definition 6.64

(
[
70
]
, Definitions 2.1, 2.6)
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
be an extriangulated category.
A non-split (i.e. non zero)
\mathbb{E}
-extension
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)
is said to be almost split if it satisfies the following conditions.

(AS1)

a_{*}(\delta)=0
for any non-section
a\in\mathcal{C}(A,A^{\prime})
.

(AS2)

c^{*}(\delta)=0
for any non-retraction
c\in\mathcal{C}(C^{\prime},C)
.
A sequence of morphisms
A\xrightarrow{x}B\xrightarrow{y}C
in
\mathcal{C}
is called an almost split sequence if it realizes some almost split extension
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)
.

A non-zero object
A\in\mathcal{C}
is
endo-local
if
\mathrm{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(A)
is local.
For any almost split
\mathbb{E}
-extension
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)
, we have that
A
and
C
are both endo-local, cf.
[
70
, Proposition 2.5]
.
Almost split extensions are unique in the following sense.

Proposition 6.65

(
[
70
]
, Proposition 2.11)
.

Let
A\in\mathcal{C}
be any object. If there are non-split extensions
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)
and
\delta^{\prime}\in\mathbb{E}(C^{\prime},A)
satisfying (AS2), then there is an isomorphism
c\in\mathcal{C}(C^{\prime},C)
such that
c^{*}(\delta)=\delta^{\prime}
.
Dually, if non-split extensions
\rho\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)
and
\rho^{\prime}\in\mathbb{E}(C,A^{\prime})
satisfy (AS1) for some
A
,
A^{\prime}
,
C\in\mathcal{C}
, then there is an isomorphism
a\in\mathcal{C}(A,A^{\prime})
such that
a_{*}(\rho)=\rho^{\prime}
.

Definition 6.66

(
[
70
]
, Definition 3.1)
.

We say that
\mathcal{C}
has right almost split extensions if for any endo-local non-projective object
A\in\mathcal{C}
, there exists an almost split extension
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(A,B)
for some
B\in\mathcal{C}
.
Dually, we say that
\mathcal{C}
has left almost split extensions if if for any endo-local non-injective object
B\in\mathcal{C}
, there exists an almost split extension
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(A,B)
for some
A\in\mathcal{C}
.
We say that
\mathcal{C}
has almost split extensions if it has right and left almost split extensions.

Let
k
be a field. Suppose
\mathcal{C}
is Krull–Schmidt.
Let
A\xrightarrow{x}B\xrightarrow{y}C
be a conflation realizing an almost split
\mathbb{E}
-extension
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)
.
Then its defect
\widetilde{\delta}
, i.e. the cokernel of
\mathcal{C}(?,y):\mathcal{C}(?,B)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(?,C)
in
\mathrm{Mod}\,\mathcal{C}
, is the simple module at
C
.
So we have
\widetilde{\delta}(C)=\mathrm{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(C)/\mathrm{rad}\mathrm{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(C)
and
\widetilde{\delta}(D)=0
for any indecomposable
D\in\mathcal{C}
which is not isomorphic to
C
.
Conversely, if a simple module
S_{C}
lies in
\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{E}
for an indecomposable object
C\in\mathcal{C}
, then by definition there is a defect
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)
such that
\widetilde{\delta}
is isomorphic to
S_{C}
.
It is clear that
\delta
satisfies (AS2).
By
[
70
, Lemma 2.14]
, we may assume
A
is indecomposable and then
\delta
is an almost split extension, whose defect is necessarily isomorphic to
S_{C}
.
The following corollary generalizes an analogous result in exact categories, cf.
[
36
, Theorem 2.26]
.

Corollary 6.67
.

Let
k
be a field.
Let
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
be an exact dg category such that the following conditions hold

1)

The
k
-category
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is Krull–Schmidt.

2)

The extriangulated category
(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
is admissible, i.e. every object in
\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{E}
has finite length (cf.
[
32
]
).

Then the lattice of exact substructures of
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
is isomorphic to the Boolean lattice of the subsets of the set of isomorphism classes of indecomposable non-projective objects in
(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
.

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{M}
be a set of representatives for each isomorphism class of non-projective indecomposable objects in
\mathcal{C}=H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.
Let us show that for each
C\in\mathcal{M}
, there exists an almost split extension with ending term
C
.
Indeed, since
C
is non-projective and
\mathcal{C}
is Krull–Schmidt, there exists a non-zero extension
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)
with
A
indecomposable.
By item 2), each defect has finite length. Let us choose
\delta
such that the length of
\widetilde{\delta}
is minimal among such extensions.
Let
c:C^{\prime}\rightarrow C
be a non-retraction morphism in
\mathcal{C}
.
Let us consider the diagram
6.59.1
in Remark
6.59
.
So there is a surjection from
\widetilde{\delta}
to
\widetilde{\mu}
where
\mu=u_{*}(\delta)
for some morphism
u:A\rightarrow E
.
Since
C
is indecomposable and
\delta
is non-zero and
c
is a non-retraction, the
\mathbb{E}
-extension
\mu
is nonzero.
We decompose
E
into indecomposables
E=\oplus_{i}E_{i}
.
Then for some
p_{i}:E\rightarrow E_{i}
, we have
\mu_{i}=(p_{i})_{*}(\mu)\neq 0
.
There is a surjection
\widetilde{\mu}\rightarrow\widetilde{\mu_{i}}
. So the composition
\widetilde{\delta}\twoheadrightarrow\widetilde{\mu}\twoheadrightarrow\widetilde{\mu_{i}}
is an isomorphism by the minimality of the length of
\widetilde{\delta}
.
Then
\widetilde{\delta}
is isomorphic to
\widetilde{\mu}
and hence
\widetilde{\theta}=0
.
It follows that
c^{*}(\theta)=0
and hence we have that
\widetilde{\delta}
is isomorphic to
S_{C}
and that
\delta
is an almost split extension.

We choose an almost split extension
\delta_{C}
for each
C\in\mathcal{M}
and put
\mathcal{R}=\{\delta_{C},C\in\mathcal{M}\}
.
Since any defect takes zero value at each projective object in
\mathcal{C}
,
the category
\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{E}
can be identified with a full subcategory of
\mathrm{Mod}\,(\mathrm{add}\mathcal{M})
.
The defects
\widetilde{\delta_{C}}
are the simple modules in
\mathrm{Mod}\,(\mathrm{add}\mathcal{M})
and hence we have that
\mathrm{def}\kern 1.00006pt\mathbb{E}
is the full subcategory of
\mathrm{Mod}\,(\mathrm{add}\mathcal{M})
consisting of objects which have finite lengths.
Recall that in a small finite length abelian category, the lattice of Serre subcategories is isomorphic to the lattice of the subsets of the set of isomorphism classes of simple objects.
Therefore, by Theorem
6.61
, the lattice of exact substructures of
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
is isomorphic to the Boolean lattice of the subsets of the set of isomorphism classes of indecomposable non-projective objects in
\mathcal{C}
.
∎

6.69.
DG relative cluster categories and Higgs categories

One of the motivations for our work is Yilin Wu’s construction of the Higgs category associated with a finite ice quiver with potential (see
[
144
]
[
142
]
for the Jacobi-finite case and
[
88
]
for the Jacobi-infinite case).

Let
(Q,F,W)
be a Jacobi-finite ice quiver with potential.
Denote by
\Gamma_{rel}
the relative Ginzburg dg algebra
\Gamma_{rel}(Q,F,W)
.
Let
e=\sum_{i\in F}e_{i}
be the idempotent associated with all frozen vertices.
Let
\mathrm{pvd}_{e}(\Gamma_{rel})
be the full subcategory of
\mathrm{pvd}(\Gamma_{rel})
of the dg
\Gamma_{rel}
-modules whose restriction to frozen vertices is acyclic.

Then the
relative cluster category

\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}(Q,F,W)
associated to
(Q,F,W)
is defined as the Verdier quotient of triangulated categories

\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel})/\mathrm{pvd}_{e}(\Gamma_{rel}).

The
relative fundamental domain

\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{\Gamma_{rel}}=\mathcal{F}^{rel}
associated to
(Q,F,W)
is defined as the following subcategory of
\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel})

\mathcal{F}^{rel}{\coloneqq}\{\mathrm{Cone}(X_{1}\xrightarrow{f}X_{0})|X_{i}\in\mathrm{add}(\Gamma_{rel})\text{ and }\mathrm{Hom}(f,I)\text{ is surjective},\forall I\in\mathcal{P}{\coloneqq}\mathrm{add}(e\Gamma_{rel})\}.

Let
\pi^{rel}:\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel})\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be the canonical quotient functor.

By
[
144
, Proposition 5.20]
, the restriction of the quotient functor
\pi^{rel}
to
\mathcal{F}^{rel}
is fully faithful.
In particular for
X,Y\in\mathcal{F}^{rel}
,
\pi^{rel}
induces an injection

\mathrm{Ext}^{1}_{\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel})}(X,Y)\rightarrow\mathrm{Ext}^{1}_{\mathcal{C}}(\pi^{rel}X,\pi^{rel}Y).

The
Higgs category
(
[
144
, Definition 5.22]
)
\mathcal{H}
is the image of
\mathcal{F}^{rel}
in
\mathcal{C}
under the quotient functor
\pi^{rel}
.
Indeed, we have the following

Lemma 6.70
.

Let
X,Y
be objects in
\mathcal{F}^{rel}
.
Then
\pi^{rel}
induces a canonical isomorphism

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel})}(X,\Sigma^{i}Y)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(\pi^{rel}X,\Sigma^{i}\pi^{rel}Y).

for any
i\leq 0
or for
Y\in\mathrm{add}\Gamma_{rel}
and
i\leq 1
.

Proof.

We first show the case when
Y=\Gamma_{rel}
and
i\leq 1
.

Recall the relative t-structure
(\mathcal{D}(\Gamma_{rel})^{rel}_{\leq 0},\mathcal{D}(\Gamma_{rel})^{rel}_{\geq 0})
on
\mathcal{D}(\Gamma_{rel})
which restricts to t-structures on
\mathrm{per}\Gamma_{rel}
and on
\mathrm{pvd}_{e}(\Gamma_{rel})
, cf.
[
144
, Propositions 4.10, 4.11]
.

We show the injectivity of the map.
Let
f:X\rightarrow\Sigma^{i}\Gamma_{rel}
be a map in
\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel})
which factors through an object
M
in
\mathrm{pvd}_{e}(\Gamma_{rel})
.

We want to show that
f
is indeed a zero map.
By definition
\Gamma_{rel}\in\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel})^{rel}_{\leq 0}
and hence
X\in\mathrm{add}\Gamma_{rel}*\mathrm{add}\Sigma\Gamma_{rel}\subset\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel})^{rel}_{\leq 0}
.
So we may suppose
M\in\mathrm{pvd}_{e}(\Gamma_{rel})^{rel}_{\leq 0}
.

By
[
144
, Corollary 3.13]
, we have

\mathrm{Hom}_{\Gamma_{rel}}(M,\Sigma^{i}\Gamma_{rel})\xrightarrow{\sim}D\mathrm{Hom}_{\Gamma_{rel}}(\Gamma_{rel},\Sigma^{3-i}M)=0

where
D=\mathrm{Hom}(-,k)
.

This shows the injectivity of the morphism.
We now show the surjectivity of the map. Consider a roof
b/s

Since
X\in\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel})^{rel}_{\leq 0}
, we may assume
\mathrm{Cone}(s)\in\mathrm{pvd}(\Gamma_{rel})^{rel}_{\leq 0}
.
Then since we have

\mathrm{Hom}_{\Gamma_{rel}}(\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(s),\Sigma^{i}\Gamma_{rel})\xrightarrow{{}_{\sim}}D\mathrm{Hom}_{\Gamma_{rel}}(\Gamma,\Sigma^{2-i}\mathrm{Cone}(s))=0,

the morphism
b
factors through
s
and this shows the surjectivity of the map.

For general
Y\in\mathcal{F}^{rel}
and
i\leq 0
, it follows from the above case by applying the homological functor
\mathrm{Hom}(X,-)
to the defining triangle for
Y
.
∎

Let
\mathrm{per}_{dg}(\Gamma_{rel})
(resp.
\mathrm{pvd}_{e}(\Gamma_{rel})_{dg}
) be the canonical dg enhancement of
\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel})
(resp.
\mathrm{pvd}_{e}(\Gamma_{rel})
).
Let
\mathcal{C}_{dg}
be the canonical dg enhancement of
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}(Q,F,W)
given by the dg quotient
\mathrm{per}_{dg}(\Gamma_{rel})/\mathrm{pvd}_{e}(\Gamma_{rel})_{dg}
.
Let
\mathcal{H}_{dg}
be the full dg subcategory of
\mathcal{C}_{dg}
consisting of objects in
\mathcal{H}
.
Let
\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{dg}
be the dg full subcategory of
\mathrm{per}_{dg}(\Gamma_{rel})
consisting of objects in
\mathcal{F}^{rel}
.

By
[
144
, Definition 5.12, Proposition 5.39]
, the dg category
\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{dg}
(resp.
\mathcal{H}_{dg}
) is extension-closed in
\mathrm{per}_{dg}(\Gamma_{rel})
(resp.
\mathcal{C}_{dg}
) and thus inherits a canonical exact dg structure.
By Lemma
6.70
, the canonical morphism from
\mathrm{per}_{dg}(\Gamma_{rel})
to
\mathcal{C}_{dg}
induces a quasi-equivalence

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{F}_{dg}^{rel}\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{H}_{dg}.

By
[
144
, Section 5.8]
, Theorem
6.1
and Proposition
6.24
, the canonical morphism

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{H}_{dg}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{dg}

characterises
\mathcal{C}_{dg}
as the bounded dg derived category of
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{H}_{dg}
.

Since
\Gamma_{rel}
is projective in the extriangulated category
\mathcal{F}^{rel}
, it follows that higher extensions
\mathbb{E}^{i}
of
\mathcal{F}^{rel}
vanish for
i\geq 2
.
Also we have
\mathrm{Ext}^{i}_{\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel})}(X,Y)=0
for
X,Y\in\mathcal{F}^{rel}
and
i\geq 2
.
Thus by Theorem
6.1
and Proposition
6.24
, the canonical morphism

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{dg}\rightarrow\mathrm{per}_{dg}(\Gamma_{rel})

characterises
\mathrm{per}_{dg}(\Gamma_{rel})
as the bounded dg derived category of
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{dg}
.

Claim: Via the canonical quasi-equivalence
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{dg}\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{H}_{dg}
, the exact dg structure on
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{dg}
is identified with the exact substructure on
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{H}_{dg}
left generated by
\mathrm{add}\Gamma_{rel}
.

Indeed, let
g:\pi^{rel}X\rightarrow\Sigma\pi^{rel}Y
be a morphism in
\mathcal{H}
.
Then by Lemma
6.70
,
g
is of the form
\pi^{rel}(f)
for some
f:X\rightarrow\Sigma Y
if and only if
g
factors though an object in
\mathrm{add}\Gamma_{rel}
.

Note that
\Gamma_{rel}
is cluster-tilting in
\mathcal{H}
, cf.
[
144
, Proposition 5.49]
. In general we have

Proposition 6.71
.

Let
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
be a connective exact dg category such that
(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{E})
is a Hom-finite, Krull–Schmidt extriangulated category with a basic cluster-tilting object
T
.
Let
\Gamma
be the dg endomorphism algebra of
T
in
\mathcal{A}
.
Let
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S}^{\prime})
be the connective exact dg category with exact substructure left generated by
\mathrm{add}T
.
Let
\mathcal{D}^{b}_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}(\mathcal{A}){\coloneqq}H^{0}(\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))
be the bounded derived category of
\mathcal{A}
with the exact structure
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
.
Then we have an equivalence of triangulated categories up to direct summand

\mathcal{D}^{b}_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{per}\Gamma.

Proof.

The dg functor

\mathrm{Hom}(T,-):\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{dg}(\Gamma)

induces a functor
D^{b}_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{per}\Gamma
.
Notice that
T
is projective in
(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{E}^{\prime})
with
\mathbb{E}^{\prime}
given by the exact structure
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
.

Since
T
is cluster-tilting, the extriangulated category
(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{E}^{\prime})
has enough projective objects
\mathrm{add}T
and is hereditary in the sense of
[
53
]
.
Also,
T
generates
\mathcal{D}^{b}_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}(\mathcal{A})
as a triangulated category.

Now the proposition follows from Theorem
6.1
and Proposition
6.24
, by a dévissage argument, cf.
[
79
, Lemma 4.2]
[
80
, 1.3]
.
∎

Remark 6.72
.

In Proposition
6.71
, if we take different basic cluster-tilting objects
T
in
(H^{0}(\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{E})
, then the exact substructures thus constructed are different because they have different projective objects.

We end this section by constructing a class of homotopy bicartesian squares in the dg category
\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{dg}
(or, by Remark
5.4
, equivalently in the dg category
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{dg}
) which are not necessarily homotopy bicartesian in the ambient pretriangulated dg category
\mathrm{per}_{dg}(\Gamma_{rel})
.
The idea is that we have a quasi-equivalence of dg categories

\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{dg}\simeq\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{H}_{dg}

which identifies the exact structure on the left hand side with a substructure of that on the right hand side.
So we only need to find conflations in
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{H}_{dg}
which are not in
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{dg}
.

Let
M
be an object in
\mathcal{F}^{rel}
of the form
\mathrm{Cone}(P\xrightarrow{f}Q)
.
Denote by
M^{*}
the dual
\mathrm{RHom}_{\Gamma_{rel}}(M,\Gamma_{rel})\in\mathrm{per}(\Gamma^{op}_{rel})
of
M
.
Then we have
H^{i}M^{*}=0
for
i\geq 2
and that
H^{1}M^{*}
is finite-dimensional.
Thus
N=\tau_{\leq 0}M^{*}
lies in
\mathrm{per}(\Gamma^{op}_{rel})
.

Claim 3: We have
H^{1}M^{*}\in\mathrm{pvd}_{e}(\Gamma^{op}_{rel})
and
M\xrightarrow{\sim}\tau_{\leq 0}N^{*}
.

Indeed, we apply the cohomological functor
\mathrm{Hom}(-,\Gamma_{rel})
to the triangle

P\xrightarrow{f}Q\rightarrow M\rightarrow\Sigma P

and we get the following exact sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}(\Sigma Q,\Sigma e\Gamma_{rel})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}(\Sigma P,\Sigma e\Gamma_{rel})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}(M,\Sigma e\Gamma_{rel})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Hom}(Q,\Sigma e\Gamma_{rel})=0.}

Thus we have
eH^{1}M^{*}=\mathrm{Hom}(M,\Sigma e\Gamma_{rel})=0
and
H^{1}M^{*}\in\mathrm{pvd}_{e}(\Gamma^{op}_{rel})
.
We have a canonical triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\Sigma^{-1}H^{1}M^{*})^{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M^{**}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N^{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma(\Sigma^{-1}H^{1}M^{*})^{*}.}

Then the claim follows by observing
(H^{1}M^{*})^{*}\in\mathcal{D}(\Gamma^{op}_{rel})_{\geq 3}
.
Indeed, we have

(H^{1}M^{*})^{*}\in\mathcal{D}(\Gamma^{op}_{rel})_{\geq 3}\cap\mathcal{D}(\Gamma^{op}_{rel})_{\leq 3}

which implies that
N^{*}\in\mathcal{D}(\Gamma_{rel}^{op})_{\leq 1}^{rel}
.

Claim 4: We have
\mathrm{Hom}(N,\Sigma^{i}\Gamma_{rel}e)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{i}(M)e=0
for
i\geq 1
and
\mathrm{Hom}(N,T)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Hom}(H^{1}M^{*},\Sigma^{2}T)
for
T\in\mathcal{D}(\Gamma^{op}_{rel})_{\leq-2}
.

Indeed, the claim follows by applying the cohomological functors
\mathrm{Hom}(-,\Sigma\Gamma_{rel}e)
and
\mathrm{Hom}(-,T)
to the triangle in
\mathrm{per}(\Gamma_{rel}^{op})

N=\tau_{\leq 0}M^{*}\rightarrow M^{*}\rightarrow\Sigma^{-1}H^{1}M^{*}\rightarrow\Sigma N.

We also have
\mathrm{Hom}(\Gamma_{rel}e,\Sigma^{\geq 1}N)=0
.

Summarising the above discussion, we have, by
[
144
, Definition 5.12]
, that
N\in\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{\Gamma^{op}_{rel}}
if and only if
\mathrm{Hom}(H^{1}M^{*},T)=0
for any
T\in\mathcal{D}(\Gamma^{op}_{rel})_{\leq-4}
.

, the following object in
\mathrm{rep}(\mathrm{Sq},\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{\Gamma^{op}_{rel}})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S^{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

Example 6.74
.

Let
(Q,F,W)
be the following ice quiver with potential

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 4}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}

where the ice part
F
is given by the blue vertices and blue arrows and the potential
W=\delta\gamma\beta\alpha
.
Then the underlying graded quiver of the corresponding relative Ginzburg algebra
\Gamma_{rel}(Q,F,W)
is given as follows

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 4}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t_{4}}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}

where
|\alpha^{*}|=-1
,
|\beta^{*}|=-1
and
|t_{4}|=-2
. The differential
d
is determined by the values on generators, which are given as follows

\displaystyle d(\alpha)=d(\beta)=d(\gamma)=d(\delta)=0,

\displaystyle d(\alpha^{*})=\delta\gamma\beta,d(\beta^{*})=\alpha\beta\gamma,d(t_{4})=\alpha\alpha^{*}-\beta^{*}\beta.

We have
e=e_{1}+e_{2}+e_{3}
. Denote by
P_{i}=e_{i}\Gamma_{rel}
.

Let
M=S_{1}
. Then we have the following triangle

P_{4}\rightarrow P_{1}\rightarrow S_{1}\rightarrow\Sigma P_{4}

such that

\mathrm{Hom}(P_{1},e\Gamma_{rel})\twoheadrightarrow\mathrm{Hom}(P_{4},e\Gamma_{rel}).

So
M\in\mathcal{F}^{rel}
.

Let
L
be the homotopy fiber of the map
P_{3}\rightarrow P_{4}
induced by
\alpha
.
Then we have a triangle

D\rightarrow L\rightarrow\Sigma^{-1}S_{4}\rightarrow\Sigma D

where
D
is the mapping cone of the map
P_{4}\rightarrow P_{1}
induced by
\beta
, which is isomorphic to
S_{1}
.

So
N=\tau_{\leq 0}M^{*}
is isomorphic to
S_{3}^{\prime}
.
Similarly we have the following triangle

P_{4}^{*}\rightarrow P_{3}^{*}\rightarrow S_{3}^{\prime}\rightarrow\Sigma P_{4}^{*}

which shows that
N\in\mathcal{F}^{rel}
.

We thus have the following diagram in
\mathcal{F}^{rel}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{4}}

which can be lifted to a homotopy bicartesian square in
\mathcal{F}^{rel}_{dg}
.

7.
The greatest exact structure on an additive dg category

We follow Rump’s idea
[
125
,
126
]
to show the existence of the greatest exact structure.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be an additive connective dg category. For simplicity, we may assume that
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is an additive category, cf. Remark
5.4
.

Definition 7.1
.

A left exact structure on
\mathcal{A}
is a class
\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{3t}(\mathcal{A})
stable under isomorphisms, consisting of homotopy short exact sequences (called conflations)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

where
i
is called an inflation and
p
is called a deflation, such that the following axioms are satisfied

Ex0

\mathrm{id}_{0}
is a deflation.

Ex1

Compositions of deflations are deflations.

Ex2

Given a deflation
p:B\rightarrow C
and any map
c:C^{\prime}\rightarrow C
in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
, the object

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

admits a homotopy pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

and
{p^{\prime}}
is also a deflation.

Ex3

If a morphism
g:B\rightarrow C
admits a homotopy kernel and for some
h:B^{\prime}\rightarrow B
the composition
gh:B^{\prime}\rightarrow C
is a deflation, then
g
is a deflation.

We call
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
or simply
\mathcal{A}
a left exact dg category.

Dually, a right exact structure on
\mathcal{A}
is given by a class of homotopy short exact sequences which satisfies the axioms
{\mathrm{Ex}0}
,
{\mathrm{Ex}1}^{op}
,
{\mathrm{Ex}2}^{op}
and
{\mathrm{Ex}3}^{op}
.

Remark 7.2
.

By the axioms
\mathrm{Ex}0
and
\mathrm{Ex}2
, the morphism
\mathrm{id}_{A}
is a deflation for each
A\in\mathcal{A}
.
By the axioms
\mathrm{Ex}0
and
\mathrm{Ex}3
, the morphism
A\rightarrow 0
is a deflation for each
A\in\mathcal{A}
.
By Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}3
, in the context of Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}2
, the 3-term h-complex

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\oplus C^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}b\\
p^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}-p{,}\;c{]}}

is a conflation.

Proposition 7.8
.

Suppose that the class

is stable under compositions and pullbacks. Assume that the morphism

for each

.

, the class

The class
P\mathcal{R}
satisfies the conditions of Proposition

. So we have

Corollary 7.9
.

The class
PQP\mathcal{R}
defines a left exact dg structure on
\mathcal{A}
, which is the unique maximal left exact dg structure on
\mathcal{A}
.

Combining Corollary
7.9
and Proposition
7.3
, we have

Theorem 7.10
.

For each additive dg category
\mathcal{A}
, the greatest exact dg structure exists.

The above theorem generalizes Rump’s result on the maximal exact structure on an additive category, cf.
[
125
]
and also
[
129
,
25
]
.

Let us turn to the special case when
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is
divisive
(=weakly idempotent complete), i.e. each split epimorphism has a kernel.
The following lemma shows that an additive dg category with homotopy kernels is divisive.

Lemma 7.11
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a dg category.
Let
\overline{p}:Y\rightarrow Z
be a split epimorphism in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
. If the object
p:Y\rightarrow Z
in
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A})
admits a homotopy kernel, then
\overline{p}
admits a kernel in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.

Proof.

Suppose we have a homotopy left exact sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

where
d(h)=-pf
.
For each object
A\in\mathcal{A}
, it induces a long exact sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ldots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{-1}\mathcal{A}(A,X)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{-1}\mathcal{A}(A,Y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{-1}\mathcal{A}(A,Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}\mathcal{A}(A,X)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}\mathcal{A}(A,Y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}\mathcal{A}(A,Z).}

Since
\overline{p}:Y\rightarrow Z
is an split epimorphism in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
, we have that the induced map
H^{-1}\mathcal{A}(A,Y)\rightarrow H^{-1}\mathcal{A}(A,Z)
is also surjective for each
A\in\mathcal{A}
.
Therefore by the above long exact sequence, we have that
\overline{f}
is a kernel of
\overline{p}
.
∎

Proposition 7.12
.

Let
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S})
be a left exact dg category such that
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is divisive.
Then there is a universal exact morphism in
\mathrm{Hqe}

F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})

to a pretriangulated dg category. Put
\mathcal{D}^{b}(\mathcal{A})=H^{0}(\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A}))
. If
\mathcal{A}
is connective, then this morphism satisfies the following properties

a)

It induces a quasi-fully faithful morphism from
\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\tau_{\leq 0}\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.
Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
be the essential image.

b)

The conflations of
\mathcal{A}
are inherited from
\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
.

c)

The inclusion
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{b}(\mathcal{A})
is stable under kernels of retracts.

d)

The inclusion
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
is stable under special pullbacks, i.e. if we are given a diagram of the following form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}

where the objects
X
,
Y
,
Z
and
W
are in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, and the second row is a conflation in
\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
, and the right square is a homotopy pullback square in
\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
, then
Y^{\prime}
is also an object in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

Sketch of proof.

By construction
\mathcal{D}^{b}_{dg}(\mathcal{A})
is the dg quotient
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})/\mathcal{N}_{dg}
where
\mathcal{N}_{dg}
is the full dg subcategory of
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
generated by the totalizations of conflations in
\mathcal{A}
.
The proof of a) is similar to the proof of Theorem
6.1
.
The assertion c) follows from the fact that
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is divisive.

We show the assertion b).
Consider a triangle in
\mathcal{D}^{b}(\mathcal{A})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma A}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\jmath}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u/t}

where
A
,
B
and
C
are objects in
\mathcal{A}
and we keep the same notation for the corresponding objects in
\mathcal{D}^{b}(\mathcal{A})
.
We proceed as in the proof of Theorem
6.1
.
We assume the roof
u/t
is of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma A}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}

where
N^{\prime}=\mathrm{Cone}(t)
is the totalization of a conflation
X^{\prime}
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\prime}}

Then the morphisms
C\rightarrow N^{\prime}
and
\Sigma^{-1}N^{\prime}\rightarrow\Sigma A
give rise to morphisms
\overline{c}:C\rightarrow C^{\prime}
and
\overline{a}:A^{\prime}\rightarrow A
in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.
Claim: the morphism
j:B\rightarrow C
admits a homotopy kernel which is homotopy short exact in
\mathcal{A}
.
Indeed, there is an isomorphism from the above triangle to the following triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(j)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cone}(j)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\jmath}}

which restricts to identities of
B
and
C
.
Let
s:A\rightarrow\Sigma^{-1}\mathrm{Cone}(j)
be the restricted morphism in
\mathcal{D}^{b}(\mathcal{A})
.
By the quasi-full faithfulness, this morphism lifts to a morphism in
\mathrm{pretr}(\mathcal{A})
and from this morphism we get a homotopy kernel of
j
which is homotopy short exact. Thus it is enough to show that
j
is a deflation.

Apply Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}2
and we get the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{\prime}}

where for simplicity we omit the homotopies and where
p
is a deflation.
Then we have the following diagram in
\mathcal{D}^{b}(\mathcal{A})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{p}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\jmath}}

By the above claim, the morphism
j:B\rightarrow C
admits a homotopy kernel in
\mathcal{A}
.
By the quasi-full faithfulness of
F
and Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}3
, we infer that
j
is a deflation.

It is direct to verify the assertion d), using Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}2
and the assertion b).
∎

Remark 7.13
.

The converse of Proposition
7.12
also holds. Let
\mathcal{D}
be a pretriangulated dg category. If
\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{D}
is a full dg subcategory which is closed under special pullback in the sense of Proposition
7.12
d) and which is stable under kernels of retracts, then
\mathcal{A}
with the conflations inherited from
\mathcal{D}
is a divisive left exact dg category.

Proposition 7.14
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be an additive dg category such that
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is divisive.
Let
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}
be a class which is stable under pullbacks.
Let
a:A\rightarrow B
and
b:B\rightarrow C
be morphisms in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.
If the composition
c=ba
belongs to
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}
, then
b
admits a homotopy kernel.

Proof.

The cospan of
c
along
b
admits a homotopy pullback
X

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}

We view
X
as a morphism from
e
to
c
in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
.
By Lemma
4.15
, the obvious morphism from
a
to
c
factors through the morphism
X
and hence the morphism
\overline{d}:D\rightarrow A
is a split epimorphism in
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
.
Since
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is divisive, it admits a kernel
K
and hence the object
d\in H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
is isomorphic to the canonical projection
K\oplus A\rightarrow A
and hence admits a homotopy kernel.
By Corollary
4.14
, the object
b
also admits a homotopy kernel.
∎

Theorem 7.15
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be an additive dg category such that
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is divisive.
Then
P\mathcal{R}
defines the greatest left exact structure on
\mathcal{A}
.

Proof.

It is clear that the class
P\mathcal{R}
is stable under compositions and pullbacks.
It remains to check Axiom
\mathrm{Ex}3
for
P\mathcal{R}
.

Let
a:A\rightarrow B
and
b:B\rightarrow C
be morphisms in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A})
such that the composition
c=ba
belongs to
P\mathcal{R}
. We claim that
b\in\mathcal{R}
.
Note that
b
admits a homotopy kernel
X
by Proposition
7.14

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

We have a morphism of 3-term h-complexes

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K\oplus A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}0{,}\;1{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}-h{,}\;0{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

where
u=[k,\;a]
,
v=\begin{bmatrix}1\\
0\end{bmatrix}
.
It is not hard to see that the right-hand square is homotopy cartesian.
So the morphism
u
belongs to
\mathcal{R}
.
By Corollary
4.14
and Proposition
4.9
, the right-hand square is homotopy bicartesian.
By Proposition
4.9
, the 3-term h-complex
X
is homotopy short exact.
Therefore
b
belongs to
\mathcal{R}
.

It remains to show that
b
belongs to
P\mathcal{R}
.
Let
f:F\rightarrow C
be any object in
H^{0}(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{A}))
.
Consider the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

By Corollary
4.11
, the homotopy pullback
c^{\prime}
of
c
along
f
is homotopic to the composition of some morphism
a^{\prime}
with the homotopy pullback
b^{\prime}
of
b
along
f
.
By the above, we have that
b^{\prime}
belongs to
\mathcal{R}
.
Thus
b
belongs to
P\mathcal{R}
.
∎

A morphism
b:B\rightarrow C
is a
semi-stable
homotopy cokernel if it belongs to
P\mathcal{R}
.
Dually, one defines the notion of
semi-stable
homotopy kernel.
A homotopy short exact sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

is
stable
if
f
is a semi-stable homotopy kernel and if
g
is a semi-stable homotopy cokernel.
If the additive dg category
\mathcal{A}
is such that
H^{0}(\mathcal{A})
is divisive, then by Theorem
7.15
, the homotopy short exact sequences in the greatest exact dg structure on
\mathcal{A}
are exactly the stable ones.

Remark 7.16
.

In
[
129
]
, the authors showed that in pre-abelian categories, i.e. categories with kernels and cokernels, the greatest exact structure consists of the class of all stable kernel-cokernel pairs.
In
[
25
]
, it was generalized to a more general class of additive categories, namely
the weakly idempotent complete ones.
In
[
126
]
, Rump gave a counterexample where not every stable short exact sequence in an additive category is in the greatest exact structure.

Example 7.17
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an abelian category having enough projectives and enough injectives.
A full subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
is resolving if it is stable under extensions, stable under kernels of epimorphisms, stable under taking direct summands and contains all the projectives, cf.
[
5
, Section 3]
. Dually one defines the notion of coresolving subcategory.
Let
\mathcal{E}
be a both resolving and coresolving subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
.
Then it is direct to check that a kernel in
\mathcal{E}
is a monomorphism in
\mathcal{C}
.
Therefore a kernel-cokernel pair in
\mathcal{E}
is a short exact sequence in
\mathcal{C}
.
Thus the inherited exact structure on
\mathcal{E}
from
\mathcal{C}
is the maximal exact structure on
\mathcal{E}
.
For example, the category
\mathrm{rep}_{\rm{l.f.}}(H)
of locally free modules over the generalized path algebra
H
is a both resolving and coresolving subcategory of the ambient abelian category
\mathrm{rep}(H)
, cf.
[
47
, Theorem 3.9]
, and thus the exact structure of
\mathrm{rep}_{\rm{l.f.}}(H)
inherited from
\mathrm{rep}(H)
is the maximal exact structure.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an arbitrary abelian category.
If
\mathcal{E}
is an extension-closed subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
which is stable under the passage to subobjects, then a kernel-cokernel pair in
\mathcal{E}
is necessarily a short exact sequence in
\mathcal{C}
. Thus the inherited exact structure on
\mathcal{E}
from
\mathcal{C}
is the maximal exact structure. For example, let
Q
be an acyclic quiver and
\mathcal{B}
an abelian category. Let
\mathrm{rep}(Q,\mathcal{B})
be the category of representations of
Q
in
\mathcal{B}
, i.e. the category of functors
Q\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
, where
Q
is considered as a category in the natural way. The monomorphism category, denoted by
\mathrm{mono}(Q,\mathcal{B})
, is a full subcategory of
\mathrm{rep}(Q,\mathcal{B})
which consists of all representations
(M_{i},M_{\alpha})_{i\in Q_{0},\alpha\in Q_{1}}
for which

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M_{i,in}:\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q_{1},t(\alpha)=i}M_{s(\alpha)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(M_{\alpha})_{\alpha}}

is a monomorphism for all vertices
i
, where
s(\alpha)
and
t(\alpha)
denote the source and target of the arrow
\alpha
.
It is clear that
\mathrm{mono}(Q,\mathcal{B})
is stable under extensions and the passage to subobjects in
\mathrm{rep}(Q,\mathcal{B})
, cf.
[
42
]
. Thus the exact structure of
\mathrm{mono}(Q,\mathcal{B})
inherited from
\mathrm{rep}(Q,\mathcal{B})
is the maximal exact structure.

Example 7.18
.

We recall the setting in Example
3.29
.
Let
A
be a finite-dimensional
k
-algebra.
Let
\mathcal{H}^{[-1,0]}(\mathrm{proj}\,A)
be the full subcategory of
\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{H}^{b}(\mathrm{proj}\,A)
consisting of two-term complexes
P^{-1}\to P^{0}
of finitely generated projective
A
-modules.
Let
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{C}^{b}_{dg}(\mathrm{proj}\,A)
be the canonical enhancement of

{\mathcal{H}}^{b}(\mathrm{proj}\,A)
and
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
its full dg subcategory on the objects
P^{-1}\to P^{0}
.
For an
A
-module
M
, we denote by
M^{*}
its
A
-dual.

Consider the algebra
A
given by a quiver with relations as follows

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 2}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 3\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}

There exists a homotopy exact squence
X
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
which is not homotopy short exact in
\mathcal{A}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

where
S_{2}
stands for the two-term complex
P_{1}\rightarrow P_{2}
.
We claim that this homotopy short exact sequence is stable.
As a consequence, the natural exact dg structure on
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is not the greatest one.

The key point is that the map
P_{3}\rightarrow P_{1}
is a right
\mathrm{add}(P_{2}\oplus P_{3})
-approximation of
P_{1}
and the map
P_{2}^{*}\rightarrow P_{1}^{*}
is a right
\mathrm{add}(P_{2}^{*}\oplus P_{3}^{*})
-approximation of
P_{1}^{*}
.

Let
T=(T^{-1}\rightarrow T^{0})
be an object in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
Consider a morphism
S_{2}\rightarrow P_{3}
in
Z^{0}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
.
Take the
A
-dual and we get

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces((T^{0})^{*}\rightarrow(T^{-1})^{*})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(P_{3}^{*}\rightarrow 0)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(P_{2}^{*}\rightarrow P_{1}^{*})\mathrlap{.}}

We have the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S_{3}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{2}^{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{1}^{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{2}^{*}\oplus(T^{-1})^{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{1}^{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(T^{-1})^{*}}

The image of the map
P_{2}^{*}\oplus(T^{-1})^{*}\rightarrow P_{1}^{*}
is either
P_{1}^{*}
so that the second row is split exact, or equals the image of the map
P_{2}^{*}\rightarrow P_{1}^{*}
so that
N=(T^{-1})^{*}
and the first column is split exact.

In the first case,
M
is a projective module and
P_{1}
is a direct summand of
T^{-1}
.
Assume that
T^{-1}
decomposes as
P_{1}\oplus K
.
Then the cospan
L

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T}

admits a homotopy pushout which is homotopy bicartesian.
So we have the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(P_{1}\oplus K\rightarrow T^{0})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(P_{2}\oplus K\rightarrow T^{0}\oplus P_{3})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P_{1}}

and it is direct to check the second row is homotopy left exact and hence homotopy exact.

In the second case, we have
M=S_{3}^{\prime}\oplus(T^{-1})^{*}
and hence the cospan
L
admits a homotopy pushout which is homotopy bicartesian.
Similarly as above, one checks that the pushout of
X
along
S_{2}\rightarrow T
is homotopy short exact.
Therefore, the morphism
S_{2}\rightarrow P_{3}
is a semi-stable homotopy kernel.
Similarly, the morphism
P_{3}\rightarrow P_{1}
is a semi-stable homotopy cokernel and hence the homotopy short exact sequence
X
is stable.

Appendix A
Extriangulated categories

In this appendix, we give two related constructions of closed subbifunctors, one of them generalizing the construction by Ogawa
[
116
, Proposition 2.1]
in the case of triangulated categories, and some diagram lemmas in extriangulated categories.

A.1.
Closed subbifunctors associated with extension-closed subcategories

Lemma A.2
.

Let
\mathcal{N}\subset\mathcal{C}
be an extension-closed subcategory.
Then we have the following closed subbifunctors of
\mathbb{E}

\mathbb{E}^{\mathcal{N}}:\mathcal{C}^{op}\times\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathrm{Ab},\;\;(C,A)\mapsto\sum_{f:N\rightarrow A,N\in\mathcal{N}}\mathrm{Im}(\mathbb{E}(C,N)\rightarrow\mathbb{E}(C,A))

and

\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}}:\mathcal{C}^{op}\times\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathrm{Ab},\;\;(C,A)\mapsto\sum_{f:C\rightarrow N,N\in\mathcal{N}}\mathrm{Im}(\mathbb{E}(N,A)\rightarrow\mathbb{E}(C,A))

such that
\mathbb{E}^{\mathcal{N}}|_{\mathbb{\mathcal{N}}}=\mathbb{E}|_{\mathbb{\mathcal{N}}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}}|_{\mathbb{\mathcal{N}}}
.
The closed subbifunctor
\mathbb{E}^{\mathcal{N}}
(resp.
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}}
) is called the subbifunctor left generated (resp. right generated) by
\mathcal{N}
.

Remark A.3
.

When
\mathcal{C}
is a Quillen exact category, this gives a way to construct Quillen exact substructures of
\mathcal{C}
.

Proof of Lemma
A.2
.

We show the case for
\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}}
.
The case for
\mathbb{E}^{\mathcal{N}}
follows by duality.
By
[
63
, Proposition 3.16]
, it is enough to show that
\mathfrak{s}|_{\mathbb{F}}
-deflations are closed under compositions.

Since
\mathcal{N}
is an additive subcategory, it is direct to check that an
\mathfrak{s}|_{\mathbb{F}}
-conflation
\delta\in\mathbb{F}(C,A)
is in the image of a map

\mathbb{E}(f,A):\mathbb{E}(N,A)\rightarrow\mathbb{E}(C,A)

for some object
N\in\mathcal{N}
and some map
f:C\rightarrow N
.

Suppose
f:X\rightarrow Y
and
g:Y\rightarrow Z
are two
\mathfrak{s}|_{\mathbb{F}}

Since
\mathcal{N}
is an extension-closed subcategory, we have
W\in\mathcal{N}
.
By Lemma
A.6
, there exists a morphism
[u,\;v]:Y^{\prime}\oplus Z\rightarrow W
such that the following sequence is an
\mathbb{E}
-triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N\oplus Y^{\prime}\oplus Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\;.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}-j\\
k^{\prime}\\
g\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}x{,}\;u{,}\;v{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\theta=y^{*}j_{*}d_{*}(\mu)}

We have the following isomorphism of sequences

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}\oplus Y\oplus Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N\oplus Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}\oplus Y\oplus Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N\oplus Y^{\prime}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}j^{\prime}\\
f\\
k^{\prime}f\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}f^{\prime}\;\;-j\;\;0\\
0\;\;-k^{\prime}\;\;1\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}j^{\prime}\\
f\\
0\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}f^{\prime}\;\;-j\;\;0\\
0\;\;0\;\;1\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{*}(\delta)\oplus 0}

where
s=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\
0&1&0\\
0&-k^{\prime}&1\end{bmatrix}
.
Thus the first row is also a conflation.

Now we apply the pasting law for homotopy cartesian squares (cf.
[
60
]
) to the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}\oplus Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N\oplus Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}j^{\prime}\\
k^{\prime}f\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}j\\
k^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces-v}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}f^{\prime}\;\;0\\
0\;\;1\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}-x{,}\;u{]}}

and by Lemma
A.8
, the morphism
[-x,\;u]
is an
\mathfrak{s}
-deflation.
We see that
gf
is an
\mathfrak{s}|_{\mathbb{F}}
-deflation.

∎

Proposition A.4
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
be an extriangulated category and
\mathcal{N}
an extension-closed subcategory.
Then we have the following closed subbifunctors of
\mathbb{E}

\mathbb{E}^{L}_{\mathcal{N}}:\mathcal{C}^{op}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathrm{Ab},\quad(C,A)\mapsto\{\delta\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)|\text{for any $N\in\mathcal{N}$ and $s:N\rightarrow C$, $s^{*}(\delta)\in\mathbb{E}^{\mathcal{N}}(N,A)$})\}

and

where

and

are the closed subbifunctors defined in Lemma

.

(nm)^{*}(\psi)\in\mathbb{E}^{\prime}(N^{\prime\prime},H)
and hence we have some morphism

and an

with
\widetilde{N}\in\mathcal{N}
and
g_{*}(\gamma)=(nm)^{*}(\psi)
.

So we have the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{N^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N^{\prime\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces lk}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces jp}

By the
\mathbb{E}
-triangle
A.4.1
, there exists a (non-unique) morphism
c:\widetilde{N^{\prime}}\rightarrow F
making the above diagram commute.
We apply axiom
(\mathrm{ET3})^{op}
to the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{N}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{N^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N^{\prime\prime}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s^{*}(\theta)}

and obtain a morphism of
\mathbb{E}
-triangles
(d,b):\gamma\rightarrow s^{*}(\theta)
.
This implies that
b^{*}(s^{*}(\theta))
is an
\mathbb{E}^{\prime}
-extension.
Since
b
is an
\mathbb{E}^{\prime}
-deflation, by
[
63
, Lemma 3.14]
we have
s^{*}(\theta)\in\mathbb{E}^{\prime}(N,A)
and hence
jp:B\rightarrow C
is an
\mathbb{F}
-deflation. This finishes the proof.
∎

A.5.
Some diagram lemmas

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
be an extriangulated category.
The following lemma is called (ET4-2) in
[
92
]
.

Lemma A.6

(
[
96
]
, Proposition 1.20)
.

Let

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}

be any
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle, let
f:A\rightarrow D
any morphism, and let

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}\delta}

be any
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle realizing
f_{*}\delta
.
Then there is a morphism
g
which gives a morphism of
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangles

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}\delta}

and moreover, the sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D\oplus B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}{-}f\\
x\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}d{,}\;g{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e^{*}\delta}

becomes an
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle.

Definition A.7

(
[
59
]
, Definition 3.1)
.

A commutative square

(A.7.1)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}

is a homotopy cartesian square if there exists an
\mathbb{E}
-triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\oplus C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}f\\
a\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}-b{,}\;u{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}

in
\mathcal{C}
. The
\mathbb{E}
-extension
\delta
is called a differential for the square.

Lemma A.8
.

Consider a homotopy cartesian square
A.7.1
with a differential
\delta
.
Then
f
is an
\mathfrak{s}
-deflation (resp.
\mathfrak{s}
-inflation) if and only if so is
u
.

Proof.

We only prove the deflation part of the statement.
Suppose that
f
is an
\mathfrak{s}
-deflation. Let

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\theta}

be an
\mathbb{E}
-triangle.
We apply
[
111
, Proposition 3.17]
to the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\oplus C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}f\\
a\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\theta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}-b{,}\;u{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}1{,}\;0{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}

and hence
u:C\rightarrow D
is also an
\mathfrak{s}
-deflation.

Conversely, suppose that
u
is an
\mathfrak{s}
-deflation.
Let

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu}

be an
\mathbb{E}
-triangle.
We have the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{*}(\mu)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu}

By the dual of Lemma
A.6
, there exists a morphism
a^{\prime}:A^{\prime}\rightarrow C
making the above diagram commute and such that the right hand side square is homotopy cartesian with a differential given by
g^{\prime}_{*}(\mu)
.
It follows that there exists an isomorphism
j:A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
such that
f^{\prime}j=f
and hence
f
is also an
\mathfrak{s}
-deflation.
∎

The following lemma is called (ET4-5) in
[
92
]
.

Lemma A.9

(
[
92
]
, Theorem 3.3)
.

Let

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta^{\prime}}

be
\mathbb{E}-
triangles and
g:B_{1}\rightarrow B_{2}
be a morphism such that
y_{2}g=y_{1}
.
Then there is a morphism
f:A_{1}\rightarrow A_{2}
which gives a morphism of
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangles

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta^{\prime}}

and moreover, the squence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}\oplus B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}{-}f\\
x_{1}\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}x_{2}{,}g{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}^{*}\delta}

becomes an
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle.

Using the above lemma, we prove a slightly stronger version of
[
111
, Proposition 3.17]
.

Lemma A.10
.

Suppose we are given
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangles

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
,
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
,
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta^{\prime}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta^{\prime\prime}}

satisfying
y_{2}\circ g=y_{1}
. Then there is an
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\theta}

which makes the following diagram commutative in
\mathcal{C}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}

and satisfy the following equalities:

(i)

f_{*}(\delta)=\delta^{\prime}
,

(ii)

(x_{1})_{*}(\theta)=\delta^{\prime\prime}
,

(iii)

h^{*}(\theta)+y_{2}^{*}(\delta)=0

and moreover, the sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}\oplus B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}{-}f\\
x_{1}\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}x_{2}{,}g{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}^{*}\delta}

becomes an
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle.

Proof.

By the previous lemma, there exists a morphism
f:A_{1}\rightarrow A_{2}
which gives a morphism of
\mathbb{E}-
triangles

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta^{\prime}}

and moreover, the sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}\oplus B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}{-}f\\
x_{1}\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}x_{2}{,}g{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}^{*}\delta}

becomes an
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle.

Thus we have the following diagram in
\mathcal{C}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}\oplus B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}0\\
1\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}{-}f\\
x_{1}\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}x_{2}{,}g{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}1{,}0{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces-f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}

By the dual of
[
111
, Proposition 3.17]
, there is an
\mathbb{E}-
triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces-f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces-\theta}

which makes the above diagram commutative in
\mathcal{C}
and
h^{*}(-\theta)=y_{2}^{*}\delta
and

\begin{bmatrix}-f\\
x_{1}\end{bmatrix}_{*}(-\theta)+\begin{bmatrix}0\\
1\end{bmatrix}_{*}(\delta^{\prime\prime})=0.

Applying the morphism
[0,1]_{*}
to the last equality, we see that
(x_{1})_{*}(\theta)=\delta^{\prime\prime}
.
∎

Similarly, we can prove a slightly stronger version of
[
111
, Proposition 3.15]
.

Lemma A.11
.

Suppose we are given
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangles

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
,
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
.
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta^{\prime}}

Then there is a commutative diagram in
\mathcal{C}
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{1}}

which satisfies

\mathfrak{s}(y_{2}^{*}\delta)=[A_{1}\xrightarrow{m_{1}}M\xrightarrow{e_{1}}B_{2}],

\mathfrak{s}(y_{1}^{*}\delta^{\prime})=[A_{2}\xrightarrow{m_{2}}M\xrightarrow{e_{2}}B_{1}],

(m_{1})_{*}(\delta)+(m_{2})_{*}(\delta^{\prime})=0

and moreover, the sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\oplus B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}{e_{1}}\\
e_{2}\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}y_{1}{,}-y_{2}{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(m_{1})_{*}(\delta)}

is an
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle.

Proof.

We apply the dual of Lemma
A.6
to the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}^{*}(\delta)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta}

Then there exists a morphism
e_{2}:M\rightarrow B_{1}
such that the above diagram commutes in
\mathcal{C}
and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\oplus B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}{e_{2}}\\
e_{1}\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}y_{1}{,}-y_{2}{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(m_{1})_{*}(\delta)}

is an
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle.

We then apply
[
111
, Proposition 3.17]
to the diagram

\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\theta}

such that the above diagram commutes (so we have
k=e_{2}
) and

(i)

(m_{2})_{*}(-\delta^{\prime})=(m_{1})_{*}(\delta)
,

(ii)

(x_{2})_{*}(\theta)=0
,

(iii)

[1,0]^{*}(\theta)+[y_{1},-y_{2}]^{*}(-\delta^{\prime})=0
.

Applying the morphism
\begin{bmatrix}1\\
0\end{bmatrix}^{*}
to the last equality, we get
\theta=y_{1}^{*}(\delta^{\prime})
.
∎

, Lemma 3.14]

]
.

Lemma A.12
.

Let

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
,
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta_{f}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E_{0}}
,
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta_{h}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
,
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta_{g}}

be
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangles satisfying
h=gf
. Then there are morphisms
d_{0}:D\rightarrow E_{0}
and
e_{0}:E_{0}\rightarrow F
such that the following

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E_{0}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta_{h}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta_{g}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}_{*}(\delta_{g})}

is a commutative diagram whose third column is an
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle, moreover,
d_{0}^{*}(\delta_{h})=\delta_{f}
and
f_{*}\delta_{h}=e_{0}^{*}(\delta_{g})
and the sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C\oplus D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E_{0}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}g\\
f{{}^{\prime}}\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}h_{0}{,}-d_{0}{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}(\delta_{h})}

is an
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle.

Proof.

By the dual of Lemma
A.6
, there exists a morphism
d_{0}:D\rightarrow E_{0}
such that

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C\oplus D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E_{0}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}g\\
f^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}h_{0}{,}-d_{0}{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\theta=f_{*}(\delta_{h})}

is an
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle and
(\mathrm{id}_{A},g,d_{0})
is a morphism of
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangles.
In particular,
d_{0}^{*}(\delta_{h})=\delta_{f}
.

Consider the following commutative diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C\oplus D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E_{0}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}0\\
-1\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{bmatrix}g\\
f^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}h_{0}{,}-d_{0}{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[}1{,}0{]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\theta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta_{g}}

By the dual of
[
111
, Proposition 3.17]
, there exists an
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{d_{0}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu}

which makes the above diagram commute (hence
d_{0}=\widetilde{d_{0}}
) and
\begin{bmatrix}0\\
-1\end{bmatrix}_{*}(\mu)+\begin{bmatrix}g\\
f^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}_{*}(\delta_{g})=0
,
e_{0}^{*}(\delta_{g})=\theta
.

Thus we have
\mu=f^{\prime}_{*}(\delta_{g})
and
e_{0}^{*}(\delta_{g})=f_{*}(\delta_{h})
.
∎

Remark A.13
.

A.12
is proved in

, Appendix B]

Definition A.14
.

A contravariant connected sequence of functors is a pair
(T,\epsilon)
where
T=(T^{i})_{i\geq 0}
is sequence of right
\mathcal{C}
-modules and
\epsilon
is a collection of morphisms
\epsilon_{\delta}^{i}:T^{i}(A)\rightarrow T^{i+1}(C)
for each
\mathbb{E}\mbox{-}
extension
\delta\in\mathbb{E}(C,A)
and
i\geq 0
which is natural with respect to morphisms of
\mathbb{E}
-extensions.

\delta
-functor if for any

Corollary A.17
.

Keep the notations as above.
Let
(R,\gamma,\mu)
be another
\delta
-functor which satisfies the above assumptions A.1–A.3.
Then there is a unique isomorphism of
\delta
-functors
\theta^{i}:R^{i}\rightarrow T^{i}

for
i\geq 0
such that
\theta^{0}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(?,-)}
.

Proof.

By Proposition
A.15
, we have that for each
i\geq 0
, the right
\mathcal{C}
-module
R^{i}(?,A)
is naturally isomorphic to
T^{i}(?,A)
in
\mathrm{Mod}\,\mathcal{C}
and the isomorphism is natural in the variable
A
and compatible with the connecting morphisms.
Hence we have an isomorphism of
\mathcal{C}
-
\mathcal{C}
-bimodules
\theta^{i}:R^{i}\rightarrow T^{i}
for each
i\geq 0
.
Similarly
R^{i}(C,-)
is naturally isomorphic to
T^{i}(C,-)
and this also gives an isomorphism of
\mathcal{C}
-
\mathcal{C}
-bimodules
\lambda^{i}:R^{i}\rightarrow T^{i}
for each
i\geq 0
.

We identify both
R^{1}
and
T^{1}
with
\mathbb{E}
and by assumption the natural isomorphisms
\theta^{1}
and
\lambda^{1}
are both given by the identity.
We only need to check that the natural isomorphisms
\theta^{i}
and
\lambda^{i}
coincide with each other for each
i\geq 2
and we proceed by induction on
i
.

Let
C
and
F
be objects in
\mathcal{C}
and
x\in R^{i}(C,F)
for
i\geq 1
.
Since
R^{i}
and
R^{i-1}
are both effaceable, there exists

-triangles
